0.title: In the Beginning Was the Word
0.overview:
The Gospel of John is the most theological document ever written. Where Matthew presents Jesus as the King of Israel, Mark as the Servant-Son, and Luke as the Saviour of the world, John presents Jesus as the eternal Word of God who became flesh and dwelt among us — the visible form of the invisible God. John wrote last, having lived longest with the mystery of the incarnation, and every sentence carries the weight of that lifelong meditation.

John's purpose is stated with unusual precision at the end of the book: "these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name" (20:31). Two things — belief and life. Not mere assent to facts, but faith in a person; and not mere existence, but the eternal life that is knowing God and knowing Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3). The entire Gospel is an extended argument for this faith, structured around seven signs and seven "I AM" declarations.

The seven signs escalate in power and publicity: water to wine (private), healing the official's son (at a distance), healing the invalid (Sabbath controversy), feeding five thousand (crowd), walking on water (disciples alone), healing the blind man (Jerusalem), raising Lazarus (public, four days dead). Each sign is a window into who Jesus is; together they build the case that "no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him" (3:2) — and more than that: unless he is God. The eighth and final sign is the resurrection itself, which the prologue has been anticipating from its first verse.

The seven "I AM" statements are the theological spine of the Gospel. Each one appropriates the divine name revealed at the burning bush (Exod 3:14 — "I AM WHO I AM") and fills it with the content of Jesus' saving work: I am the bread of life; the light of the world; the door; the good shepherd; the resurrection and the life; the way, the truth, and the life; the true vine. These are not metaphors about a human teacher but divine self-disclosures of the Son of God. When Jesus says "Before Abraham was, I am" (8:58), his hearers pick up stones to throw at him — they know exactly what he is claiming.

Who wrote it? The Gospel names its author only as the disciple whom Jesus loved, who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things (21:24; cf. 19:35). He was one of the inner circle at the Last Supper, and he never names himself or his brother James, though he names almost every other disciple. The early church, from Irenaeus on, identified him as John the son of Zebedee, writing in old age at Ephesus, probably between AD 80 and 95. Some scholars think the beloved disciple was a Jerusalem follower other than one of the Twelve, or that the Gospel was finished by his community. But the internal evidence fits John, the son of Zebedee, best, and the church’s testimony is early and consistent.

Why is it so different from Matthew, Mark and Luke? John has no parables, few miracles and long discourses; much of his story is set in Judea and Jerusalem, across at least three Passovers; and the great “I am” sayings are his alone. He was not correcting the others but completing them. He chose his material deliberately, so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (20:30–31), and says plainly that he left out much more than he included (21:25). Where the others mostly give the Galilean ministry, John adds what happened in Jerusalem and what it meant.

Unique to John is the Farewell Discourse (chapters 13–17) — five chapters of intimate instruction given to the disciples on the night of his betrayal. Here Jesus gives his most extended teaching on the Holy Spirit ("another Helper"), on union with him ("abide in me"), on the world's hatred, on the coming joy, and on the prayer that will sustain the church to the end of the age. The High Priestly Prayer of chapter 17 — Jesus praying for his disciples and for all who will believe through their word — is the most sacred text in Scripture. John's Gospel ends not with a great commission on a mountain but with a question on a beach: "Do you love me?" Everything hangs on the answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Prologue: The Word Became Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before anything existed, the Word already was. He was with God, and he was God. Everything came into being through him, and in him was the life that is light for humanity, a light that darkness has never put out. God sent John to testify about the light so that all might believe, though John himself was not the light. The true light was coming into the world he had made, yet the world did not recognise him, and his own people did not welcome him. But to all who received him and trusted in his name, he gave the right to become God’s children, born not by human descent or decision but of God. The Word became human and lived among us, and we saw his glory, the glory of the Father’s one and only Son, full of grace and truth. John testified that the one coming after him outranked him, because he existed before him. From his abundance we have all received grace on top of grace. The law came through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God, but the only Son, himself God and closest to the Father, has made him known.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Word (Logos) is not an abstract philosophical principle but the personal Son of God through whom all things were made and in whom life and light reside. John's Christology is the highest in the New Testament: Jesus is fully God, co-eternal with the Father, the agent of creation, the source of life. The incarnation does not diminish his deity — 'the Word became flesh' while remaining the Word. Grace and truth come through Jesus Christ; the law came through Moses. The contrast is not abolition but fulfillment: the law pointed to the one in whom grace and truth are personally embodied.

Verse 2 is a safeguard rather than a repetition. Having said the Word was God, John at once restores the distinction — He was in the beginning with God — so that the identification cannot swallow the persons. The Prologue's architecture is carried by its verbs: the Word simply was, while all things were made, and in verse 14 the Word himself became flesh. He never became God; he became flesh.

The new birth of verse 13 is stated in three negatives before its single positive: not by descent, not by natural desire, not by the decision of any human head of a house — and therefore not by anything a person can inherit, produce or decide. Sonship is conferred, not achieved. The right of verse 12 is exousia, a granted legal standing, and the word used of believers in this Gospel is children (1:12; 11:52), while the Son is reserved for Jesus alone — a distinction that protects the uniqueness of Christ and enlarges rather than reduces the gift.

Grace and truth in verses 14 and 17 echo the name God proclaimed over Moses at Sinai — abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod. 34:6) — which is why verse 17 must not be read as setting Moses against Christ — a reading Jesus himself forbids at 5:46. Moses was shown the glory from behind and told to write it down; the Prologue claims that the same grace and truth have now arrived in person. And verse 18 closes the door natural religion keeps trying: God has never been seen as he is, and the only one who has never left his side has come out and told us — the telling being a life rather than a lecture.
verseByVerse.examples:
The Prologue is the key that opens the entire Gospel: whoever grasps who Jesus is before reading a single miracle will interpret everything correctly. 'The Word was God' (not 'a god') is one of the clearest affirmations of Christ's full deity in all of Scripture. And the Logos would have resonated with both Jewish (the creative Word of God) and Greek (the rational principle of the universe) audiences — John is announcing that the one both traditions were groping toward has arrived in person.

The darkness has not overcome it is the sentence a reader in a dark season needs: the light has never yet been extinguished, however far it has been reduced — and the church's own history is the evidence, since it has been down to a very few candles more than once and has never gone out. The verse does not promise that the darkness will feel defeated; it says the dark did not put the light out, and the shining verb is in the present tense while the failure to overcome is in the past.

The pastoral force of the three denials in verse 13 is usually missed. Because nothing whatever in the new birth was contributed by the one being born, there is nothing in it he can later fail to keep up — which is the answer to the Christian who cannot locate a moment of conversion and has concluded it never happened. No one remembers being born; the evidence of a birth is not a memory but a pulse. John gives the tests himself in his first letter, where believing the Son is the present-tense proof of a birth already completed in the past (1 Jn. 5:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the very beginning, the Word already existed. The Word was with God, in personal relationship with him, and the Word was himself God. He was with God from the beginning.

In the beginning. The first words of Genesis 1:1. John begins a new creation story, and places the Word before creation: when the beginning began, the Word already “was”.

The Word. Logos. For Jewish readers, God’s word creates (Psalm 33:6), reveals (Jeremiah 1:4) and saves (Isaiah 55:11), and Wisdom was with God at creation (Proverbs 8:22–31). For Greeks, the logos was the rational principle ordering the universe. John takes up both and says something neither said: the Word is a person, and he became flesh (v. 14).

With God, and was God. Distinct from the Father (“with God”) yet sharing his nature (“was God”). Here is the foundation of the doctrine of the Trinity: one God, more than one person.

What it does not mean. Not that the Word is a lesser divine being. The Jehovah’s Witnesses’ “the Word was a god” rests on the absence of the Greek article. But a predicate noun placed before the verb commonly lacks the article; the construction stresses nature: all that God is, the Word is. And John uses “God” without the article for the Father too (vv. 6, 18). Nor does “the Word was God” mean the Word is the Father (modalism): he was “with” God. Verdict: the historic Christian reading, as at Nicaea: the Son is true God from true God, of one being with the Father.

For worship. John 20:28 closes the Gospel with Thomas’s words, “My Lord and my God!” This verse opens it. Worship Jesus as God.
verseByVerse.note: “In the beginning” deliberately echoes the first words of Genesis. “The Word” (Greek logos) was a term both Jews and Greeks understood: God’s self-expression, through which he created and revealed himself.

parallels.desc: in the beginning God created
by the word of the LORD the heavens were made
his name is the Word of God

verseByVerse.quote: "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through him God made everything; nothing at all came into existence without him. In him was life, and that life was the light of humanity.

Agent of creation. The Word is not part of creation but its maker (Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2). Everything that exists owes its existence to Christ.

Life and light. Two of John’s great words. As in Genesis, life and light come from God’s word. In Christ is the life that gives life (5:26; 11:25) and the light by which people see God and themselves (8:12).

Textual note. Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation. Some early writers ended the sentence after “not anything was made” and read “what has come into being in him was life”. Verdict: the usual punctuation (ESV) gives the clearer sense, though the alternative is ancient.

On a Tuesday. Everything you handle today, wood, metal, data, food, was made through Christ. Work with it gratefully and well (Colossians 3:17).

parallels.desc: “Let there be light”
all things were created through him

verseByVerse.quote: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light keeps shining in the darkness, and the darkness has not overpowered it. There was a man sent by God, called John.

Shines. Present tense: the light still shines.

Overcome or understood? The Greek verb can mean “grasp” in either sense: seize and master, or comprehend (KJV “comprehended”). John may intend both: the darkness neither understood the light nor extinguished it, as the cross and resurrection will show. Verdict: “overcome” fits the conflict running through the Gospel best.

John. The Baptist, never called “the Baptist” in this Gospel. His role is witness. Sent from God, like the prophets, and like Jesus himself (the word “sent” is used of Jesus some forty times in John).

For worship. No darkness in the world or in you is too deep for Christ’s light. Praise him that it has not been put out.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “overcome” can also be rendered “understood.” The John of verse 6 is John the Baptist.

parallels.desc: John’s ministry begins

verseByVerse.quote: "He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John came as a witness, to testify about the light, so that through him everyone might believe. He himself was not the light; he came to testify about it.

Witness. A key word in John (some forty-seven times as verb and noun). The Gospel is a courtroom: John the Baptist, Jesus’ works, the Scriptures, the Father, the Spirit and the disciples all testify (5:31–39; 15:26–27).

Not the light. Perhaps aimed at followers of John who exalted him too highly (Acts 19:1–7). John gladly makes himself small (3:30).

On a Tuesday. Your task is to point to Christ, not to yourself. Witness means saying what you know of him, plainly.

parallels.desc: he was a burning and shining lamp

verseByVerse.quote: "The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The true light, who gives light to every human being, was coming into the world. He was in the world, the world had been made through him, and yet the world did not recognise him.

True. Real, ultimate, as opposed to partial lights (6:32; 15:1).

Gives light to everyone. Christ is the source of all human understanding, conscience and knowledge of God in creation (Romans 1:19–20; 2:14–15).

Where Christians differ: the light in every person. Quakers spoke of an “inner light” in all, and some inclusivists argue that people may be saved by responding to this general light without hearing of Christ. Reformed interpreters answer that this light leaves people without excuse but does not by itself save: the world “did not know him”, and salvation comes by receiving him and believing in his name (v. 12; 14:6; Acts 4:12). Verdict: the app’s exclusivist view, held humbly: Christ enlightens all, but saves those who trust him; hence the urgency of mission.

The world. In John, usually humanity organised against God (15:18–19), yet the object of God’s love (3:16).

The tragedy. The Maker visits what he made, and it does not know him.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came to what was his own, and his own people did not welcome him. But to all who did receive him, those who trust in his name, he gave the right to become God’s children.

His own. First “his own things” (his own home, Israel’s land and temple), then “his own people”. Like a man coming home to find the door locked.

Received and believed. Receiving Christ and believing in his name are the same act: welcoming him as he is. “His name” means his person and character.

The right. Exousia, authority or entitlement. Adoption is a legal status, not a feeling (Romans 8:15–17; Galatians 4:4–7).

What it does not mean. Not that all people are already God’s children in this sense. All are his creatures; those who receive Christ become his children.

For worship. “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God” (1 John 3:1).
verseByVerse.note: “His own” is Israel, God’s own people.

parallels.desc: sons of God through faith

verseByVerse.quote: "who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These children were born not of human descent, nor of physical desire, nor of a husband’s decision, but of God. And the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us. We have seen his glory, the glory of the Father’s only Son, full of grace and truth.

Born of God. Not by ancestry (“blood”), natural desire or human will. New birth is God’s work (3:3–8). Faith (v. 12) and new birth (v. 13) belong together, but the source is God. Where Christians differ: which comes first? Arminians hold that faith comes first and God then gives new birth; Reformed theology holds that God’s regenerating work enables faith, though they occur together (1 John 5:1; Ephesians 2:4–8). Verdict: regeneration is the root, faith the first fruit; the believer is never born again against his will, but by a will made new.

Textual note. A few early Latin writers (Tertullian, Irenaeus) read “who was born” (singular), applying the verse to Jesus’ virgin birth. No Greek manuscript has it. Verdict: the plural is original.

Became flesh. The Word did not stop being God, nor merely appear human: he took a full human nature, body and soul (Philippians 2:6–7; 1 John 4:2). Flesh means weakness and mortality. Against the Docetists, who said Christ only seemed human, and the Gnostics, who despised matter, John insists on the incarnation.

Dwelt. Eskēnōsen, tabernacled. God’s glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34); now it is seen in Jesus.

Only Son. Monogenēs, unique, one of a kind. The church has used it to teach the Son’s eternal generation from the Father.

Grace and truth. The words of God’s self-description to Moses, “steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6).

For worship. The God who filled the tabernacle took a body so that he could be seen, touched and nailed to a cross. Kneel before the incarnate Lord.
verseByVerse.note: “Dwelt” means literally “pitched his tent” — God’s presence among his people, as in the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: that I may dwell in their midst
abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness
born of the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "(John bore witness about him, and cried out, 'This was he of whom I said, "He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me."') For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John testified about him, crying out that this was the one he had spoken of: the one coming after him ranks above him, because he existed before him. From his fullness we have all received grace upon grace.

After, before, before. Jesus came after John in time and ministry, but ranks before him because he existed before him, though born six months later (Luke 1:36). A riddle that only pre-existence solves.

Fullness. All the riches of God dwell in Christ (Colossians 1:19; 2:9), and believers share in them.

Grace upon grace. Literally “grace instead of grace”: one wave of grace replacing another, endlessly; or the grace of the new covenant following that of the old (v. 17).

On a Tuesday. Whatever you need today, patience, courage, wisdom, there is more grace in Christ than you will use up.
verseByVerse.note: John was born about six months before Jesus; “he was before me” points to Jesus’ existence before his birth.

parallels.desc: in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell

verseByVerse.quote: "For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; the only Son, himself God, who is closest to the Father’s heart, has made him known.

Moses and Christ. Not law bad and grace good: the law was itself a gift. But Moses was a servant through whom it was given; grace and truth came in person in Jesus (Hebrews 3:5–6).

No one has seen God. Moses asked to see God’s glory and saw only his back (Exodus 33:18–23). Now God is seen in the Son (14:9).

Textual note. The earliest manuscripts (two papyri from about AD 200, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) read “the only God” (monogenēs theos); later ones “the only Son” (KJV “the only begotten Son”). Verdict: “only God” is original and the harder reading; the ESV renders it “God the only Son”. The verse ends the prologue as it began: the Word is God (v. 1).

At the Father’s side. Literally “in the bosom”, the place of intimacy, as the beloved disciple at the supper (13:23).

Made him known. Exēgēsato, from which “exegesis”: Jesus is God’s interpretation of himself.

For worship. Do you want to know what God is like? Look at Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the readings “the only One, who is God” and, in some manuscripts, “the only Son.” “At the Father’s side” is literally “in the bosom of the Father” — the place of closest intimacy.

parallels.desc: no one may see me and live
whoever has seen me has seen the Father

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–51 — The Testimony of John and the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When priests and Levites from Jerusalem ask John who he is, he states plainly that he is not the Messiah, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet, but the voice in the wilderness Isaiah spoke of, calling people to make the Lord’s road straight. Asked why he baptises, he says he baptises with water, but among them stands one they do not know, whose sandal he is unfit to untie. Next day, seeing Jesus, John calls him the Lamb of God who takes away the world’s sin, the one who ranks above him because he was before him. John testifies that he saw the Spirit come down like a dove and remain on Jesus, the sign God had given him of the one who baptises with the Spirit; so he declares that this is the Son of God. The following day two of John’s disciples hear him call Jesus the Lamb of God and follow Jesus. He asks what they are looking for; they ask where he is staying, and he invites them to come and see. One of them, Andrew, brings his brother Simon, telling him they have found the Messiah, and Jesus names Simon Cephas, Peter. Next day Jesus calls Philip, who tells Nathanael they have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael scoffs at Nazareth, but comes, and Jesus greets him as a true Israelite without deceit and says he saw him under the fig tree before Philip called him. Nathanael confesses him Son of God and King of Israel. Jesus promises he will see greater things: heaven opened and God’s angels going up and down on the Son of Man.
verseByVerse.theology:
The gathering of the first disciples in John 1 is a theology of testimony: John testifies to Jesus; Andrew testifies to Simon; Philip testifies to Nathanael. The gospel spreads through personal witness. Each person who encounters Jesus becomes a testimony to others. The titles accumulate — Lamb of God, Son of God, Rabbi, Messiah, King of Israel, Son of Man — each one true, each one partial, each one pointing toward the one who exceeds all titles. Faith begins with testimony, but it must end with personal encounter: 'Come and see.'

Two guards belong to this section. The first concerns the phrase the Jews, which appears here for the first time and some seventy times in the Gospel: in John it functions as shorthand for the Jerusalem religious authorities, not for a people. The author is a Jew, every disciple is a Jew, and Jesus says in this same book that salvation is from the Jews (4:22). What is recorded is an argument inside a family about the family's own hope, and reading it as one people's verdict on another inverts it — a misreading Christians have made at terrible cost.

The second concerns the Lamb. Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (v. 29) should not be assigned lazily to one background. John's own frame is Passover: he alone dates the condemnation to the hour the lambs were killed (19:14) and applies the Passover regulation about unbroken bones to the body on the cross (19:36). But the words spoken here — takes away the sin — echo Isaiah, since of all the candidate lambs only the servant of Isaiah 53 bears sin. Genesis 22 supplies the unanswered question (where is the lamb?), and the daily sacrifice explains why there had to be a last one. The verb is a present participle and the noun is singular: not a list of offences but the whole condition, taken up in order to be carried away.

The gathering of the disciples also settles the relation between this Gospel and the others. The call by the Sea of Galilee in Matthew and Mark is not an alternative version of this meeting but a later and decisive summons; here men are introduced to Jesus and begin to believe, and later they leave the nets for good. Faith by stages is the normal pattern, not a defective one — which is also the burden of vv. 50-51, where a man who has believed for minutes is told he will see greater things, and the greater things turn out to include a cross.
verseByVerse.examples:
'Behold, the Lamb of God' is the most comprehensive atonement statement in the New Testament: the lamb of Passover (Exod. 12), the lamb of the daily sacrifice (Exod. 29:38-42), the suffering servant who is led like a lamb to slaughter (Isa. 53:7), and the apocalyptic Lamb who alone is worthy (Rev. 5) — all in one person. And Andrew's first act after meeting Jesus is to find his brother: the natural overflow of genuine encounter with Christ is the desire for others to share it.

The pastoral centre of this section is that nobody in it recruits by argument. Andrew fetches his own brother — the hardest possible person, and the one least impressed by him — with a five-word sentence containing no case at all. Philip's testimony is theologically magnificent and incomplete twice over (Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph — nothing of Bethlehem, nothing of the virgin birth), and John lets both gaps stand on the page because Nathanael came anyway. Nobody is waiting for a witness to be finished before he is useful.

Two cautions worth carrying out of it. Andrew won his brother the same day, and that is the exception rather than the pattern; Jesus' own brothers did not believe during his lifetime (7:5). Anyone who has prayed for a relative for decades is not being rebuked by this chapter. And I saw you under the fig tree should be handled on both sides: it is the comfort of the believer whose faithfulness nobody is counting, and it is exposure for the reader who would rather his private life stayed private — with the point being that the one who has complete access to it is the one who came to take away the sin of the world, and he mentions the tree and says nothing else.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, "Who are you?" He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, "I am not the Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is John’s testimony when the Jewish authorities in Jerusalem send priests and Levites to ask who he is. He states it openly, without evasion: he is not the Messiah.

The Jews. In John often the religious leadership in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole: Jesus, John and the disciples were all Jews (4:22). The phrase must never be used to fuel hatred of Jewish people.

An official inquiry. Priests and Levites, temple officials, investigate a popular preacher baptising crowds.

Confessed, did not deny, confessed. Triple emphasis. John refuses a title many would have given him (Luke 3:15).

On a Tuesday. When people praise you too highly, say plainly what you are not.
verseByVerse.note: In John’s Gospel “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities in Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: whether he might be the Christ

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, "What then? Are you Elijah?" He said, "I am not." "Are you the Prophet?" And he answered, "No."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask whether he is Elijah, then. He says he is not. Are you the Prophet? No.

Elijah. Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah’s return before the day of the LORD. Jesus said John was the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; 17:12), meaning John fulfilled Elijah’s role (Luke 1:17). John denies being Elijah literally returned, as many expected.

The Prophet. The prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15–18), whom some expected as a separate figure (6:14; 7:40). The New Testament identifies him with Jesus (Acts 3:22).

Shorter and shorter. “I am not.” “No.” John has no interest in himself.
verseByVerse.note: Many expected Elijah to return before the Messiah; “the Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised.

parallels.desc: I will send you Elijah
a prophet like me
he is Elijah who is to come

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?" He said, "I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of the Lord,' as the prophet Isaiah said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they press him: who is he? They need an answer for those who sent them. What does he say about himself? He replies that he is the voice of one calling out in the wilderness to make straight the Lord’s road, as the prophet Isaiah said.

Isaiah 40:3. The opening of Isaiah’s message of comfort: the LORD himself is coming to rescue his people, and a herald prepares his way. John applies it to Jesus: the Lord whose road he prepares is Jesus.

A voice. Not a title but a function. A voice is heard and then fades; the message matters.

For worship. The coming of Jesus is the coming of the LORD. Make room for him.

parallels.desc: the voice in the wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: (Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
These men had been sent by the Pharisees.

The Pharisees. Priests and Levites were usually Sadducees, but the Pharisees were concerned with purity rites like baptism. This aside prepares for the conflict to come.

verseByVerse.quote: They asked him, "Then why are you baptizing, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?" John answered them, "I baptize with water, but among you stands one you do not know."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask him why he is baptising, then, if he is not the Messiah, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet. John answers that he baptises with water, but among them stands someone they do not know.

Why baptise? Jews baptised Gentile converts. For John to baptise Jews implied they too needed to repent and be made ready, as if outsiders. That needed authority.

One you do not know. Jesus is already among them, unrecognised (v. 10). John’s water points to him.

On a Tuesday. Christ may be nearer than people think. Help them notice him.

verseByVerse.quote: "even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie." These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the one coming after John, whose sandal strap John is not worthy to untie. This happened at Bethany on the far side of the Jordan, where John was baptising.

A slave’s job. Rabbinic tradition said a disciple should do for his teacher everything a slave does, except untie his sandals. John says he is unworthy even of that.

Bethany across the Jordan. Not the village near Jerusalem (11:1). Its exact site is uncertain; a site east of the Jordan near Jericho is widely accepted. Textual note. Some manuscripts read “Bethabara” (KJV), from Origen, who could not find a Bethany there. Verdict: Bethany is original.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job. This Bethany lay east of the Jordan — not the Bethany near Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: where John had been baptizing at first

verseByVerse.quote: The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! This is he of whom I said, 'After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day John sees Jesus coming towards him and says, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” This is the one of whom he said that a man coming after him ranks ahead of him, because he existed before him.

The Lamb of God. A rich image. The Passover lamb, whose blood saved Israel (Exodus 12; 1 Corinthians 5:7; and in John, Jesus dies as the Passover lambs are killed, 19:14, 36). The daily lambs of the temple sacrifices (Exodus 29:38–42). The Servant led like a lamb to the slaughter, bearing the sins of many (Isaiah 53:7, 12). The lamb God would provide (Genesis 22:8).

Takes away. Carries off, removes: the work of a sacrifice.

The sin of the world. Singular: the world’s sin as a whole. Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Arminians and many others read “the world” as every individual, and see Christ’s death as making salvation possible for all. Reformed theology reads “the world” in John as humanity without distinction, Gentiles as well as Jews (11:51–52; 1 John 2:2), and holds that Christ actually takes away the sin of all who will be saved (10:11, 15; 17:9). Verdict: the app’s view of definite atonement: Christ’s death is sufficient for all and offered freely to all, and it truly secures the salvation of his people from every nation. No one who comes will be turned away (6:37).

For worship. Look at the Lamb. Your sin, carried off.
verseByVerse.note: Lambs were offered daily in the temple and at Passover; Isaiah’s servant goes “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter.”

parallels.desc: the Passover lamb
God will provide the lamb

verseByVerse.quote: "I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John says he himself did not know him, but he came baptising with water for this purpose: that Jesus might be revealed to Israel.

Did not know him. John and Jesus were relatives (Luke 1:36) and may have met, but John did not know him as the Messiah until God showed him (v. 33). Knowing Christ is a matter of revelation, not acquaintance.

The purpose of baptism. John’s whole ministry existed to make Jesus known.

verseByVerse.quote: And John bore witness: "I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him. I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, 'He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
John testifies that he saw the Spirit come down from heaven like a dove and remain on him. He did not know him, but God, who sent him to baptise with water, had told him that the one on whom he saw the Spirit come down and remain is the one who baptises with the Holy Spirit.

The dove. John does not narrate Jesus’ baptism, but this is it (Mark 1:10). The dove may recall the Spirit hovering over the waters (Genesis 1:2) or Noah’s dove announcing a new world (Genesis 8:11).

Remained. John’s word “abide” (menō), used often of the Father, Son and believers (15:4–10). The Spirit came on prophets for a time; on Jesus he remains (Isaiah 11:2; 61:1).

Baptises with the Spirit. Jesus pours out the Spirit (20:22; Acts 2:33). The difference between John and Jesus: John uses water; Jesus gives God himself.

For worship. The Spirit who rested on Jesus is the Spirit he gives to his people. Thank him for that gift.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him

verseByVerse.quote: "And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John has seen it, and he testifies that this is the Son of God.

Seen and testified. Eyewitness testimony, the basis of the Gospel (19:35; 1 John 1:1–3).

Textual note. Some early manuscripts read “the Chosen One of God” (ESV margin), echoing Isaiah 42:1, where the Spirit rests on God’s chosen servant. It may be original, the “Son of God” being a later change to match the rest of the Gospel; or the reverse. Verdict: a genuinely close call; “Son of God” is better attested, and either way Jesus is God’s unique Servant-Son.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Chosen One of God.”

parallels.desc: my Chosen One

verseByVerse.quote: The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day John is standing there again with two of his disciples. He watches Jesus walking by and says, “Behold, the Lamb of God!”

Looked. An intent gaze.

Repeated. No longer a sermon to crowds, but a word to two disciples. John knows its effect: they will leave him.

On a Tuesday. The best mentoring sends people on to Christ, even if it means losing them.

verseByVerse.quote: The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the two disciples hear him say this, they follow Jesus.

Followed. Literally walking behind him, but the word becomes the word for discipleship (8:12; 12:26). Hearing about the Lamb leads to following him.

For worship. John’s joy was to decrease (3:29–30). Rejoice whenever someone moves from you to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, 'What are you seeking?' And they said to him, 'Rabbi' (which means Teacher), 'where are you staying?' He said to them, 'Come and you will see.' So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turns, sees them following, and asks what they are seeking. They call him Rabbi, Teacher, and ask where he is staying. He tells them to come and they will see. So they go, see where he is staying, and spend that day with him. It is about four in the afternoon.

What are you seeking? Jesus’ first words in John: a question about desire. He asks it still (18:4; 20:15).

Staying. The verb “abide” again (v. 32). They want more than an address: they want to be with him.

Come and you will see. An invitation, not an argument. Discipleship begins with spending time with Jesus.

The tenth hour. About 4 p.m. if counted from sunrise. The eyewitness remembers the hour that changed his life. One of the two is unnamed, perhaps the beloved disciple himself.

On a Tuesday. Invite friends to “come and see”: to read a Gospel with you, or come to church. Let Jesus speak for himself.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the tenth hour was about 4 p.m. — late enough that they stayed the rest of the day.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother. He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which means Christ).
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the two who heard John and followed Jesus is Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. The first thing he does is find his brother Simon and tell him they have found the Messiah, which means Christ.

Andrew. Always bringing someone to Jesus: his brother here, the boy with the loaves (6:8–9), the Greeks (12:22).

Messiah. The Hebrew Mashiach and the Greek Christos, “anointed one”: the promised king of David’s line. John translates for Greek readers. Only John uses the word “Messiah” in the New Testament (here and 4:25).

On a Tuesday. Start with your own family, gently and patiently. Andrew is not famous, but he brought Peter.
verseByVerse.note: “Messiah” (Hebrew) and “Christ” (Greek) both mean “anointed one” — the promised king.

parallels.desc: Andrew and Simon called by the lake

verseByVerse.quote: He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, "You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas" (which means Peter).
verseByVerse.commentary:
He brings him to Jesus. Jesus looks at him and says that he is Simon, son of John, but will be called Cephas, which means Peter.

Looked at him. The same intent gaze as John’s (v. 36). Jesus sees who Simon is and who he will become.

Rock. Kēphas in Aramaic, Petros in Greek. Simon is anything but rock-like in the Gospels, but Jesus names him for what grace will make him (21:15–19). Matthew 16:18 develops the name.

For worship. Jesus knows you completely and names you for what he will make of you. Thank him for his patience.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that Cephas (Aramaic) and Peter (Greek) both mean “rock.”

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, "Follow me." Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day Jesus decides to go to Galilee. He finds Philip and tells him to follow him. Philip, like Andrew and Peter, comes from the town of Bethsaida.

He found. Andrew found Peter; now Jesus finds Philip. Behind every human finding is the Lord who seeks (Luke 19:10).

Follow me. The simplest and most demanding call (21:19, 22).

Bethsaida. A fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, where Jewish and Gentile cultures met; Philip and Andrew have Greek names (12:21–22).
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: Philip found Nathanael and said to him, "We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip finds Nathanael and tells him they have found the one Moses wrote about in the Law and the prophets also wrote about: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.

The whole Old Testament. Moses and the Prophets point to Christ (5:39, 46; Luke 24:27).

Son of Joseph. As people knew him (6:42). John’s readers know from the prologue he is more; John does not deny the virgin birth but lets the irony stand.

Nathanael. Named only in John (also 21:2). Often identified with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip in the other Gospels’ lists.
verseByVerse.note: Nathanael is not named in the other Gospels; he is often identified with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip in their lists.

parallels.desc: Nathanael of Cana

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Philip said to him, "Come and see." Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, "Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathanael asks whether anything good can come from Nazareth. Philip simply says, “Come and see.” Jesus sees Nathanael coming and says of him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!”

Nazareth. A small village of perhaps a few hundred people, never mentioned in the Old Testament, Josephus or the Talmud. Nathanael came from nearby Cana (21:2): local rivalry may be in play.

Come and see. Philip does not argue. He repeats Jesus’ own invitation (v. 39).

No deceit. Perhaps contrasting Nathanael with Jacob, the deceiver (Genesis 27:35), who became Israel. A true Israelite is honest, even in his doubts.

On a Tuesday. Honest objections are not a barrier to Jesus. Invite the sceptic to come and see.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was an obscure village; it is never named in the Old Testament. “No deceit” may contrast Nathanael with Jacob, the deceiver who became Israel.

parallels.desc: your brother came deceitfully
in whose spirit there is no deceit

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "How do you know me?" Jesus answered him, "Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathanael asks how Jesus knows him. Jesus answers that before Philip called him, when he was under the fig tree, he saw him.

Under the fig tree. A place of shade, rest, and, in later Jewish tradition, of studying the law; also a picture of peace in the messianic age (Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10). Perhaps Nathanael had been praying or reading there, and Jesus knew it.

Supernatural knowledge. Jesus knows people’s hearts (2:24–25; 4:17–18).

For worship. “O LORD, you have searched me and known me!” (Psalm 139:1). The one who sees you is the one who saves you.
verseByVerse.note: Sitting under one’s own fig tree was a picture of peace and security.

parallels.desc: every man under his vine and under his fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael answered him, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!" Jesus answered him, "Because I said to you, 'I saw you under the fig tree,' do you believe? You will see greater things than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathanael replies, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” Jesus asks whether he believes because he said he saw him under the fig tree. He will see greater things than these.

Son of God, King of Israel. Probably both royal titles here (Psalm 2:6–7; 2 Samuel 7:14): Nathanael confesses Jesus as Messiah. John’s readers know “Son of God” means more (v. 18; 20:31).

Greater things. Signs, the cross, the resurrection. Faith that begins with a small sign is led on to greater sight.

On a Tuesday. Whatever first drew you to Christ, he has more to show you. Keep following.

parallels.desc: my King, my Son
the King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells them solemnly that they will see heaven opened, and the angels of God going up and coming down on the Son of Man.

Truly, truly. “Amen, amen”: doubled only in John (twenty-five times), a solemn affirmation of Jesus’ own authority.

You plural. The promise is to all the disciples.

Jacob’s ladder. Genesis 28:12: Jacob dreams of a stairway with angels going up and down, and calls the place Bethel, “house of God”. Jesus is the true Bethel, the meeting place of heaven and earth, the true temple (2:19–21). The true Israelite (v. 47) will see what Jacob saw, in Jesus.

Son of Man. Jesus’ favourite title for himself, from Daniel 7:13–14, the heavenly figure given everlasting dominion, and in John the one lifted up on the cross (3:14; 12:32–34).

For worship. Heaven is open in Jesus. Come to God through him; there is no other ladder.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “you” is plural: the promise is for all the disciples. “Truly, truly” is a solemn formula found only in John.

parallels.desc: Jacob’s ladder, angels ascending and descending

1.title: The Word Made Flesh
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.<sup>2</sup>He was in the beginning with God.<sup>3</sup>All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made.<sup>4</sup>In him was life, and the life was the light of men.<sup>5</sup>The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.<sup>6</sup>There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.<sup>7</sup>He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him.<sup>8</sup>He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light.<sup>9</sup>The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.<sup>10</sup>He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him.<sup>11</sup>He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him.<sup>12</sup>But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,<sup>13</sup>who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God.<sup>14</sup>And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.<sup>15</sup>(John bore witness about him, and cried out, “This was he of whom I said, ’He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me.’”)<sup>16</sup>For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.<sup>17</sup>For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.<sup>18</sup>No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known.<sup>19</sup>And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?”<sup>20</sup>He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, “I am not the Christ.”<sup>21</sup>And they asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” And he answered, “No.”<sup>22</sup>So they said to him, “Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”<sup>23</sup>He said, “I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, ’Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as the prophet Isaiah said.”<sup>24</sup>(Now they had water, but among you stands one you do not know,<sup>27</sup>even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie.”<sup>28</sup>These things took place in Bethany across the said to me, ’He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.’<sup>34</sup>And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of
