Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas” (which means Peter).<sup>43</sup>The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, “Follow me.”<sup>44</sup>Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.<sup>45</sup>Philip found Nathanael and said to him, “We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”<sup>46</sup>Nathanael said to him, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”<sup>47</sup>Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!”<sup>48</sup>Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”<sup>49</sup>Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”<sup>50</sup>Jesus answered him, “Because I said to you, ’I saw you under the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these.”<sup>51</sup>And he said to him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
1.overview:
John opens not at Bethlehem but before creation. The prologue (vv. 1–18) is the overture to the whole Gospel: the Word who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made, has become flesh and lived among us, and in him we have seen the glory of the Father’s only Son, full of grace and truth. The great themes of the book appear here first: life and light, darkness that cannot overcome the light, witness, the world that does not know him, his own people who do not receive him, and the gift of becoming God’s children through faith, by a birth from God.

The narrative then begins with a week of witness. John the Baptist tells the Jerusalem delegation that he is not the Messiah, not Elijah, not the Prophet, only a voice preparing the way. He points to Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, the one on whom the Spirit came and remained, the Son of God. Two of John’s disciples follow Jesus; Andrew brings his brother Simon, whom Jesus renames Cephas; Philip finds Nathanael, who doubts that anything good comes from Nazareth until Jesus shows he knows him, and then confesses him Son of God and King of Israel. Jesus promises greater things: heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man, Jacob’s ladder fulfilled in himself. One title after another is given to Jesus in this chapter: Word, God, Light, Lamb, Son of God, Rabbi, Messiah, King of Israel, Son of Man. The rest of the Gospel shows what they mean.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Wedding at Cana: Water into Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three days later there is a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and Jesus’ mother is there; Jesus and his disciples have also been invited. When the wine runs out, his mother tells him they have no wine. Jesus answers, addressing her as “woman”, that this is not their concern, for his hour has not yet come. She tells the servants to do whatever he says. Nearby stand six stone water jars used for Jewish purification rites, each holding twenty to thirty gallons. Jesus tells the servants to fill them with water, and they fill them to the brim. Then he tells them to draw some out and take it to the man in charge of the feast. He tastes the water that has become wine, not knowing where it came from, though the servants know. He calls the bridegroom over and remarks that people normally serve the best wine first and the cheaper wine once the guests have drunk freely, but he has saved the best until now. This, the first of his signs, Jesus does at Cana, revealing his glory, and his disciples believe in him. Afterwards he goes down to Capernaum with his mother, brothers and disciples, and stays there a few days.
verseByVerse.theology:
John calls the miracles of Jesus 'signs' (semeia) — they are not mere wonders but pointers to a deeper reality. The water-into-wine sign points to who Jesus is (the one who brings the new wine of the kingdom) and what his mission accomplishes (the transformation of the old into the new, abundance replacing scarcity, joy replacing labor). 'His hour had not yet come' — the hour of the cross, the hour of glorification, which will be the ultimate sign to which all others point. The disciples see the sign, believe, and their faith is the intended fruit of every sign in this Gospel.

The material of the sign is the point of the sign. The six jars were there for the Jewish rites of purification — the physical apparatus of a whole system for dealing with uncleanness — and Jesus does not replace the vessels but fills them. The water of ceremonial cleansing becomes the wine of a wedding feast: not the destruction of the old order but its transformation into joy. The quantity settles the tone. A hundred and twenty to a hundred and eighty gallons, at a village wedding, is not a measured response to a stated need; the disproportion is itself the message.

Semeion is established here as this Gospel's word for a miracle, and the choice is deliberate: John never uses the Synoptics' dynamis (mighty work). A sign is a signpost, valueless if you stop at it, and the crowds of chapter 6 will do exactly that. Seven signs are selected, and 20:30-31 states the purpose. He manifested his glory pays the claim of 1:14 — and the first instalment of that glory is a wedding present given anonymously in an unknown village. And his disciples believed in him, though they had already believed (1:41, 45, 49): faith in this Gospel grows and is tested rather than being settled once.
verseByVerse.examples:
The abundance of the provision — six jars of twenty to thirty gallons each — is a sign of the inexhaustible generosity of the kingdom. Jesus honors the institution of marriage by performing his first miracle at a wedding. And 'the best wine last' is the pattern of the gospel: the world offers its best first and then disappoints, but Christ gives his best at the end — the resurrection, the new creation, the eternal feast.

The pastoral register of the first sign is lower than readers expect and deliberately so. Nobody is ill and nobody is dying; a family has run out of drink and will be humiliated for years in a culture where hospitality was an obligation with teeth. The first miracle of the incarnate Son was performed because somebody was going to be embarrassed — which sets the threshold for what may be brought to him far below where most praying puts it. Mary's four words state the trouble and propose nothing: They have no wine.

You have kept the good wine until now is the gospel's shape against the world's. Everything else front-loads — the advertisement better than the product, youth spent early, the decline negotiated afterwards. But the promise must be guarded: it is not an assurance that circumstances improve, and it should not be handed to a suffering Christian as though it were. Plenty of lives get harder. What is promised is a better end, not an easier road — which is precisely why it speaks to the reader who has concluded his best years are behind him.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two days later there is a wedding at Cana in Galilee. Jesus’ mother is there, and Jesus and his disciples have been invited too.

The third day. Counting from the call of Philip and Nathanael (1:43): the end of a week of new beginnings, perhaps echoing the days of creation. Readers may also hear a hint of resurrection.

Cana. Probably Khirbet Qana, about nine miles north of Nazareth. Nathanael’s home town (21:2).

A wedding. Village weddings lasted up to a week, with the whole community feasting. Jesus begins his signs not in the temple but at a family celebration.

The mother of Jesus. Never named in John. She appears here, at the start of his signs, and at the cross (19:25–27).

On a Tuesday. Jesus goes to weddings. Ordinary joys, family meals and celebrations are places where he is welcome. Invite him in.
verseByVerse.note: Cana was a village in Galilee, a few miles north of Nazareth. A wedding feast could last a week.

verseByVerse.quote: When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, "They have no wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the wine runs out, Jesus’ mother tells him they have no wine.

A social disaster. In an honour culture, running out of wine would shame the bridegroom’s family for years; there may even have been a legal obligation to provide.

Mary’s words. She simply states the need, as Martha and Mary later do (11:3). A model of prayer: telling Jesus the problem and trusting him with it.

Wine. In Scripture, a gift that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15) and a symbol of the joy of God’s kingdom (Isaiah 25:6). Its lack can picture a joyless religion.
verseByVerse.note: Running out of wine would have shamed the family publicly.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jesus said to her, 'Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.' His mother said to the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus replies, “Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.” His mother tells the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”

Woman. Not rude in Greek; Jesus uses it tenderly from the cross (19:26). But it is not a son’s usual word. It marks a new relationship: his mission is set by his Father, not his family.

What to me and to you? A Semitic idiom of distance, meaning roughly “that is not our concern” (compare 2 Kings 3:13). Jesus will act, but on his own terms.

My hour. In John, the hour of his death, resurrection and glorification (7:30; 12:23; 13:1; 17:1). Even at a wedding, Jesus has the cross in view.

Do whatever he tells you. Mary’s last recorded words in John, and her best counsel to all. Compare Pharaoh about Joseph (Genesis 41:55).

Where Christians differ: Mary’s intercession. Roman Catholic and Orthodox teaching sees this episode as showing Mary’s power to intercede, and encourages prayer through her. Protestants answer that Jesus gently distances himself from her request here, that Christ is the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), and that Scripture never calls believers to pray to the saints. Verdict: honour Mary as the Lord’s faithful servant and follow her counsel: go to Jesus directly, and do what he says.
verseByVerse.note: “Woman” was a respectful form of address, not a rude one. Jesus’ “hour” in John is the time of his death and glorification.

parallels.desc: “Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do”

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus said to the servants, "Fill the jars with water." And they filled them up to the brim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six stone water jars are standing there, used for the Jewish purification rites, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus tells the servants to fill the jars with water, and they fill them to the brim.

Stone jars. Stone, unlike pottery, was held not to become ritually unclean; archaeologists have found such vessels across Judea and Galilee from this period. The water was for washing hands and vessels (Mark 7:3–4).

Six. Perhaps significant: one short of seven, the number of completeness. The old order is incomplete.

120 to 180 gallons. About 500 to 700 litres. More than the feast could ever need.

To the brim. The servants obey fully. Nothing could be added, so no one could suspect a trick.

On a Tuesday. Obedience often looks unremarkable: carrying water. Do what Jesus says, fully, even when you cannot see why.
verseByVerse.note: Stone jars did not become ritually unclean, so they were used for purification water. The ESV notes that each held two or three measures — twenty to thirty gallons: well over a hundred gallons in all.

parallels.desc: the washings of the Jews

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast." So they took it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he tells them to draw some out and take it to the master of the feast, and they do.

The master of the feast. A head waiter or a trusted guest who managed the banquet and tasted the wine.

Faith in action. The servants carry what they had poured in as water to the man in charge. The miracle happens somewhere between the jar and the cup, without word or gesture.
verseByVerse.note: The master of the feast was the guest put in charge of the celebration.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him, 'Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the master of the feast tastes the water now turned into wine, not knowing where it came from, though the servants who drew it know, he calls the bridegroom. Everyone, he says, serves the good wine first and the poorer wine once people have drunk freely; but he has kept the good wine until now.

The servants knew. Those who obey see what the important people miss.

The best wine last. A picture of the gospel: God has saved the best for the age of the Messiah (Hebrews 1:1–2). And for the believer, the best is always still to come.

Where Christians differ: wine and alcohol. Some Christians, especially since the nineteenth-century temperance movement, have argued that this was unfermented grape juice and that total abstinence is required. The word is the ordinary word for wine, and the master’s comment about guests who have “drunk freely” shows it was fermented. Scripture praises wine as God’s gift (Psalm 104:15) and forbids drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 23:29–35). Verdict: drinking in moderation is permitted; drunkenness is sin; abstaining is a wise and loving choice for many, for the sake of health, a weaker brother or a past addiction (Romans 14:21). Neither drinkers nor abstainers should judge the other.

For worship. Thank God that in Christ he has kept the best until now.

parallels.desc: a feast of well-aged wine
the mountains shall drip sweet wine

verseByVerse.quote: "This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him. After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does this, the first of his signs, at Cana in Galilee, and reveals his glory; and his disciples believe in him. Afterwards he goes down to Capernaum with his mother, his brothers and his disciples, and they stay there a few days.

Signs. John never calls Jesus’ miracles “mighty works” but “signs”: acts that point beyond themselves to who he is. John records seven before the cross (2:1–11; 4:46–54; 5:1–9; 6:1–14; 6:16–21; 9:1–7; 11:1–44), written so that readers may believe (20:30–31).

His glory. The glory seen in the Word made flesh (1:14). Few at the feast saw it; the disciples did, and believed.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ chief purpose was to rescue parties. The sign shows that he brings the joy of the new age, transforming the old rites of purification into the wine of the kingdom.

His brothers. Probably younger sons of Joseph and Mary (Mark 6:3; Matthew 1:25). Where Christians differ. Roman Catholic teaching holds Mary’s perpetual virginity and reads these as cousins; Orthodox tradition as sons of Joseph from an earlier marriage. Protestants generally take the plain meaning. Verdict: the natural reading is that they were Jesus’ half-brothers, though the question does not touch the gospel.

For worship. Praise Jesus, whose first sign was to turn want into overflowing joy.
verseByVerse.note: John calls Jesus’ miracles “signs” — pointers to who he is. Capernaum was a fishing town on the lake shore.

parallels.desc: these are written so that you may believe

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Temple Cleansing and the New Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Near Passover Jesus goes up to Jerusalem and finds the temple courts full of dealers in cattle, sheep and doves, and money-changers at their tables. He plaits a whip from cords and drives out the traders and their animals, flings the coins to the ground, upsets the tables and orders the dove-sellers to take their goods away: his Father’s house is not a place of business. The disciples recall the psalm about zeal for God’s house devouring the righteous one. The authorities demand a sign to back his action. Jesus tells them that if they tear this temple down, he will rebuild it in three days. They scoff that Herod’s temple has been forty-six years in the building. But Jesus is speaking of his own body, and after he rises the disciples remember and believe both Scripture and his word. At the festival many trust in him because of his signs, yet Jesus does not trust himself to them, for he knows human hearts without being told.
verseByVerse.theology:
The temple cleansing is an act of prophetic authority: Jesus acts as the Lord coming suddenly to his temple (Mal. 3:1), purifying the house of prayer from the commercial transactions that have turned worship into a market. The zeal that consumes him is zeal for the Father's house — the passion of the Son for the honor of the Father. 'My Father's house' — his first recorded words in Luke (2:49) and his claim here: the temple belongs to his Father, and he has authority over it because he is the Son.

The temple thread runs the length of Scripture and this passage is its hinge. In 1:14 the Word dwelt among us and we have seen his glory; here the tabernacle has become the temple, and John states that the temple is a body (v. 21); and the Bible ends with a city in which John saw no temple at all, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev. 21:22). My Father's house (v. 16) is the claim that licenses the whip — the same phrase Luke records from him at twelve years old in the same building (Lk. 2:49).

Verse 22 supplies this Gospel's account of how understanding arrives. The disciples heard the saying at the time and grasped nothing of it for three years; the resurrection made the old sentence legible and the memory surfaced with its meaning attached — which is the promise of 14:26 in operation. They believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken, two objects of one verb, with no distinction drawn between them.

Verses 23-25 must not be used to unsettle the wrong reader. What is described is faith produced by spectacle and not yet tested — the crowd of chapter 6 who turn back at the first hard saying (6:66). John uses of them the identical phrase he used of the saved in 1:12, believed in his name: the difference is not in the vocabulary but in what the faith does when the wine runs out. Anxiety about whether one's faith is real is not a symptom of this condition; the people described here were entirely untroubled. And Jesus withholding himself is not Jesus withdrawing — the next thing he does is give Nicodemus the fullest account of the new birth in the Bible.
verseByVerse.examples:
The buying and selling were not wicked in themselves but had invaded the sacred space set apart for prayer, turning the house of God into a place of commerce. The sign of the temple's destruction and raising in three days is the central sign of the entire Gospel: the cross and resurrection are the ultimate manifestation of Jesus's glory, the event to which all other signs point.

The anger of this scene needs handling in both directions. It is not incompatible with meekness: anger is what love does when what it loves is being damaged, and he stops to make the whip of cords himself (v. 15) — this is deliberate, not a loss of temper. But the passage is not a warrant for aggression on God's behalf. Two things separate it from that: all of it is aimed at the dishonouring of God and the exclusion of the powerless, and none of it at a slight to himself, since under personal injury he did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7; 1 Pet. 2:23); and it is the Son acting in his own house with the owner's authority.

The searching application is not the easy one about churches selling things. It is the Court of the Gentiles question: whether anything in the ordinary operation of a congregation — its assumptions, its vocabulary, the things everyone knows and nobody explains — makes it hard for an outsider to get near God. Nobody in Jerusalem had decided to exclude the nations. They had simply needed the space.

And the chapter's last word runs straight into the next scene: the printers' chapter break hides a joint. Verse 25 ends he himself knew what was in man (anthropos), and John's next sentence begins Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus — the general statement and its illustration set against each other like a caption and a photograph.

verseByVerse.quote: The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Jewish Passover is near, Jesus goes up to Jerusalem. In the temple he finds people selling cattle, sheep and doves, and money-changers seated at their tables.

Passover. John mentions three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), the basis for the view that Jesus’ ministry lasted about three years.

The temple market. In the Court of the Gentiles, the only area where non-Jews could pray. Pilgrims needed approved animals for sacrifice and Tyrian silver coins for the temple tax. A convenience had become a noisy bazaar, and probably a profitable monopoly for the high priest’s family.

Where Christians differ: one cleansing or two? The other Gospels place a temple cleansing in the last week (Mark 11:15–17). Some think John moved it to the beginning for theological reasons. Others hold that Jesus cleansed the temple twice, at the start and end of his ministry; the details and sayings differ. Verdict: two cleansings is the more natural reading of both accounts, though the Gospel writers do sometimes order material by theme; either way the event is historical.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax. John places this cleansing early; the other Gospels record one in the last week.

verseByVerse.quote: And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And he told those who sold the pigeons, "Take these things away; do not make my Father's house a house of trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Making a whip out of cords, he drives them all out of the temple, sheep and cattle as well. He scatters the money-changers’ coins and overturns their tables. To the dove-sellers he says, “Take these things away; do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.”

A whip of cords. Probably made from the rushes or ropes used for the animals; weapons were forbidden in the temple. It was used to drive the animals; there is no suggestion that Jesus beat people.

My Father’s house. An astonishing claim: the temple is his Father’s house, and he is the Son with authority over it (Luke 2:49; Malachi 3:1–3). Zechariah 14:21 foresaw a day when there would be no trader in the house of the LORD.

Where Christians differ: Jesus and anger. Some use this passage to justify violence; some pacifists find it uncomfortable. Jesus’ act was a prophetic sign of judgment by the Lord of the temple, not a model for vigilante force. Verdict: anger at the corruption of worship can be holy (Ephesians 4:26), but its expression must be controlled and lawful. Christians are not authorised to take the whip.

On a Tuesday. Ask what clutters worship in your church or your heart: commerce, convenience, performance, distraction. Let Christ clear it out.

parallels.desc: no longer a trader in the house of the LORD
my Father’s house

verseByVerse.quote: "His disciples remembered that it was written, 'Zeal for your house will consume me.' So the Jews said to him, 'What sign do you show us for doing these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples remember that it is written, “Zeal for your house will consume me.” The Jewish leaders ask what sign he can show them to prove his right to do this.

Psalm 69:9. A psalm of the suffering righteous one, quoted often of Jesus (15:25; 19:28–29; Romans 15:3). “Will consume” looks ahead: his zeal for God’s house will cost him his life.

A sign? They do not deny the wrong; they question his authority. Jesus will give one sign: his resurrection (Matthew 12:38–40).

For worship. Jesus was consumed by zeal for God’s glory. Ask him to share that zeal with you.

parallels.desc: zeal for your house has consumed me

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The Jews then said, "It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The Jewish leaders reply that this temple has taken forty-six years to build, and he will raise it in three days?

A riddle. “Destroy” is an ironic command: if you destroy it, as you will. Misquoted at his trial as a threat to destroy the temple (Mark 14:58; 15:29).

Forty-six years. Herod the Great began rebuilding in 20/19 BC, which dates this Passover to about AD 27/28. The work was not finished until AD 63, seven years before the Romans destroyed it.

Raise. The word used of resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple around 20 BC; forty-six years brings us to about AD 27. The work went on for decades more.

parallels.desc: the charge at his trial

verseByVerse.quote: But he was speaking about the temple of his body. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the temple he means is his body. When he is raised from the dead, his disciples remember that he said this, and they believe the Scripture and the word Jesus had spoken.

The true temple. The temple was where God dwelt among his people and where sin was atoned for. Jesus’ body is now the dwelling place of God (1:14) and the place of sacrifice. After his resurrection the church is his body and God’s temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22).

Remembered. Much of what Jesus said was understood only after Easter, through the Spirit (12:16; 14:26).

What it does not mean. Not that God will rebuild a physical temple as the centre of worship. The temple has found its fulfilment in Christ (4:21–24; Revelation 21:22).

For worship. You meet God not in a building but in Christ, crucified and risen. Come to him.

parallels.desc: they remembered his words

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing. But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus is in Jerusalem at the Passover festival, many believe in his name when they see the signs he is doing. But Jesus does not entrust himself to them, because he knows all people.

Believed … did not entrust. A wordplay: the same verb. They “believed” in him, but he did not “believe” in them. Their faith rested on signs and was shallow (6:26; 8:31–59).

Where Christians differ: can true faith be lost? Some see such passages as true believers who later fall away. Reformed theology distinguishes between temporary faith, which never truly unites to Christ, and saving faith, which perseveres (1 John 2:19; John 10:27–29). Verdict: those whom Christ keeps are kept forever; faith that rests only on spectacle may prove false. Examine yourself, not to doubt, but to rest on Christ himself (2 Corinthians 13:5).

parallels.desc: I the LORD search the heart

verseByVerse.quote: and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He needs no one to testify about human beings, for he himself knows what is in each person.

He knew. Divine knowledge of the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:9–10). Jesus has already shown it with Peter and Nathanael (1:42, 48), and will with the Samaritan woman (4:17–18).

A warning and a comfort. A warning: Jesus is not fooled by enthusiasm. A comfort: he knows the worst about us, and loves us still (13:1; 21:17).

For worship. “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you” (21:17).

parallels.desc: you alone know the hearts of all

2.title: The First Sign: Water into Wine
2.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.<sup>2</sup>Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.<sup>3</sup>When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.”<sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.”<sup>5</sup>His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”<sup>6</sup>Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons.<sup>7</sup>Jesus said to the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them up to the brim.<sup>8</sup>And he said to them, “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.” So they took it.<sup>9</sup>When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom<sup>10</sup>and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.”<sup>11</sup>This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him.<sup>12</sup>After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days.<sup>13</sup>The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.<sup>14</sup>In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.<sup>15</sup>And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables.<sup>16</sup>And he told those who sold the pigeons, “Take these things away; do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.”<sup>17</sup>His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me.”<sup>18</sup>So the Jews said to him, “What sign do you show us for doing these things?”<sup>19</sup>Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”<sup>20</sup>The Jews then said, “It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?”<sup>21</sup>But he was speaking about the temple of his body.<sup>22</sup>When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.<sup>23</sup>Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing.<sup>24</sup>But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people<sup>25</sup>and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
2.overview:
Two scenes open Jesus’ public ministry, one in a village home and one in the temple, and both announce that something new has come. At a wedding in Cana, when the wine runs out, Jesus turns some 150 gallons of water standing in stone jars for Jewish purification into wine better than any served before. It is the first of the seven “signs” John records, and through it Jesus reveals his glory and his disciples believe. The prophets pictured the messianic age as a feast overflowing with wine (Isaiah 25:6; Amos 9:13); the water of the old purification rites gives way to the wine of the kingdom.

At Passover in Jerusalem Jesus drives the traders and money-changers from the temple court with a whip of cords, forbidding them to make his Father’s house a market. Asked for a sign to justify his authority, he says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” His hearers think of Herod’s building, forty-six years in the making; John explains that he meant his body, and the disciples understood after the resurrection. The meeting place of God and people is now Jesus himself. Many in Jerusalem believe because of his signs, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them, for he knows what is in every human heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Nicodemus and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nicodemus, a Pharisee on the ruling council, visits Jesus by night and acknowledges him as a teacher sent by God, because of his signs. Jesus tells him that without a birth from above no one can see God’s kingdom. Nicodemus takes it literally: can an old man be born a second time? Jesus explains that entry to the kingdom requires birth by water and the Spirit. Human nature can only reproduce itself; the Spirit gives new life, unseen and unpredictable as the wind. Israel’s teacher should have understood. Jesus speaks of what he has seen, yet his testimony is refused. The Son of Man, who alone has come down from heaven, must be raised up as Moses raised the bronze serpent, so that all who trust him may have eternal life. The reason is God’s love for the world: he gave his unique Son, so that no one who believes in him will be lost, but will live for ever. The Son came to rescue, not to condemn. Believers face no condemnation; unbelievers are condemned already. The light has come, but people chose darkness because their deeds were evil and they feared exposure, while those who practise the truth come to the light gladly.
verseByVerse.theology:
The new birth is the work of the Spirit, who blows where he wills. No human being can produce it, control it, or predict it; the Spirit sovereignly regenerates those whom God has given to the Son. The lifting up of the Son of Man — as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness — is the means by which eternal life comes to those who look in faith. God's motive is love for the world; his means is the gift of his Son; his purpose is salvation, not condemnation. The light has come, and the verdict of each person is revealed by whether they come to the light or flee from it.

The kingdom of God — the dominant phrase of the other three Gospels — occurs in John only here, at verses 3 and 5, and never again. And the verb shifts between them: without this birth a man cannot see the kingdom (v. 3) and cannot enter it (v. 5). The problem is not that he is outside a door he can see; he cannot perceive the country. This is why argument alone never works, and why Nicodemus is the proof of it.

Verse 6 states the impossibility as a principle of kind, not of quantity: like produces like, and nothing in creation generates something of a higher order than itself. Flesh here is not the body — this Gospel has just said the Word became flesh and meant it as the highest news in the world — but human nature working with its own resources, including the best of them. So the failure of religious effort is not a failure of sincerity or degree. Effort was never the mechanism.

Verse 16 requires two corrections that make it larger rather than smaller. So loved renders houtos, an adverb of manner rather than degree: in this way God loved — he gave. The size of the love is not asserted but demonstrated. And the world in this Gospel is not a neutral term for the planet's population but humanity organised against God (1:10; 7:7; 15:18-19). The object of the love was the thing set against him. Verse 17's not to condemn is a statement of purpose, not a denial that judgement exists — verse 18 says the opposite in the same breath. A lifeboat does not go out to drown anyone; that the drowning is real is why it was launched.
verseByVerse.examples:
'Born again' (or 'born from above') is among the most comprehensive descriptions of salvation in the New Testament: it captures the totality of the transformation (rebirth, not reform), its source (from above, from God), and its necessity (without it, the kingdom cannot be seen). Nicodemus's night visit is the first of several encounters in John where the darkness represents the condition of the human soul before the light breaks in. John 3:16 is not a formula to be memorized but a universe to be explored: every word contains inexhaustible depth.

Nicodemus is not finished at the end of this conversation, and the arc is the answer to anyone who thinks the night visit was a failure. He appears twice more, each time further into the open: in chapter 7 he speaks up in the council for due process and is shouted down (7:50-51); and after the crucifixion, when the twelve have scattered and there is nothing left to gain, he comes to a Roman execution in daylight with about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (19:39) — a quantity fit for the burial of a king, carried through the streets by a member of the Sanhedrin. The man who came at night buried him in the afternoon.

The bronze serpent repays being staged rather than cited. Israel complains; snakes come; people are dying through the camp. God's remedy is not to remove the snakes but to have Moses cast an image of the very thing killing them and raise it on a pole — an image, commanded by the God who forbade images, of the instrument of death — and the only requirement laid on a dying man is that he look. It is deliberately the one thing someone face down in the sand can still do. (Israel kept the bronze snake, and seven centuries later Hezekiah found them burning incense to it and smashed it, calling it Nehushtan — 2 Kgs. 18:4. Even the instrument of mercy becomes an idol if the look lands on it rather than through it.)

Verse 10 is the verse for the reader who knows his Bible and feels nothing. Nicodemus knows the texts and can almost certainly recite them; what he has never done is apply the promise of a new heart to himself, because he has spent his life being told, accurately, that his conduct is exemplary. Note the tone of the rebuke, though: Jesus asks a question, does not end the conversation, and goes on to give this one bewildered official more sustained teaching on the new birth than anyone else receives in the Gospels.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, "Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader of the Jews, comes to Jesus at night. He addresses him as Rabbi and says that they know he is a teacher come from God, because no one could do the signs he does unless God were with him.

Nicodemus. A Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin (7:50), wealthy (19:39), learned. If any man could earn God’s favour, he could.

By night. Perhaps from caution or fear (19:38–39), perhaps for an unhurried conversation. In John, night also has a symbolic ring (13:30): he comes out of darkness towards the light (v. 19–21).

We know. He speaks for a group, perhaps of sympathetic Pharisees. His estimate of Jesus is high but not high enough: a teacher, not the Son.

On a Tuesday. Respectable, religious people also need to come to Jesus. Do not assume the churchgoer, the professional or the theologian has no need of new birth.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus was a member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council. Coming by night may have been for secrecy or simply for quiet conversation.

parallels.desc: Nicodemus speaks up in the council
he brings spices for Jesus’ burial

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers him solemnly that unless someone is born again, from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God.

Born again or from above? Anōthen means both “again” and “from above” (3:31; 19:11). Jesus means both: a second birth, and one that comes from God.

See the kingdom. Experience God’s reign; enter it (v. 5). The only place the kingdom of God is mentioned in John.

Not improvement but rebirth. Jesus does not tell Nicodemus to try harder. A birth is not something you achieve; it happens to you.

What it does not mean. “Born again” is not a special class of Christian, nor a single emotional experience. Every true Christian is born again; no one can be a Christian without it.

For worship. Thank God for the new life he gave you, which you could not give yourself (1 Peter 1:3).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “again” (Greek anōthen) can also be rendered “from above.” Nicodemus hears one sense; Jesus means both.

parallels.desc: born of God
born again to a living hope

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus said to him, "How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?" Jesus answered, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus asks how anyone can be born when old: can he enter his mother’s womb a second time? Jesus answers solemnly that unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.

A literal misunderstanding. A pattern in John (2:20; 4:11; 6:52): people take Jesus’ words physically, which lets him explain them. Nicodemus may also be wistful: how can a man as old and set as I am start again?

Water and Spirit. Ezekiel 36:25–27: God will sprinkle clean water to cleanse his people and give them a new heart and his Spirit. The “teacher of Israel” (v. 10) should have known it.

Where Christians differ: what is the water? Roman Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran traditions see Christian baptism here, through which God regenerates. Others think of natural birth (amniotic water, v. 6). Many Reformed interpreters see the Ezekiel promise: one birth, cleansing and renewal by the Spirit, of which baptism is the later sign (Titus 3:5). Verdict: the Ezekiel background is decisive: “water and Spirit” together describe the one inward work of God that cleanses and renews; baptism signifies it but does not effect it.
verseByVerse.note: Water and Spirit together recall Ezekiel’s promise of cleansing and a new heart.

parallels.desc: I will sprinkle clean water on you and put my Spirit within you
the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.

Like produces like. Human nature can only produce more human nature, fallen and limited. Only the Spirit can produce spiritual life.

Flesh. Here not sinful nature as in Paul, but human life as such, weak and mortal (1:13–14). Even so, it cannot reach God.

On a Tuesday. You cannot raise your children, persuade your friends or argue your colleagues into the kingdom. Pray for the Spirit to give new birth.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel that I said to you, 'You must be born again.' The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus should not be surprised that Jesus told him he must be born again. The wind blows where it wants; you hear its sound but do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.

You must. “You” plural: not just Nicodemus but all.

Wind and Spirit. One Greek word, pneuma (Hebrew ruach), means both. Ezekiel 37:9–14: the breath of God brings dry bones to life.

Sovereign and free. The wind is not controlled by us. The Spirit regenerates whom he wills (1:13). We cannot see him at work, but we see the effects.

Where Christians differ: decision and new birth. Much popular evangelism speaks as though a person is born again by deciding to be. Reformed theology answers that the decision of faith is real and necessary, but it is the fruit of the Spirit’s prior work, as a cry is the sign of a birth, not its cause. Verdict: preach freely and call everyone to believe; trust the Spirit, not technique, to give life.

For worship. Pray with Ezekiel for the breath of God to “breathe on these slain” (Ezekiel 37:9) in your family, church and town.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the same Greek word (pneuma) means both “wind” and “spirit.”

parallels.desc: you do not know the way the spirit comes
come from the four winds, O breath

verseByVerse.quote: "Nicodemus said to him, 'How can these things be?' Jesus answered him, 'Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus asks how these things can be. Jesus replies that he is Israel’s teacher and yet does not understand them.

The teacher. With the definite article: a recognised authority. The Old Testament spoke of a new heart and spirit (Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26). He knew the texts but not their meaning.

Nicodemus’s last words here. He fades from the conversation. But he reappears defending Jesus (7:50–51) and burying him (19:39). The wind was blowing.

On a Tuesday. Knowing the Bible is not the same as knowing its Lord. Ask God to make what you know become life.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus calls him “the teacher of Israel” — a recognised authority who should have known the prophets’ promises.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells him solemnly that they speak of what they know and testify to what they have seen, but they do not accept their testimony. If Jesus has told them earthly things and they do not believe, how will they believe if he tells them heavenly things?

We and you. Plurals: Jesus and his disciples speaking to Nicodemus’s circle, and through them John’s church speaking to the synagogue of his day.

Earthly things. The new birth happens on earth, in people. Heavenly things, the mysteries of God’s nature and plan, are still harder. If they stumble at the first, they cannot reach the second.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “you” in these verses is plural: Jesus is addressing Nicodemus’s whole circle.

verseByVerse.quote: "No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man. And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so the Son of Man must be lifted up.

Only the Son of Man. No mystic or prophet has climbed to heaven to bring back its secrets. The only one who can tell heavenly things is the one who came from there (1:18).

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “who is in heaven” (KJV). The earliest omit it. Verdict: probably not original, though its theology is true: the Son never ceased to be God in heaven while on earth.

The bronze serpent. Numbers 21:4–9: Israel was dying from snakebite as judgment for their grumbling; God told Moses to set a bronze serpent on a pole, and whoever looked at it lived. The remedy took the form of the curse.

Lifted up. In John, both crucifixion and exaltation (8:28; 12:32–33). The cross is Christ’s glory.

Must. Divine necessity: there is no other way.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who is in heaven.” In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: the bronze serpent on a pole
he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die

verseByVerse.quote: "that whoever believes in him may have eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that everyone who believes may have eternal life in him.

Look and live. As dying Israelites looked at the serpent, so sinners look to the crucified Christ in faith. Not a work, simply a look of trust (Isaiah 45:22). C. H. Spurgeon was converted at fifteen on hearing a lay preacher say: Look unto me, and be ye saved.

Eternal life. The first use of John’s great phrase (17 times). Not just endless life but the life of the age to come, the life of God himself, beginning now (17:3).

Where do Jesus’ words end? Ancient manuscripts had no quotation marks. Many interpreters think Jesus’ words end at verse 15 and verses 16–21 are John’s reflection. Verdict: uncertain and unimportant: John writes inspired Scripture either way.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some interpreters end Jesus’ words at verse 15 and read verses 16–21 as John’s comment.

verseByVerse.quote: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God loved the world in this way: he gave his one and only Son, so that everyone who trusts in him will not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn it, but so that the world might be saved through him.

So loved. “So” means “in this way” more than “so much”: the stress is on how God loved, by giving his Son (1 John 4:9–10). Of course the measure is also immense.

The world. In John, humanity in rebellion against God. The wonder is not that the world is big but that it is bad, and God loved it anyway (Romans 5:8).

Gave. Sent into the world and given up to death (Romans 8:32). The echo of Abraham and Isaac, his only son (Genesis 22:2, 12), is hard to miss.

Perish. Not annihilation but ruin, final loss: the opposite of eternal life (10:28).

Where Christians differ: God’s love and the world. Arminians read this verse as proof that Christ died equally for every person, intending to save all. Reformed interpreters agree that God has a real love for all humanity, shown in the free offer of the gospel to “whoever”, and also that he has a special, saving love for his people, whom the Son lays down his life for (10:11; 15:13; Ephesians 5:25). Verdict: preach this verse to everyone without hesitation: God’s love is real, the offer is sincere, and whoever believes will be saved. Definite atonement does not narrow the offer; it guarantees that the offer will be effective.

Not to condemn. The purpose of the first coming was rescue. Judgment is a sad by-product of refusing the rescue (v. 18).

For worship. Say it slowly, inserting your name: God so loved me that he gave his Son for me.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that verse 16 can also be rendered “For this is how God loved the world” — the stress is on the manner of his love.

parallels.desc: your son, your only son

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, for not believing in the name of God’s only Son. This is the verdict: the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.

Not condemned. Justification is present and final: no condemnation for those in Christ (5:24; Romans 8:1).

Condemned already. Unbelief is not a neutral position. Humanity is already under judgment; refusing the Son leaves a person where they are.

Loved darkness. The root of unbelief is moral, not merely intellectual. People avoid the light because it would expose them.

What it does not mean. Not that those who have never heard are condemned for rejecting what they never heard; they are judged for sins against the light they had (Romans 2:12). But Jesus’ point is that rejecting him is the final sin.

parallels.desc: no condemnation

verseByVerse.quote: "For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed. But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who does evil hates the light and avoids it, so that their deeds will not be exposed. But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be seen plainly that their works have been done in God.

Hiding. Since Eden, sinners hide (Genesis 3:8). The light of Christ is threatening to those who want to keep their secrets.

Does what is true. A Hebrew idiom: lives faithfully. Such people come to the light not because they are sinless but because they want God’s truth more than their own reputation.

Carried out in God. Even their good works are God’s doing (Ephesians 2:10; Philippians 2:13).

On a Tuesday. Is there something you are keeping in the dark: an expense claim, a browser history, a resentment? Bring it into the light. Confession is the way to freedom (1 John 1:7–9).

parallels.desc: expose the works of darkness

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — John's Final Testimony: The Bridegroom's Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus and his disciples spend time in the Judean countryside, baptising, while John is still free and baptising at Aenon near Salim, where water is plentiful. After a dispute about purification, John’s disciples complain that everyone is now going to Jesus. John answers that people receive only what heaven gives. He is not the Messiah but the one sent ahead, like the friend of the bridegroom, whose joy is complete when he hears the groom’s voice. Jesus’ influence must grow while John’s shrinks. The one from heaven is over all and speaks what he has seen, though few accept it; those who do confirm that God tells the truth. God gives him the Spirit without limit, and the Father, who loves the Son, has entrusted everything to him. To trust the Son is to have eternal life; to refuse him is to remain under God’s wrath.
verseByVerse.theology:
John the Baptist's final words in this Gospel are also its most concentrated theological summary: Jesus comes from above, speaks the words of God, gives the Spirit without measure, and holds in his hands both eternal life and God's wrath. There is no middle ground: whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him. The Baptist who began by pointing to the Lamb of God ends by declaring the eternal stakes of the decision about him.

Verse 30 contains a word that is usually missed: both verbs carry must. Not I ought to step back graciously but a divine necessity — the same word Jesus used at verse 14 of the Son of Man being lifted up. The rise of one and the waning of the other are a single arrangement, and it was not the Baptist's to negotiate. These are among his last recorded words in this Gospel (some think he speaks on to verse 36); he does not appear again except in the past tense.

The closing verses hold eternal life and wrath in the same frame, and the pairing at verse 36 is deliberately asymmetrical: not believes against does not believe, but believes against does not obey (apeitheo, refuses to be persuaded). The unbelief in view is not doubt politely held but the refusal of a person who has a right to be obeyed.

And the final verb is this Gospel's own great word. The wrath of God remains on him is menei, from meno — the abiding word, whose first appearance was the Spirit coming down and remaining on Jesus (1:32-33), which reappeared when the first disciples asked where he was staying and then stayed (1:38-39), and which carries the whole of chapter 15. Something abides on everyone. On Christ the Spirit rests and does not lift; in his people he himself abides; and on the one who refuses him the wrath he was already under simply stays, because nothing has happened to move it. Nothing arrives — which is the same truth as condemned already at verse 18, said with a different verb, and which is also where the mercy lies: what remains can be lifted, and this chapter has already said how.
verseByVerse.examples:
'He must increase, but I must decrease' is the defining characteristic of all genuine ministry — the minister who builds his own kingdom rather than Christ's has misunderstood the calling. The image of the friend of the bridegroom captures perfectly the joy of the one who serves another's marriage rather than his own: he is not jealous, not diminished, but fulfilled in the fulfillment of the one he loves.

The friend of the bridegroom is sharper than a general lesson in humility once the role is understood. He stood beside the groom and served the wedding. The wedding was in a real sense his project — and the moment the bridegroom's voice was heard inside, his work was finished and his job was to go home. The Greek doubles the joy for emphasis: he rejoices with joy, and the perfect tense of verse 29 says that joy is now standing complete, at the exact moment the crowds transfer. He is not managing a loss. He is at the height of his life. And if Jesus is the bridegroom there is a bride, and she is not the audience at the wedding — she is the one being married.

Verse 30 must not be left sentimental, because of what it cost, as the other Gospels tell it. Within months John was arrested for telling the truth about a marriage, and from that cell he sent to ask whether Jesus was after all the one who was to come (Matt. 11:2-3) — not the question of a serenely fulfilled man, but of one whose decrease had gone further than he bargained for. He was beheaded without trial to settle a promise made in front of dinner guests. And Jesus' verdict, delivered while he was in that cell doubting, was that among those born of women no one greater had arisen (Matt. 11:11).

This is the passage for anyone being replaced — the younger colleague who is plainly better at it, the role handed on, the retirement that arrived before the sense of usefulness did, the body doing less than last year. The world has no account of those except loss. Note where the weight of the sentence actually falls: he must increase is doing all the work, and the second clause is only its shadow. Nobody in Scripture is asked to shrink for the sake of shrinking; the decrease is bearable, and is even a completed joy, solely because of who fills the space.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing. John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Jesus and his disciples go into the Judean countryside, where he stays with them and baptises. John too is baptising at Aenon near Salim, because there is plenty of water there, and people keep coming to be baptised.

Jesus baptising. John clarifies at 4:2 that it was his disciples who baptised. This baptism was probably like John’s, a sign of repentance, before Christian baptism after the resurrection (Matthew 28:19).

Aenon near Salim. Aenon means “springs”. Probably in the Jordan valley south of Scythopolis, or in Samaria near Shechem. Its location is uncertain.

Plentiful water. Some see here a hint of immersion. Where Christians differ: the mode of baptism. Baptists and many others hold that baptism by immersion best fits the word (baptizō, dip) and the picture of burial (Romans 6:4). Others allow pouring or sprinkling, noting the word’s wider use (Mark 7:4) and the picture of the Spirit poured out. Verdict: immersion is the clearest expression of the meaning and the likeliest New Testament practice, but the validity of baptism does not hang on the quantity of water.
verseByVerse.note: The location of Aenon (“springs”) near Salim is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: (for John had not yet been put in prison)
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was before John was thrown into prison.

Filling a gap. Mark begins Jesus’ Galilean ministry after John’s arrest (Mark 1:14). John’s Gospel shows an earlier, overlapping ministry in Judea. The Gospels complement one another.

Assumed knowledge. John expects readers already to know that John the Baptist was imprisoned, probably from the other Gospels or common teaching.
verseByVerse.note: The other Gospels begin Jesus’ Galilean ministry after John’s arrest; John fills in an earlier period.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a discussion arose between some of John's disciples and a Jew over purification. And they came to John and said to him, "Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness — look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A dispute arises between John’s disciples and a Jew about purification. They come to John and tell him, as Rabbi, that the man who was with him across the Jordan, whom he testified about, is baptising, and everyone is going to him.

Purification. Perhaps the relative value of John’s baptism, Jesus’ baptism and Jewish washings (2:6).

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “Jews” (plural). Verdict: the singular, the harder reading, is probably original.

Rivalry. John’s disciples are jealous for their master. They do not even name Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Beware of jealousy when another church, ministry or colleague is growing faster than yours.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, "A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John answers that a person can receive only what is given from heaven.

Gifts and roles. Each ministry is God’s assignment (1 Corinthians 3:5–7; 4:7). John’s role was given; so is Jesus’. There is no room for competition.

On a Tuesday. Contentment begins with knowing that your role, gifts and place are given by God. Do your part gladly.

parallels.desc: what do you have that you did not receive?

verseByVerse.quote: "You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, 'I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.' The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They themselves can bear witness that he said he is not the Messiah but has been sent ahead of him. The bride belongs to the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and listens for him, is overjoyed when he hears the bridegroom’s voice. That joy of John’s is now complete.

The bridegroom. God is Israel’s husband in the prophets (Isaiah 54:5; 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20). John gives that role to Jesus (Mark 2:19–20; Ephesians 5:25–27; Revelation 19:7).

The friend. The best man, who arranged the wedding and waited to hear the bridegroom’s arrival. His job was to bring the bride to the groom, not to keep her.

Complete joy. John’s joy is not diminished but fulfilled by Jesus’ success.

For worship. The church is Christ’s bride, not ours. Rejoice to hear his voice.
verseByVerse.note: The friend of the bridegroom arranged the wedding and brought bride and groom together — his joy was the groom’s joy.

parallels.desc: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride

verseByVerse.quote: "He must increase, but I must decrease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must increase, but I must decrease.

Must. Divine necessity: this is God’s plan, and John embraces it.

Increase and decrease. Like the morning star fading before the sun. John’s last recorded words in this Gospel are his best.

What it does not mean. Not self-hatred, but self-forgetfulness. John is not crushed; his joy is full (v. 29).

On a Tuesday. Pray this verse over your ambitions, your reputation and your ministry. Let Christ have the credit.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all. He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who comes from above is above all. The one who is from the earth belongs to the earth and speaks as one from the earth. The one who comes from heaven is above all. He testifies to what he has seen and heard, yet no one accepts his testimony.

Who speaks? Perhaps John the Baptist continuing, perhaps the Gospel writer reflecting (as possibly in vv. 16–21). The theme returns to verses 11–13.

Above all. Jesus is not one prophet among many; he outranks every human messenger, John the Baptist included.

No one. An overstatement for emphasis, qualified in the next verse.

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit the second “is above all”. Verdict: probably original; the meaning is unaffected.

parallels.desc: you are from below, I am from above

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever accepts his testimony has certified that God is true.

A seal. Like stamping a document with a signet: believing Jesus is endorsing God’s truthfulness. Conversely, refusing him calls God a liar (1 John 5:10).

For worship. Set your seal today: God is true.
verseByVerse.note: To set one’s seal to something is to certify it as true.

parallels.desc: let God be true

verseByVerse.quote: "For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the one whom God has sent speaks God’s words, because God gives the Spirit without measure. The Father loves the Son and has put everything into his hands.

Without measure. Prophets received the Spirit in measure, for particular tasks. The Son has the Spirit fully and permanently (1:32–33; Isaiah 11:2).

Textual note. Some manuscripts add “God” as the explicit giver. Verdict: an interpretative addition, but correct: the Father gives the Spirit to the Son.

The Father loves the Son. The eternal love within the Trinity (17:24), the source of the Son’s authority (5:20; 13:3; Matthew 28:18).

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but God’s wrath remains on him.

Has. Present tense: eternal life now (5:24).

Believe and obey. The contrast is believing versus disobeying. Unbelief is disobedience to God’s command to trust his Son (1 John 3:23); true faith obeys (Romans 1:5).

The wrath of God. The only mention of wrath in John. God’s settled, holy opposition to sin, not a temper tantrum. It “remains”: it is already there, and stays unless removed. Christ bore it for those who believe (Romans 3:25; 5:9; 1 John 2:2).

Where Christians differ: wrath. Some modern writers think a loving God cannot be angry, and reinterpret wrath as impersonal consequences. Scripture presents it as God’s own personal response to evil, consistent with his love. Verdict: the wrath is real and personal; propitiation is good news only because it is.

For worship. Thank Jesus that the wrath which would have remained on you was carried by him.

parallels.desc: the wrath of God is revealed

3.overview:
Nicodemus, a Pharisee and member of the ruling council, comes to Jesus at night with a respectful compliment: Jesus must be a teacher from God. Jesus answers with a statement that sweeps away all religious achievement: no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, or born from above. The Greek word means both, and Nicodemus hears only the first. Jesus explains that this birth is “of water and the Spirit”, the cleansing and new heart God promised through Ezekiel; it is as free and mysterious as the wind. The teacher of Israel ought to have known. The Son of Man, who came down from heaven, must be lifted up as Moses lifted the bronze serpent, so that whoever believes may have eternal life.

Then come the most famous words in the Bible: God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. God sent his Son to save, not to condemn; but those who refuse him stand condemned already, because they love darkness rather than light. In the second half of the chapter John the Baptist, told that everyone is going to Jesus, rejoices like the bridegroom’s friend: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” The chapter ends with the choice that runs through the whole Gospel: whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but God’s wrath remains on him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–42 — The Woman at the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Leaving Judea for Galilee, Jesus takes the road through Samaria and rests at noon by Jacob’s well near Sychar. When a Samaritan woman comes to draw water, he asks her for a drink, to her amazement, since Jews and Samaritans keep apart. He tells her that if she knew who was asking, she would ask him for living water. She objects that he has no bucket; is he greater than Jacob? He answers that well water leaves people thirsty again, but the water he gives becomes a spring of eternal life within. She asks for it. He tells her to call her husband, and when she says she has none, he reveals that she has had five, and her present partner is not her husband. She calls him a prophet and raises the dispute over whether to worship on Gerizim or in Jerusalem. Jesus says the time has come when the place will not matter: the Father, who is spirit, seeks worshippers in spirit and truth, though salvation comes from the Jews. She mentions the coming Messiah, and Jesus tells her that he is the one. The returning disciples are surprised but silent. Leaving her jar, she brings the townspeople to see the man who knew her whole life. Jesus tells the disciples his food is doing his Father’s will, and the fields are ripe for harvest now. Many Samaritans believe through her word, and more through his, confessing him the Saviour of the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The living water Jesus offers is not a religious program or a moral reformation; it is himself — the inexhaustible source of eternal life. 'The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' Jesus does not merely point to the source of life; he is the source. The worship in Spirit and truth for which the Father seeks is not worship in a particular location but worship in the reality of who God is (truth) and by the power of God's own Spirit — the worship that the new covenant makes possible through the regeneration that Nicodemus could not understand.

The living water is explained by John himself later in the book. Standing in the temple Jesus cries out about rivers of living water, and the narrator adds the interpretation — this he said about the Spirit (7:38-39). So the gift offered at the well is the indwelling Spirit, the same new birth from above that Nicodemus could not grasp one chapter earlier, now pictured as a spring rather than a well. The distinction matters: a well is a store that must be gone to, lowered into and hauled from; a spring is water arriving from underneath under its own pressure, and the verb for welling up means to leap. What Jesus gives does not merely satisfy the drinker — it turns the drinker into a source.

Worship in spirit and truth is not sincerity set against ritual. Spirit is the Holy Spirit who enables it, and truth in this Gospel is a person before it is a quality (14:6) — so both halves are gifts rather than techniques. What is ruled out is worship that is correct and dead, and worship that is warm and invented: truth without Spirit is a corpse, Spirit without truth is a mood. And God is spirit (v. 24) does not mean God is vague or impersonal — the God described here speaks, seeks, loves and sends — but that he has no body and no location, and therefore cannot be arrived at or run out of.

The decisive clause is the Father is seeking such people to worship him (v. 23). Worship is ordinarily conceived as the search conducted from this end; here God is the one out looking, which is precisely what the chapter has been narrating since verse 4. A woman went to a well to fetch water and found somebody already sitting there who had come by a road many of his countrymen avoided. Note too that salvation is from the Jews is from, not for: the privilege was a channel and never a possession.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's method with the Samaritan woman is a model of contextual evangelism: he begins with her felt need (water), moves to her deeper need (the living water), exposes the root issue (her relationships), and leads her to the question of worship and the identity of the Messiah. He does not condemn; he illumines. The woman's testimony — 'Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did' — is the most basic form of Christian witness: here is someone who knows me completely and has not rejected me.

The five husbands deserve more care than they usually get. John never calls this woman immoral; Jesus never mentions sin to her, never calls her to repent, and never says sin no more — which he does say to the woman of chapter 8 and the man of chapter 5. A woman could not divorce in that world, so five marriages behind her means five times widowed or five times dismissed, or some mixture — things done to her at least as readily as by her. The town does not behave as a town behaves toward someone it has cast out: she speaks, they listen, they come (vv. 29-30, 39). The honest answer is that we are not told, and it matters that it be said, because women have sat through sermons on this chapter and been handed a shame the passage never assigns. (The old reading of the five husbands as an allegory of the five nations resettled in Samaria in 2 Kgs. 17 should also be resisted: it dissolves a real woman into a diagram, which is the one thing this passage refuses to do to her.)

Her testimony is instructive precisely because it is so poor by our standards. One fact, about herself; overstated (all that I ever did, when he had named one arrangement); no doctrine; and a closing line phrased in Greek to expect the answer no — nearer to this couldn't be the Christ, could it? And the town emptied. What travels is not the completeness of the account but the evidence that something has happened to the person giving it. Notice what her sentence leaves out: she never says and he did not despise me, because that is the tone of the whole remark. Being completely known had turned out not to be the disaster she would have predicted — which is the thing most people are most afraid of.

The harvest section is for the discouraged sower, and there are many. One sows and another reaps contains no promise that the sower sees it; the parent who prayed for thirty years, the teacher whose class drifted, the missionary who left with nothing to report are all inside that saying. The promise is in the verse before: sower and reaper rejoice together. In ordinary farming the reaper takes the visible result; here the arrangement is deliberately made so that neither can celebrate without the other.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John (although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus learns that the Pharisees have heard he is making and baptising more disciples than John, although in fact it is his disciples, not Jesus himself, who baptise.

Rising attention. The Pharisees, who investigated John (1:24), now watch Jesus. He withdraws to avoid a premature confrontation: his hour has not yet come.

Not Jesus himself. A correction of 3:22. Perhaps so that no one could boast of being baptised by Jesus personally (compare 1 Corinthians 1:14–17).

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “the Lord” for the first “Jesus”. Verdict: either may be original; the sense is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: he left Judea and departed again for Galilee. And he had to pass through Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He leaves Judea and goes back to Galilee. He has to pass through Samaria.

Had to. Geographically, the direct route from Judea to Galilee ran through Samaria, a three-day walk; strict Jews sometimes went round by the Jordan valley. But “had to” (edei) is John’s word for divine necessity (3:14, 30). Jesus had an appointment.

Samaria. The hill country between Judea and Galilee, home of the Samaritans.

On a Tuesday. Your daily routes, commute, school run, office, may be divine appointments. Watch for who God puts in your way.
verseByVerse.note: Samaria lay between Judea and Galilee. Many Jews travelled round it by the Jordan valley; the direct route went through it.

parallels.desc: Philip preaches in Samaria

verseByVerse.quote: So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob's well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He comes to a Samaritan town called Sychar, near the land Jacob gave his son Joseph. Jacob’s well is there, and Jesus, tired from the journey, sits down by the well. It is about noon.

Sychar. Probably the village of Askar, near ancient Shechem, at the foot of Mounts Gerizim and Ebal.

Jacob’s field. Genesis 33:18–19; 48:22; Joseph was buried there (Joshua 24:32).

Jacob’s well. Still shown today near Nablus, over 100 feet deep, one of the most securely identified sites in the Gospels.

Wearied. The eternal Word was tired (1:14). Jesus knows human exhaustion (Hebrews 4:15).

Noon. The hottest time of day, an unusual hour for drawing water; women normally came in the cool of the morning or evening. Perhaps she was avoiding others.

For worship. The Lord who never tires (Isaiah 40:28) became tired for us. Bring him your weariness.
verseByVerse.note: Jacob’s well is still shown near Shechem (modern Nablus) at the foot of Mount Gerizim. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon — the heat of the day.

parallels.desc: Jacob buys land at Shechem
Joseph buried there

verseByVerse.quote: A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Samaritan woman comes to draw water, and Jesus asks her for a drink.
