Three barriers. She is a woman, a Samaritan, and, as will emerge, a woman with a troubled reputation. A rabbi would not normally speak with an unknown woman in public, let alone a Samaritan.

Give me a drink. Jesus begins by asking a favour. He makes himself the one in need, honouring her.

A well and a meeting. In Genesis and Exodus, betrothals happen at wells (Genesis 24; 29; Exodus 2:15–21). John’s readers, who have just heard of Jesus the bridegroom (3:29), may notice the echo.

On a Tuesday. Starting a conversation by asking for help can open doors. Let people serve you; it treats them with dignity.
verseByVerse.note: A Jewish teacher would not normally speak with a woman in public, still less a Samaritan.

parallels.desc: meetings at a well

verseByVerse.quote: (For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.) The Samaritan woman said to him, "How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?" (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples have gone into town to buy food. The Samaritan woman asks how he, a Jew, can ask her, a Samaritan woman, for a drink, since Jews do not associate with Samaritans.

Samaritans. Descendants of Israelites of the northern kingdom who intermarried with peoples settled there by Assyria after 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24–41). They had their own temple on Mount Gerizim and their own version of the five books of Moses. The Jewish leader John Hyrcanus destroyed their temple about 128 BC; Samaritans defiled the Jerusalem temple with human bones about AD 6–9. Hatred ran deep.

No dealings. Probably meaning they would not share vessels, since Jews regarded Samaritan women as permanently unclean. Jesus is willing to drink from her jar.

Textual note. A few manuscripts omit the explanation in brackets. Verdict: it is original, a note for Gentile readers.

On a Tuesday. Who are the “Samaritans” in your world, the people your group avoids? Christ crosses that line; follow him across it.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans were a mixed people descended from Israelites and settlers brought in by Assyria; Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility. The ESV notes that the last sentence may mean Jews did not share vessels with Samaritans.

parallels.desc: the settling of Samaria

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered her, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers that if she knew God’s gift and who it is asking her for a drink, she would have asked him, and he would have given her living water.

If you knew. She does not know two things: the gift and the giver. Both are revealed by the end of the conversation.

Living water. In everyday speech, running water from a spring, better than still water in a cistern. In Scripture, God himself is “the fountain of living waters” (Jeremiah 2:13), and the Spirit is poured out like water (Isaiah 44:3). Later John explains: Jesus meant the Spirit (7:37–39).

A gift. Not earned, not bought: asked for (Isaiah 55:1).

For worship. Ask him for living water today.
verseByVerse.note: “Living water” normally meant fresh, flowing water from a spring, as opposed to still water in a cistern.

parallels.desc: the fountain of living waters

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman points out that he has no bucket, and the well is deep. Where would he get this living water? Is he greater than their father Jacob, who gave them the well and drank from it himself, with his sons and his animals?

Literal again. Like Nicodemus, she thinks of physical water.

Our father Jacob. Samaritans claimed descent from Joseph’s sons Ephraim and Manasseh.

Greater than Jacob? Irony: the answer is yes (compare 8:53, “greater than our father Abraham?”). Jacob gave a well; Jesus gives himself.
verseByVerse.note: The well is deep — said to be over 100 feet.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells her that everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again.

The thirst that returns. True of water, and of every earthly satisfaction: money, success, relationships, pleasure. Augustine: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

On a Tuesday. Notice where you go back again and again to satisfy a thirst: a screen, a purchase, praise. Ask what thirst lies beneath it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' The woman said to him, 'Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whoever drinks the water he will give will never be thirsty again; it will become in them a spring of water welling up to eternal life. The woman asks for this water, so that she will not get thirsty or have to keep coming here to draw.

A spring within. Not a jar to be refilled, but a source inside, bubbling up continually. The Spirit’s indwelling life (7:38–39; Isaiah 58:11).

Never thirst. Not that believers never long for God, but that the deepest thirst is met at its source, and keeps being met.

Welling up. The verb is used of leaping: lively, irrepressible.

Her request. She still misunderstands, but she asks. A beginning.

parallels.desc: like a spring of water whose waters do not fail

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Go, call your husband, and come here." The woman answered him, "I have no husband." Jesus said to her, "You are right in saying, 'I have no husband';"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells her to go and call her husband and come back. She replies that she has no husband. Jesus agrees that she is right to say she has no husband.

Why the husband? Living water cannot be received while the thirst is hidden. Jesus moves from her request to her real need.

A half-truth. Technically true, as Jesus acknowledges; but he knows the rest.

On a Tuesday. Grace is not avoidance. Real love sometimes asks the question that touches the wound.

verseByVerse.quote: "for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For she has had five husbands, and the man she has now is not her husband. What she has said is true.

Five husbands. In a small town, five marriages would have marked her. We are not told why hers ended: death, divorce, or both. Women could not usually initiate divorce, so she may have been sent away more than once.

What it does not mean. The text does not tell us she was a prostitute, or that her past was all her fault. But it does show that her present relationship is outside marriage, and Jesus names it.

Where Christians differ: her story. Some modern readers see her mainly as a victim of a harsh system; traditional readers as a sinful woman. Verdict: probably both: a woman sinned against and sinning, whose life Jesus knows completely. He neither excuses nor crushes; he exposes in order to heal.

For worship. Jesus knows everything you have ever done (v. 29), and still offers you living water.

parallels.desc: he knew what was in man

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman says she can see he is a prophet. Their ancestors worshipped on this mountain, but the Jews say Jerusalem is the place where people must worship.

A prophet. His knowledge of her past convinces her. Samaritans expected a prophet like Moses, the Taheb (“restorer”).

This mountain. Mount Gerizim, towering over the well. Samaritans held it was where Abraham offered Isaac and where Moses commanded blessing (Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:12). Their temple there had been destroyed by the Jews.

Changing the subject? Perhaps, to avoid her shame. Or perhaps a real question: if her life is so wrong, where can she find God and forgiveness? Jesus answers her seriously.
verseByVerse.note: “This mountain” is Mount Gerizim, where the Samaritans worshipped; a Samaritan temple had stood there until the Jews destroyed it more than a century before.

parallels.desc: the blessing on Mount Gerizim
the place the LORD will choose

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells her, addressing her as “woman”, to believe him: the time is coming when they will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.

Believe me. A unique phrase in the Gospels.

Neither … nor. The question of holy places is about to be made obsolete. With Jesus himself as the true temple (2:19–21), worship is no longer tied to a location. The destruction of the Jerusalem temple in AD 70 confirmed it.

The Father. Jesus introduces a Samaritan woman to God as Father.

parallels.desc: in every place incense will be offered to my name

verseByVerse.quote: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Samaritans worship what they do not know; the Jews worship what they know, for salvation comes from the Jews. But the time is coming, and has now arrived, when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is looking for such people to worship him.

You do not know. Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses and rejected the prophets and the Writings, which revealed more of God and his Messiah. Jesus does not pretend all religions are equally true.

Salvation is from the Jews. The Messiah is a Jew, of David’s line (Romans 9:4–5). God’s plan runs through Israel for the world.

Now here. With Jesus, the future has arrived.

The Father seeks. Astonishing: God is looking for worshippers. He sought this woman.
verseByVerse.note: The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses.

parallels.desc: out of Zion shall go the law

verseByVerse.quote: "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.

God is spirit. Not physical, not confined to a place (1 Kings 8:27; Acts 17:24–25). One of John’s three great statements: God is spirit, light (1 John 1:5) and love (1 John 4:8).

In spirit and truth. In the Spirit, whom Jesus gives, and in truth, through Jesus, who is the truth (14:6). Not merely sincere inwardness, but worship enabled by the Spirit and shaped by God’s revelation in Christ.

Where Christians differ: forms of worship. Liturgical traditions stress structure and beauty; free-church traditions stress spontaneity; the Reformed regulative principle holds that public worship should include only what Scripture commands (Westminster Confession 21.1). This verse does not settle the forms, but it governs all of them: worship must be by the Spirit and according to truth. Verdict: the app’s Reformed instinct to let Scripture shape public worship, held with charity: reading, preaching, prayer, song, sacraments; neither a building nor a style makes worship true.

For worship. You can worship God today at the sink, the desk or the hospital bed, by his Spirit and through his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: "The woman said to him, 'I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.' Jesus said to her, 'I who speak to you am he.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman says she knows that Messiah, called Christ, is coming, and when he comes he will explain everything to them. Jesus tells her, “I who speak to you am he.”

Explain everything. The Samaritan hope was of a teacher-prophet (Deuteronomy 18:15–18).

I am he. Literally “I am, the one speaking to you.” Jesus’ first open claim to be Messiah in John, made not to the religious leaders but to a Samaritan woman with a broken past. And the “I am” recalls God’s name (Exodus 3:14), which John will make much of (6:20; 8:58; 18:5–6).

For worship. The Christ reveals himself to the outsider. Praise him for coming to you.
verseByVerse.note: The Samaritans expected a coming prophet like Moses. Jesus’ “I who speak to you am he” is literally “I am, the one speaking to you.”

verseByVerse.quote: Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, "What do you seek?" or, "Why are you talking with her?" So the woman left her water jar and went away into town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just then his disciples come back. They are amazed that he is talking with a woman, but no one asks what he wants or why he is talking with her. Then the woman leaves her water jar and goes into town.

Marvelled. At a rabbi talking with a woman, never mind a Samaritan. Their silence shows respect, and perhaps disapproval.

The water jar left. She came for water and forgot it. A small, telling detail: she has found what she was really thirsty for. Perhaps also so that Jesus could drink.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself what errand you are so absorbed in that you would not leave it for Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to the people, "Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?" They went out of the town and were coming to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She tells the people to come and see a man who told her everything she ever did. Could this be the Christ? They leave the town and make their way to him.

The people. The very people she may have avoided at noon. Her shame is replaced by witness.

Everything I ever did. An exaggeration of joy: he knew it all and did not reject her.

A question. She does not argue; she invites, and wonders aloud. Humble witness is powerful.

On a Tuesday. You do not need theological training to say “Come and see.” Tell people what Jesus has done for you.

verseByVerse.quote: Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, "Rabbi, eat." But he said to them, "I have food to eat that you do not know about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meanwhile the disciples urge him to eat. But he tells them he has food to eat that they know nothing about.

Rabbi, eat. They have brought food (v. 8) and see he is tired.

Other food. As with water (v. 10), Jesus speaks of a deeper nourishment.

parallels.desc: man shall not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples said to one another, "Has anyone brought him something to eat?" Jesus said to them, "My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the disciples ask one another whether someone has brought him food. Jesus says that his food is to do the will of the one who sent him and to finish his work.

Literal again. Even the disciples misunderstand.

My food. Deuteronomy 8:3, quoted in Jesus’ temptation (Matthew 4:4). Doing God’s will sustains him more than bread.

To accomplish. To complete. On the cross he will say, “It is finished” (19:30; 17:4).

On a Tuesday. Work done for God can feed the soul. When obedience is costly, remember that it is also nourishing.

parallels.desc: having accomplished the work

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you not say, 'There are yet four months, then comes the harvest'? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest. Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks whether they do not say there are still four months until harvest. He tells them to open their eyes and look: the fields are already white for harvest. The reaper is already receiving wages and gathering a crop for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together.

Four months. Perhaps a proverb about the interval between sowing and harvest, or a time note: it was about four months to harvest, so December to January.

White for harvest. Grain ripening to pale gold. Perhaps, as Jesus speaks, the Samaritans in white garments are streaming across the fields towards them (v. 30).

Rejoice together. In the age of the Messiah, sowing and reaping overlap (Amos 9:13).

On a Tuesday. Look up. People around you may be more ready for the gospel than you think.
verseByVerse.note: Crops were sown in winter and harvested in spring; “four months” was roughly the gap between sowing and harvest, and the saying may have been proverbial.

parallels.desc: the ploughman shall overtake the reaper

verseByVerse.quote: "For here the saying holds true, 'One sows and another reaps.' I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here the saying holds true that one sows and another reaps. Jesus has sent them to reap what they did not labour for. Others have done the hard work, and they have entered into the fruit of it.

Others laboured. The prophets, John the Baptist, the woman herself, and above all Jesus. The disciples will reap where others sowed (Acts 8:4–17, when the gospel comes to Samaria).

No room for pride. No harvest is ours alone (1 Corinthians 3:6–9).

On a Tuesday. If you are sowing with no visible fruit, take heart: someone will reap. If you are reaping, honour those who sowed.

parallels.desc: cities you did not build
I planted, Apollos watered

verseByVerse.quote: Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman's testimony, "He told me all that I ever did." So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many Samaritans from that town believe in him because of the woman’s testimony that he told her everything she ever did. So when they come to him, they ask him to stay with them, and he stays two days.

Her testimony. The same word used of John the Baptist’s witness (1:7). A Samaritan woman is the first evangelist in John’s Gospel to bring a whole town.

Stay. The word “abide” again (1:38–39). A Jew lodges with Samaritans.

For worship. Thank God for those whose simple testimony first pointed you to Christ.

parallels.desc: Samaria receives the word

verseByVerse.quote: And many more believed because of his word. They said to the woman, "It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many more believe because of his word. They tell the woman that they no longer believe just because of what she said, for they have heard him themselves and know that he really is the Saviour of the world.

Second-hand to first-hand. Testimony brings people to Jesus; his own word confirms faith. Good evangelism aims to introduce people to Christ himself, especially through Scripture.

Saviour of the world. Not of Jews only. A title used of Roman emperors; here Samaritans give it to Jesus. In the New Testament only here and 1 John 4:14.

For worship. Join the Samaritans’ confession: this is indeed the Saviour of the world, and mine.

parallels.desc: the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 43–54 — The Official's Son: The Second Sign
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After two days Jesus goes on to Galilee, though he has said a prophet is not honoured in his own country. The Galileans receive him, having seen what he did at the festival in Jerusalem. He returns to Cana, where he turned water into wine. A royal official from Capernaum, whose son is dying, hears that Jesus is back and comes to beg him to come and heal the boy. Jesus says that unless people see miraculous signs they will not believe. The official pleads with him to come before his child dies. Jesus tells him to go home: his son will live. The man takes Jesus at his word and sets off. On the way his servants meet him with news that the boy is alive and well. Asking when he improved, he learns the fever left at one in the afternoon the day before, the very hour Jesus spoke. He and his whole household believe. This is the second sign Jesus performs after coming from Judea to Galilee.
verseByVerse.theology:
The second sign illustrates the highest form of faith: believing the word of Jesus without the supporting evidence of a visible miracle. Jesus speaks ('your son will live'), the official believes, and he goes. The confirmation comes later — the servants meet him with the news, and when he checks the timing, it matches exactly. This is the progression of faith in John's Gospel: sign-faith (the disciples at Cana), word-faith (the official), and ultimately cross-and-resurrection-faith (Thomas). Each stage is genuine faith; each stage is a step deeper into trust in the person of Jesus.

The two Cana signs are numbered (2:11; 4:54) and the counting then stops for the rest of the book, which means the numbering exists only to tie these two together. They frame everything between: a member of the ruling council who could not follow the plainest thing, and a Samaritan woman who understood enough to fetch a town.

Watch what changes between them. At the wedding Jesus was present, the water was in front of him, and he instructed servants who were standing there. Here he is twenty miles away and does nothing but speak. The first sign needed his hands on the situation; the second needed only his voice, and the voice worked across a day's journey as though the journey were not there. The escalation is the direction of the whole book — and it prepares the position every reader after the ascension occupies: no touch, no presence, no visible confirmation, only a word and a distance and the walking. John says at the close that he wrote it down so that people who were never in the room might believe (20:30-31).

Note also that the man believes twice. In verse 50 he believed the word — trust in a promise about his son. In verse 53 he himself believed, with no object named, which in this Gospel is the word for what a person does about Christ rather than about a request. The household followed him; that is not a formula and must never be used to reproach faithful people whose households have not, but it is worth noting what they had to go on — a man who came home, a boy who was well, and a father who could tell them the hour.
verseByVerse.examples:
The official's faith is remarkable because he believes before he sees — he accepts the word of Jesus as sufficient ground for confidence when everything he can see argues for despair. This is the pattern of all mature faith: not the absence of evidence but trust in the word of the one who cannot lie, prior to the confirming experience.

The finest detail in the episode is one word in the servants' report: the fever left him yesterday at the seventh hour. Jesus spoke at about one in the afternoon, and Capernaum is some twenty miles away and downhill — a distance a determined man could nearly cover by nightfall. The father did not cover it. He stopped for the night and came down the next day. Nobody whose only son is dying stops for the night if any part of him is still calculating. The most convincing evidence that this man took Christ at his word is that he did not hurry home.

Verse 50 is where the miracle actually sits, and it happens before the other one is known about. He had walked all day for one thing — to bring Jesus back down to the house — and he is sent home without him. Everything he came for is refused. What he has instead is five words about a child who was at the point of death when he left. And he went. Every hour of that walk the alternative explanation was available: that he had been fobbed off, that he should have insisted, that a real healer would have come.

The pastoral note belongs to the father's prayer, which was a bad one by any measure — no theology, no composure, one sentence repeated under pressure — and was answered immediately and generously. Nothing in the account suggests Jesus was waiting for a better-formed request. And his original assumption, that God must be brought to the place, should be treated gently rather than corrected: it is what people ask when they love somebody and are frightened. The answer he received was not smaller than the one he asked for. It was the same answer, delivered without the twenty miles.

verseByVerse.quote: After the two days he departed for Galilee. (For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the two days he leaves for Galilee. Jesus himself had stated that a prophet has no honour in his own home country.

His own country. In the other Gospels, Nazareth (Mark 6:4). In John, perhaps Judea, Jesus’ true “home” as the Messiah from Bethlehem and the city of the temple, where he had been coolly received; or Galilee, where the welcome (v. 45) is shallow, based on signs. Verdict: probably Galilee, where the welcome was enthusiasm, not true honour (v. 48).

On a Tuesday. Witness can be hardest among those who know us best. Do not be discouraged by family indifference (7:5).

verseByVerse.quote: So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he arrives in Galilee, the Galileans welcome him, because they had seen everything he did in Jerusalem at the festival, since they too had been there.

A welcome of a kind. They are impressed by signs (2:23). Their enthusiasm will cool when he refuses to be the kind of Messiah they want (6:15, 66).

verseByVerse.quote: So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill. When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he comes again to Cana in Galilee, where he had turned water into wine. In Capernaum there is a royal official whose son is ill. Hearing that Jesus has come from Judea to Galilee, he goes to him and begs him to come down and heal his son, who is close to death.

A royal official. Basilikos, probably an officer of Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, whom people called king. Perhaps a Gentile; certainly a man of power, helpless before death.

Come down. Capernaum is about 20 miles away and some 1,300 feet lower, by the lake. He thinks Jesus must be present to heal.

The same as the centurion? Matthew 8:5–13 and Luke 7:1–10 tell of a centurion’s servant healed at a distance in Capernaum. The details differ (servant or son, Jewish elders, the centurion’s humility). Verdict: probably a different event; Jesus healed many.

On a Tuesday. Illness in a child humbles every parent. Bring your fears to Jesus, as this father did.
verseByVerse.note: The official was probably in the service of Herod Antipas. Capernaum lay down by the lake, about 20 miles from Cana.

parallels.desc: a similar healing of a centurion’s servant

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to him, "Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says to him that unless they see signs and wonders, they will not believe.

You plural. A rebuke to the Galileans generally: they want spectacle.

Signs and wonders. The only time this phrase appears in John. Jesus does perform signs, but faith that demands them is immature (20:29).

What it does not mean. Not a refusal to help, but a test that draws out stronger faith.
verseByVerse.note: The “you” here is plural — Jesus speaks to the Galileans in general.

verseByVerse.quote: The official said to him, "Sir, come down before my child dies." Jesus said to him, "Go; your son will live." The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The official pleads with him, calling him Sir, to come down before his child dies. Jesus tells him to go: his son will live. The man believes the word Jesus speaks and sets off.

Desperate faith. He does not argue about signs; he simply begs.

Go; your son lives. Literally “your son lives”, present tense. No touch, no visit, only a word.

He believed the word. Faith now rests not on seeing but on Jesus’ promise. The model for every reader of this Gospel (20:29–31).

On a Tuesday. Faith often means going home before you see the answer, trusting what Christ has said.

For worship. Thank Jesus whose word is enough.

parallels.desc: he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he is still on the way down, his servants meet him with the news that his son is living.

The next day. He apparently did not rush home that night (v. 52): a sign of settled trust.

Living. The servants use the same words Jesus used.

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him, "Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him." The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him, "Your son will live." And he himself believed, and all his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asks them at what time the boy began to improve, and they tell him the fever left him at one o’clock the previous afternoon. The father realises that was the very hour Jesus told him his son would live. He and his whole household believe.

The seventh hour. About 1 p.m. The timing confirms that Jesus’ word did it.

Believed again. His faith grows from trusting the word (v. 50) to settled faith in Jesus, with his household. Faith is a journey.

His household. Family and servants. Compare Cornelius, Lydia and the jailer (Acts 10:2; 16:15, 34).

For worship. Psalm 107:20: he sent out his word and healed them.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the seventh hour was about 1 p.m.

parallels.desc: he believed, with his entire household

verseByVerse.quote: This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the second sign Jesus does after coming from Judea to Galilee.

The second sign. Both Cana signs follow a similar shape: a request, an apparent rebuff, persistent trust, a word, a result discovered by servants, and faith. Together they frame a section showing Jesus as the giver of new joy and new life.

Life through his word. The theme of the next chapter: the Son gives life to whom he will (5:21, 24).

parallels.desc: the first sign

4.title: The Woman at the Well
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John<sup>2</sup>(although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),<sup>3</sup>he left Judea and departed again for Galilee.<sup>4</sup>And he had to pass through Samaria.<sup>5</sup>So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.<sup>6</sup>Jacob’s well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.<sup>7</sup>A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”<sup>8</sup>(For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.)<sup>9</sup>The Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)<sup>10</sup>Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ’Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”<sup>11</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water?<sup>12</sup>Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock.”<sup>13</sup>Jesus said to her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again,<sup>14</sup>but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.”<sup>15</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.”<sup>16</sup>Jesus said to her, “Go, call your husband, and come here.”<sup>17</sup>The woman answered him, “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her, “You are right in saying, ’I have no husband’;<sup>18</sup>for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true.”<sup>19</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.<sup>20</sup>Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.”<sup>21</sup>Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father.<sup>22</sup>You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.<sup>23</sup>But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him.<sup>24</sup>God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”<sup>25</sup>The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.”<sup>26</sup>Jesus said to her, “I who speak to you am he.”<sup>27</sup>Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, “What do you seek?” or, “Why are you talking with her?”<sup>28</sup>So the woman left her water jar and went away into town and said to the people,<sup>29</sup>“Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?”<sup>30</sup>They went out of the town and were coming to him.<sup>31</sup>Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.”<sup>32</sup>But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you do not know about.”<sup>33</sup>So the disciples said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.<sup>35</sup>Do you not say, ’There are yet four months, then comes the harvest’? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest.<sup>36</sup>Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together.<sup>37</sup>For here the saying holds true, ’One sows and another reaps.’<sup>38</sup>I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”<sup>39</sup>Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman’s testimony, “He told me all that I ever did.”<sup>40</sup>So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.<sup>41</sup>And many more believed because of his word.<sup>42</sup>They said to the woman, “It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world.”<sup>43</sup>After the two days he departed for Galilee.<sup>44</sup>(For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.)<sup>45</sup>So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.<sup>46</sup>So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill.<sup>47</sup>When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.<sup>48</sup>So Jesus said to him, “Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe.”<sup>49</sup>The official said to him, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”<sup>50</sup>Jesus said to him, “Go; your son will live.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.<sup>51</sup>As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.<sup>52</sup>So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him, “Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.”<sup>53</sup>The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him, “Your son will live.” And he himself believed, and all his household.<sup>54</sup>This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.
4.overview:
Chapter 3 showed Jesus with a respected Jewish teacher at night; chapter 4 shows him with an unnamed Samaritan woman at noon. Travelling north through Samaria, tired and thirsty, he sits by Jacob’s well and asks her for a drink, crossing three barriers at once: race, sex and religion. He offers her “living water”, a spring of eternal life welling up inside, and she misunderstands, as Nicodemus did. Then he gently exposes her life: five husbands, and the present man not her husband. She turns to the old dispute between Samaritans and Jews about where to worship; Jesus answers that the hour has come when the place no longer matters, for the Father seeks worshippers in spirit and truth. When she speaks of the coming Messiah, he tells her plainly, “I who speak to you am he.”

She leaves her water jar and brings the town to “come, see a man who told me all that I ever did.” Meanwhile Jesus tells his puzzled disciples that his food is to do his Father’s will, and that the fields are already white for harvest. Many Samaritans believe, first through her testimony and then through his own word, and confess him as “the Savior of the world.” Back in Cana, a royal official begs Jesus to come and heal his dying son; Jesus simply says, “Go; your son will live,” and the man believes and goes. His servants meet him with the news that the fever left at the very hour Jesus spoke. This is the second sign: the word of Jesus gives life at a distance. Together the stories show the gospel crossing every boundary, and faith growing from hearing to trusting his word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At a festival in Jerusalem, Jesus visits the pool of Bethesda by the Sheep Gate, where crowds of the blind, lame and paralysed lie under its colonnades. One man has been disabled for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks whether he wants to be healed. The man complains that no one helps him into the water when it stirs, and others always get there first. Jesus commands him to stand, lift his mat and walk, and at once he does. Because it is the Sabbath, the authorities rebuke him for carrying the mat; he blames the man who healed him, whose name he does not know, as Jesus has disappeared in the crowd. Later Jesus meets him in the temple and warns him to leave his sin behind, lest something worse befall him. The man reports to the authorities that it was Jesus, and they start to harass Jesus for Sabbath work. Jesus replies that his Father is still at work and so is he. Now they are more intent on killing him, for he not only breaks the Sabbath but claims God as his own Father, making himself God’s equal.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sabbath healing reveals Jesus's divine authority by the very nature of the opposition it generates. When Jesus says 'My Father is working until now, and I am working,' the Jewish leaders understand immediately what he is claiming: equality with God, the same authority over the Sabbath that God the Father has. This is not a misunderstanding that Jesus corrects; it is a correct understanding that Jesus confirms. The discourse that follows is the most comprehensive statement of the Son's relationship to the Father in the Gospels: the Son does nothing on his own, only what he sees the Father doing; the Father has given all judgment to the Son; the Son gives life to whom he will.

The Sabbath argument lands inside a debate the rabbis were already having. They knew God does not stop working on the seventh day — children are born and people die on it, and the giving of life and the judging of the dead were the standard examples of divine work that never ceases. The accepted solution was that God is exempt, since the whole universe is his house and he carries nothing out of it. Jesus takes that exemption for himself (My Father is working until now, and I am working) and then, over the next few verses, claims precisely the two works it was famous for: giving life (v. 21) and executing judgment (v. 22).

Verse 18 must not be softened. John does not write that they thought he was making himself equal with God, or that they misunderstood; he reports it as what was happening. The narrator agrees with their reading of the words and disagrees only with what they did about it. This closes off the idea that Jesus was a teacher of ethics whom his followers later inflated: nobody organises an execution over the golden rule. The possessive is the point — his own Father, private and particular, in a way that made his working and God's working one working.

Neither charge is right as they put it. He was not breaking the Sabbath; he was breaking their reading of it, and never once broke the law of God. And he was not making himself equal with God either — for the opposite reason. He made himself nothing. He was stating what was already the case, which is a larger offence than the one they charged.
verseByVerse.examples:
The thirty-eight-year illness is not incidental but emblematic: the man has exhausted every human resource and lies waiting for something that never comes by human effort. Jesus's intervention is sovereign and uninvited — the man does not ask for healing, does not know who Jesus is, and does not believe in him before the miracle. The healing comes entirely from Christ's initiative, which is the pattern of all saving grace. 'Do you want to be healed?' is the most searching question Jesus could ask, because chronic suffering can become a settled identity that is comfortable in its own way.

Do you want to be healed? sounds close to an insult to a man who has lain by a healing pool for thirty-eight years, and Jesus does not ask it of everyone he heals, which means it is meant for this history. Something happens to a want that has been disappointed for that long: it goes quiet, gets managed, and turns into a routine, until a life is built around the waiting and the waiting is the life. That is not weakness of character; most people can manage it in months. The question is the most respectful thing in the passage — he does not heal the man over his head, but asks somebody who has not been asked anything in decades what he actually wants.

This is the verse for the reader who long ago stopped asking for something: the marriage that has been like this for years, the child who does not call, the prayer abandoned around its fifth anniversary. The test is whether one can still say plainly what would be different if God moved — or whether the answer comes out as an explanation of why it will not happen, which is exactly what the man says next.

Two further mercies are worth naming. The healing came unrequested to a man who had given up asking, without faith, without confession, without his even knowing the name of the one who did it — grace arriving on its own initiative. And the mat was not left at the pool: a healed man walking away is a private mercy nobody need ever know about, but a healed man carrying his bed through the city is a public claim, the evidence held up in both arms. It is possible to be genuinely healed and entirely discreet about it. He is told to pick it up.

verseByVerse.quote: After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some time later there is a Jewish festival, and Jesus goes up to Jerusalem. In the city, by the Sheep Gate, there is a pool called Bethesda in Aramaic, surrounded by five covered colonnades.

Which feast? Unnamed; perhaps Tabernacles, Passover or Pentecost. Textual note. Some manuscripts read “the feast”, which would point to Passover or Tabernacles. Verdict: “a feast” is better attested; John does not say which.

Bethesda. Probably “house of mercy” or “house of the outpouring”. Textual note. Manuscripts also read Bethsaida and Bethzatha. The Copper Scroll from Qumran names a site “Beth Eshdathayin”, supporting Bethesda. Verdict: Bethesda.

Five porches. Once dismissed as symbolic (the five books of Moses), but excavations near St Anne’s Church have uncovered two large pools with colonnades on four sides and one across the dividing wall: exactly five. John knew Jerusalem before AD 70.

Is. Present tense: “there is a pool”. Some argue John wrote before the city was destroyed; or he uses a vivid present.
verseByVerse.note: The Sheep Gate was in the north wall, near the temple. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Bethsaida. Archaeologists have uncovered twin pools there with colonnades on four sides and one across the middle.

parallels.desc: the Sheep Gate

verseByVerse.quote: In these lay a multitude of invalids — blind, lame, and paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In these colonnades lie a great number of sick people: blind, lame and paralysed.

A picture of humanity. A crowd of the helpless, waiting for a cure that rarely comes.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add the end of verse 3 and verse 4: that they waited for the water to move, because an angel stirred it at times and the first one in was healed (KJV). The earliest manuscripts lack it, and some that have it mark it as doubtful. Verdict: not original; a scribe’s explanation of verse 7, reflecting a popular belief. Some think the pool was part of a healing shrine, perhaps to the pagan healing god Asclepius in Roman times.

What it does not mean. Scripture does not endorse the legend. Jesus bypasses the pool entirely.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 4, about an angel stirring the water and the first one in being healed — a popular belief explaining why the sick waited there.

verseByVerse.quote: One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, "Do you want to be healed?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One man there has been ill for thirty-eight years. When Jesus sees him lying there and knows he has been ill a long time, he asks whether he wants to be healed.

Thirty-eight years. Longer than many people then lived. Perhaps also an echo of Israel’s thirty-eight years in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 2:14).

Jesus chooses. Out of many sick people, Jesus goes to one, not because he asked, but because Jesus saw and knew. Grace is sovereign and personal.

Do you want to be healed? Not a cruel question. After decades of illness, healing would mean a new life, work and responsibility. Some prefer their familiar misery.

On a Tuesday. Jesus asks you the same question about a sin, a habit or a grudge: do you really want to be made well?
verseByVerse.note: Thirty-eight years may echo Israel’s thirty-eight years of wandering before entering the land (Deut 2:14), though John does not draw the link.

parallels.desc: thirty-eight years until that generation perished

verseByVerse.quote: The sick man answered him, "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sick man answers, calling him Sir, that he has no one to put him into the pool when the water is stirred up; while he is trying to get there, someone else goes down ahead of him.

No answer. He does not say yes. He explains why he cannot be healed. He is focused on the pool, the method he believes in.

No one. A lonely man in a crowd. The stirring water was probably an intermittent spring.

On a Tuesday. Notice the lonely in crowded places: hospitals, care homes, churches. Be the one who helps.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Get up, take up your bed, and walk." And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells him to get up, pick up his mat and walk. At once the man is healed; he picks up his mat and walks. That day is a Sabbath.

A word of command. No pool, no touch, no request of faith. Jesus’ word does what it says (Mark 2:11).

At once. Thirty-eight years of wasted muscle restored instantly.

The Sabbath. Mentioned last, like a sting in the tail. The Mishnah lists carrying an object from one domain to another among thirty-nine forbidden kinds of work, drawing on Jeremiah 17:21–22 and Nehemiah 13:15–19.
verseByVerse.note: The bed was a light mat. Carrying a load on the Sabbath was forbidden by tradition, drawing on the prophets.

parallels.desc: a similar command to a paralytic
bear no burden on the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, "It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Jewish leaders tell the healed man that it is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for him to carry his mat.

Blind to the miracle. A man crippled for thirty-eight years is walking, and they see only a breach of regulations.

Not lawful. Not by the law of Moses, which forbade work but did not define carrying a mat as work, but by the tradition built around it (Mark 7:8).

On a Tuesday. Religious rules can blind us to God’s grace in someone’s life. Rejoice first; question later, if at all.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities.

verseByVerse.quote: But he answered them, "The man who healed me, that man said to me, 'Take up your bed, and walk.'" They asked him, "Who is the man who said to you, 'Take up your bed and walk'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answers that the man who healed him told him to pick up his mat and walk. They ask who the man is who told him that.

Blame-shifting. He passes the responsibility to his healer.

Who told you? They ask not “who healed you?” but “who told you to break the Sabbath?” The miracle does not interest them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The healed man does not know who it was, because Jesus had slipped away into the crowd there.

No faith required. The man did not know who Jesus was. Jesus healed him before he knew him: grace before knowledge.

Withdrawn. Jesus avoids publicity.

verseByVerse.quote: "Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, 'See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.' The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Later Jesus finds him in the temple and tells him that he has been made well. He must stop sinning, or something worse may happen to him. The man goes away and tells the Jewish leaders that it was Jesus who healed him.

Jesus found him. Jesus seeks him out again, for his soul.

Sin no more. As to the woman in 8:11 (a passage of disputed authenticity). Whether this man’s illness was caused by sin is not said. Jesus elsewhere denies a simple link (9:2–3).

Something worse. Final judgment (v. 29) is worse than thirty-eight years of paralysis.

Where Christians differ: sin and sickness. Some teach that all illness results from personal sin or lack of faith. Scripture teaches that sickness entered the world through sin (Romans 5:12; 8:20–22), that occasionally a particular sin brings illness (1 Corinthians 11:30), but that usually no personal link should be assumed (John 9:3; Job). Verdict: never tell a sick person their illness is their fault; do call everyone to turn from sin.

The man tells. Whether innocently or as an informer, he reports Jesus. Contrast the blind man of chapter 9, who defends Jesus. Not every healing leads to faith.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus does not say all illness is punishment for sin, but warns that sin leads to worse than illness.

parallels.desc: go, and from now on sin no more

verseByVerse.quote: And this was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered them, "My Father is working until now, and I am working."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Jesus does these things on the Sabbath, the Jewish leaders begin to persecute him. But Jesus answers that his Father is still working, and he is working too.

Persecuting. The beginning of the hostility that leads to the cross.

My Father is working. Jewish teachers debated how God could rest on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2–3) yet keep the world in being; they concluded that God works on the Sabbath, sustaining life, giving birth and death, and judging. Jesus claims the same prerogative: he works as his Father works.

My Father. Not “our Father”. Jesus claims a unique relationship.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath. Compare Mark 2:23–3:6. Verdict: the app’s view that the Sabbath finds its fulfilment in Christ, who gives true rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10); the Lord’s Day is a glad privilege for worship, rest and mercy, not a burden of rules.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish teachers recognised that God keeps working on the Sabbath, sustaining the world; Jesus claims the same right.

parallels.desc: lord even of the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is why the Jewish leaders try even harder to kill him: not only is he breaking the Sabbath, but he is calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.

They understood. Some modern writers claim Jesus never claimed to be God. His enemies heard the claim clearly (10:33; 19:7).

Equal with God. John’s narrative comment confirms they understood him correctly (1:1; 20:28). Jesus’ reply (vv. 19–30) does not deny it but explains it.

For worship. Worship the Son as equal with the Father, as the church has always confessed: “God from God, Light from Light” (Nicene Creed).

parallels.desc: you, being a man, make yourself God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–47 — The Son's Authority: Witness and Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus explains that the Son acts in perfect union with the Father, doing whatever he sees the Father do, because the Father loves him and shows him all things. Like the Father, the Son gives life to whom he wills, and the Father has entrusted all judgment to him, so that the Son may be honoured as the Father is. Whoever hears Jesus and trusts the Father has eternal life already and has passed beyond condemnation. Even now the spiritually dead hear his voice and live, and one day everyone in the tombs will hear it and rise, to life or to judgment. Jesus does not testify alone: John the Baptist bore witness, Jesus’ works bear witness, the Father bears witness, and so do the Scriptures, which his hearers study while refusing to come to him for life. They seek honour from each other rather than from God. Moses, their hope, will accuse them, for he wrote about Jesus; if they do not believe Moses, they will not believe Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
The discourse on the Son's authority establishes that Jesus is not merely a great teacher or prophet but the one to whom the Father has delegated the twin divine prerogatives of life-giving and judgment. These are not shared with any creature; they belong to God alone. Yet the Father has given them to the Son precisely so that all will honor the Son as they honor the Father. The four witnesses — John, works, Father, Scripture — are not offered as proofs that compel belief but as witnesses whose rejection reveals the condition of the rejecting heart: no love of God, no desire for the glory that comes from God.

Life in himself (v. 26) is the highest thing said about God in the chapter. Everything that lives has life on loan — a tree from soil and light, a man from food and breath — and every such supply can be cut, which is why everything that lives also dies. To have life in himself is to hold it as a property rather than a supply, with nothing behind it that could fail; theologians call it aseity, and it belongs to God alone. That the Father granted the Son to have it is not an event in time and does not make it derived in the ordinary sense: it states the eternal relation between Father and Son. What the Father is, the Son is.

Verse 23 fixes the measure of honour with two words — just as — and forecloses the most popular way of handling Jesus. There is no arrangement in which a person keeps God and declines Christ; it is not offered. And the direction is the reverse of what is usually assumed: the Father has given life and judgment to the Son precisely so that all may honour the Son. Withholding that honour is not modesty on God's behalf but a failure to give the Father what he has said he wants.

Verse 29 sounds like salvation by works and cannot be, since verse 24 gives life to whoever hears my word and believes. The good and the evil are evidence rather than currency — the visible form of a life that had already crossed from death to life, or had not. And the apparent contradiction between 5:31 (if I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true) and 8:14 (even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true) resolves by what each answers: the first concerns legal standing, the second factual accuracy. He does not need corroboration in order to be right; he offers it because they need it in order to be persuaded.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's claim to give life to whom he will (v. 21) and to execute judgment (v. 22) is either the most arrogant statement in human history or the most important truth in human history — there is no middle ground. The discourse forces a decision: either this man is deluded and dangerous, or he is who he says he is. The sequence of judgments in the discourse — present hearing (v. 24), coming resurrection (vv. 28-29) — establishes that the final judgment is already operative in every person's response to Christ.

Verse 35 is the saddest in the chapter and the tense is what makes it unbearable. He was a burning and shining lamp — the ordinary household oil lamp, the thing carried into a room after dark, and this Gospel has been careful that the Baptist was not the light (1:8). And they were willing to rejoice in it for a while. The whole country went out to the Jordan; it was the religious event of the decade; and it lasted about as long as such things last. By the time Jesus speaks, John's ministry is over. The mechanism has not changed — there is a way of consuming preaching as an experience, genuinely moved and warmly discussing it afterwards, and ending the season exactly where one started. The enjoyment is not fraudulent, which is what makes it dangerous: it feels like a response and it is a reaction.

Verse 39's search was no casual reading — these men counted the letters and knew which word stood at the centre of the Torah. They got a preposition wrong: they thought the life was located in the text, obtainable by handling it. Jesus does not deny that Scripture gives life; he denies the address. The distance between the scroll and the person was about four feet, and they would not cross it. It is entirely possible to conduct a serious study of Scripture as a closed system — the tracing of themes, the resolving of difficulties, the satisfaction of a passage coming clear — and for the whole exercise to terminate in itself. The test takes ten seconds: after the last passage studied, did it end in knowing something, or in wanting him?

Verse 44 is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus calls believing impossible for a stated reason, and the reason is an economy. Doxa means both glory and reputation, and these men held a currency they issued to one another — standing, deference, the seat at the front — which can only be earned inside the system and therefore only kept by not leaving. The way out is in the same verse and is not an instruction to care less about honour: the glory that comes from the only God. He does not tell them to want no approval. He tells them they are seeking it from a bankrupt issuer.

And the chapter's arrangement is its own argument. It opens with a man who could not reach the water, had nobody, and did not know the name of the one who healed him — and he was made whole. It closes with the best-taught men in the nation, holding every witness heaven could produce, who would not come. He got up. The men with all the evidence stayed sitting down.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus said to them, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells them solemnly that the Son can do nothing on his own initiative, only what he sees the Father doing; whatever the Father does, the Son does as well. For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything he is doing, and he will show him greater works than these, to their amazement.

Nothing of his own accord. Not weakness, but perfect unity. The Son never acts independently of the Father, because he shares the Father’s will and nature.

Whatever the Father does. A creature could do some things God does; only God could do everything God does.

Where Christians differ: is the Son subordinate? Arians in the fourth century, and Jehovah’s Witnesses today, read “the Son can do nothing” as proof that he is a lesser being. Some recent evangelicals have taught an eternal subordination of the Son’s will to the Father. The historic doctrine (Nicaea, Augustine, the Reformers) holds that the Father, Son and Spirit are one in essence and will, that their works are inseparable, and that the Son’s dependence expresses his eternal relation to the Father as Son and his humble obedience as incarnate. Verdict: equality of being, order of relations, one will: the Son does what the Father does because they are one God (10:30).

Greater works. Raising the dead and judging (vv. 21–22), and the resurrection itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whomever he wishes. The Father judges no one, but has entrusted all judgment to the Son.

Life-giver. Raising the dead was God’s prerogative (Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6; 2 Kings 5:7). The Son does it, and freely.

To whom he will. The Son’s sovereign will in salvation (compare 1:13; 6:37, 44). Grace is not owed.

All judgment. The Judge of all the earth (Genesis 18:25) has entrusted judgment to Jesus (Acts 17:31). The one who will judge you is the one who died for sinners.

parallels.desc: I kill and I make alive

verseByVerse.quote: "that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that everyone may honour the Son just as they honour the Father. Whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him.

Just as. Equal honour: worship. Isaiah 42:8: God will not give his glory to another. He gives it to the Son because the Son is not another God.

No honouring the Father without the Son. A claim that rules out treating Jesus as merely a great teacher, and rules out any religion that honours God while rejecting Christ (1 John 2:23).

For worship. Sing to Christ as to God, as the earliest Christians did (Pliny, about AD 112).

parallels.desc: no one who denies the Son has the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life. Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells them solemnly that whoever hears his word and believes the one who sent him has eternal life. He does not come into judgment but has passed from death to life. The hour is coming, and has now come, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.

Has eternal life. Present possession, not merely future hope.

Not into judgment. Not condemnation (3:18; Romans 8:1). Believers will appear before Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), but not to be condemned.

Passed from death to life. A completed move: spiritually dead people (Ephesians 2:1–5) are made alive by Christ’s voice.

Is now here. The “first resurrection” of the soul happens now, at conversion. Where Christians differ. Amillennialists see here support for reading Revelation 20:4–6 as the spiritual life believers have now, with one bodily resurrection of all at the end (vv. 28–29). Premillennialists see two bodily resurrections separated by the millennium. Verdict: the app’s amillennial view: a resurrection of the soul now (v. 25) and of the body for all at the last day (vv. 28–29).

For worship. Thank Christ that his voice reached you when you were dead.

parallels.desc: dead in trespasses, made alive

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself. And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself. And he has given him authority to judge, because he is the Son of Man.

Life in himself. Self-existent life, not borrowed: the life of God. The Father has eternally “given” it, not as to a creature, but in the eternal relationship of Father and Son (1:4).

Son of Man. The figure of Daniel 7:13–14 who receives dominion and judgment. Because he shares our humanity, he is a fitting Judge (Hebrews 4:15).

parallels.desc: one like a son of man given dominion

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They should not be amazed at this, for a time is coming when everyone in the tombs will hear his voice and come out: those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.

All. A single general resurrection of righteous and wicked (Daniel 12:2; Acts 24:15).

Hear his voice. As Lazarus will (11:43): a preview.

Done good, done evil. Where Christians differ: judged by works? Some read this as salvation by works. Others see a contradiction with verse 24. Reformed interpreters answer that good works are the evidence, not the ground, of salvation: those who have truly believed (v. 24) show it in the good they do (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:18). The final judgment publicly displays the reality of faith. Verdict: justification by faith alone, judgment according to works, with no contradiction.

The resurrection of judgment. The wicked are raised bodily to face condemnation (Matthew 10:28). The app’s traditional view of hell, held with sorrow.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, some to shame

verseByVerse.quote: "I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me. If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus can do nothing on his own. He judges as he hears, and his judgment is just, because he seeks not his own will but the will of the one who sent him. If he alone testifies about himself, his testimony is not valid.

Just judgment. A judge whose will is perfectly one with God’s cannot be corrupt (Isaiah 11:3–4).

Not true. In the legal sense: not admissible on its own. The law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus will call them.

A trial. The rest of the chapter reads like a court case in which the accused calls witnesses, and the accusers are found guilty.
verseByVerse.note: The law required two or three witnesses; a man’s testimony about himself did not count as valid evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: "There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is another who testifies about him, and he knows that the testimony this other gives about him is true.

Another. The Father (v. 37). Some think John the Baptist (v. 33), but Jesus is about to say that he does not depend on human testimony (v. 34).
verseByVerse.note: The other witness is probably the Father (v. 37), though some take it as John the Baptist (v. 33).

verseByVerse.quote: "You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth. Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sent messengers to John, and he testified to the truth. Not that Jesus accepts human testimony, but he mentions it so that they may be saved.

John’s witness. The delegation of 1:19–28. John pointed to Jesus.

That you may be saved. Even in controversy, Jesus seeks his opponents’ salvation.

On a Tuesday. In arguments, aim not to win but to help the other person to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John was a lamp that burned and gave light, and for a while they were happy to enjoy his light.

A lamp, not the light. John was a lamp (lychnos), lit from another source (1:8). Psalm 132:17: a lamp for the LORD’s anointed.

For a while. They enjoyed John as a novelty but did not follow where he pointed.

On a Tuesday. It is possible to enjoy a preacher without obeying his message. Do not be a sermon tourist.

parallels.desc: I have prepared a lamp for my anointed

verseByVerse.quote: "But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus has testimony greater than John’s. The works the Father has given him to complete, the very works he is doing, testify that the Father has sent him. And the Father who sent him has himself testified about him.

The works. The signs and the whole of his ministry (10:25, 37–38; 14:11).

The Father’s witness. Perhaps at Jesus’ baptism (1:33), and supremely in the Scriptures (v. 39) and the resurrection.

parallels.desc: the Father’s voice at the baptism

verseByVerse.quote: "His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen, and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have never heard the Father’s voice or seen his form, and his word does not live in them, because they do not believe the one he has sent.

Never heard, never seen. Unlike Israel at Sinai, who heard God’s voice (Deuteronomy 4:12; 5:24), or Moses, who saw his form (Numbers 12:8). The present generation, rejecting the Son, has no real access to God at all.

His word not abiding. They have the Scriptures in their hands but not in their hearts.

parallels.desc: you heard the sound of words, but saw no form

verseByVerse.quote: "You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They study the Scriptures diligently because they think that in them they have eternal life. These are the very Scriptures that testify about him, yet they refuse to come to him to have life.

Search. Probably indicative (“you search”) rather than a command. They studied intensely; rabbis counted letters.

The Scriptures testify about me. The key to the Old Testament is Christ (Luke 24:27, 44; 2 Corinthians 3:14–16). To read it without him is to miss its point.

Refuse to come. The problem is the will, not the intellect (v. 40; Matthew 23:37).

What it does not mean. Not that Bible study is bad, but that it is a means, not an end. Life is in Christ, to whom the Scriptures lead.

On a Tuesday. When you read the Bible, ask, “What does this show me of Christ?” and then come to him in prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not receive glory from people. But I know that you do not have the love of God within you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not accept glory from people. But he knows them, and knows they do not have the love of God in them.

Not seeking glory. His motive is not human applause.

The love of God. Probably their love for God. For all their religious zeal, they do not love God, or they would love his Son (8:42; 1 John 5:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him. How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has come in his Father’s name, and they do not accept him; if someone else comes in his own name, they will accept him. How can they believe when they accept glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?

In his own name. False messiahs who came on their own authority found followers. Josephus lists several; Simon bar Kokhba led a revolt in AD 132 and was hailed by Rabbi Akiva as Messiah.

Glory from one another. The craving for human approval makes faith impossible, because faith means accepting God’s verdict on us and on Christ (12:42–43).

On a Tuesday. Whose approval are you living for, colleagues, followers, family? Seek the praise that comes from God (Romans 2:29).

parallels.desc: Theudas and Judas the Galilean

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They should not think Jesus will accuse them before the Father. Their accuser is Moses, on whom they have set their hope. If they believed Moses, they would believe Jesus, because Moses wrote about him.

Moses the accuser. The one they trust as their advocate will testify against them, for the law itself condemns sinners (Deuteronomy 31:26; Romans 3:19–20).

He wrote of me. The promise of the seed (Genesis 3:15; 22:18), the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the bronze serpent (Numbers 21), the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15). Moses’ whole system pointed forward (Hebrews 10:1).

For worship. Thank God that the law which accuses us points us to the one who fulfils it for us (Romans 10:4).

parallels.desc: a witness against you

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if they do not believe what Moses wrote, how will they believe what Jesus says?

Writings and words. They revere Moses’ written law above spoken teaching. But their unbelief towards Moses’ real meaning blocks their faith in Jesus.

The unity of Scripture. Old and New Testaments stand or fall together. Christians who neglect the Old Testament lose much of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Read Moses this year, looking for Christ in Genesis to Deuteronomy.

5.title: The Son Has Life in Himself
5.text: <sup>1</sup>After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.<sup>3</sup>In these lay a multitude of invalids—blind, lame, and paralyzed.<sup>5</sup>One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years.<sup>6</sup>When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to be healed?”<sup>7</sup>The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me.”<sup>8</sup>Jesus said to him, “Get up, take up your bed, and walk.”<sup>9</sup>And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.<sup>10</sup>So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, “It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed.”<sup>11</sup>But he answered them, “The man who healed me, that man said to me, ’Take up your bed, and walk.’”<sup>12</sup>They asked him, “Who is the man who said to you, ’Take up your bed and walk’?”<sup>13</sup>Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.<sup>14</sup>Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, “See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.”<sup>15</sup>The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him.<sup>16</sup>And this was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath.<sup>17</sup>But Jesus answered them, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”<sup>18</sup>This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.<sup>19</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise.<sup>20</sup>For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.<sup>21</sup>For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will.<sup>22</sup>For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,<sup>23</sup>that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.<sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life.
