He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.<sup>25</sup>“Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.<sup>26</sup>For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.<sup>27</sup>And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.<sup>28</sup>Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice<sup>29</sup>and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.<sup>30</sup>“I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me.<sup>31</sup>If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true.<sup>32</sup>There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true.<sup>33</sup>You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth.<sup>34</sup>Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved.<sup>35</sup>He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.<sup>36</sup>But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me.<sup>37</sup>And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me. His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen,<sup>38</sup>and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent.<sup>39</sup>You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me,<sup>40</sup>yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life.<sup>41</sup>I do not receive glory from people.<sup>42</sup>But I know that you do not have the love of God within you.<sup>43</sup>I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me. 5.overview:
The third sign takes place in Jerusalem at the pool of Bethesda, whose five colonnades archaeologists have uncovered near the Sheep Gate. Among the crowds of sick people waiting for the water to stir lies a man who has been an invalid for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks whether he wants to be well, then tells him to pick up his mat and walk, and he does. But it is the Sabbath, and the authorities challenge the man for carrying his mat. When they learn it was Jesus, they begin to persecute him, and Jesus answers, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” They understand him exactly: he is calling God his own Father and making himself equal with God, and they now seek to kill him.

Jesus’ reply (vv. 19–47) is one of the richest statements of his identity in the Gospels. The Son does nothing on his own, but whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. Like the Father he gives life to whom he will, and the Father has entrusted all judgment to him, so that all should honour the Son as they honour the Father. Whoever hears his word and believes has eternal life now and has passed from death to life; and an hour is coming when all the dead will hear his voice and rise, to life or to judgment. Then, as in a courtroom, Jesus calls his witnesses: John the Baptist, his own works, the Father, and the Scriptures. His hearers search the Scriptures for life but refuse to come to the one they speak of; they seek glory from one another, not from God. Moses himself, whom they trust, will accuse them, for he wrote about Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some time later Jesus crosses the Sea of Galilee, followed by a huge crowd drawn by his healings. He goes up a hillside with his disciples. Passover is near. Seeing the crowd approach, he asks Philip where they could buy bread for them all, to test him, since he already knows what he will do. Philip calculates that even two hundred days’ wages would not buy each a mouthful. Andrew mentions a boy with five small barley loaves and two fish, but what use are they? Jesus has the people sit on the grass, about five thousand men. He takes the loaves, gives thanks and distributes them, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. When all are satisfied, he tells the disciples to collect the leftovers so that nothing is wasted, and they fill twelve baskets. Seeing the sign, the people declare him the Prophet who was to come, and Jesus, knowing they mean to seize him and make him king, withdraws alone to the hills. At evening the disciples set off by boat for Capernaum in the dark, without him. A strong wind whips up the lake. After rowing three or four miles they see Jesus walking on the water towards them and are terrified, but he tells them it is he and not to fear. They gladly take him aboard, and at once the boat reaches the shore.
verseByVerse.theology: The feeding miracle and the sea-walking are connected signs: together they reveal Jesus as the one who commands both provision and chaos, who is both the Lord of creation and the bread of life. 'It is I' on the water (v. 20) is followed at once by the great 'I am' discourses of John's Gospel, beginning with 'I am the bread of life' in the discourse that follows. The crowd that wants to make Jesus an earthly king misunderstands the sign: they want the bread without the Bread-giver, the miracle without the meaning, the provision without the person.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' plan to divide the available food among five thousand is not faithlessness but the appropriate response of stewards who account for what they have. Jesus's question to Philip — 'where are we to buy bread?' — is a test, not a request for information. The walking on water is the most theologically revealing of the nature miracles: Jesus walks on the sea, which in the Old Testament is the domain of chaos and the realm only God can command (Job 38:16; Ps. 77:19).

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias. And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Jesus crosses to the far side of the Sea of Galilee, also called the Sea of Tiberias. A large crowd keeps following him because they have seen the signs he does in healing the sick.

Tiberias. The city Herod Antipas founded about AD 20 and named after the emperor; the lake took its name later, which suggests John writes for readers late in the first century.

Following for signs. Their motive is mixed (v. 26).

All four Gospels. Matthew 14:13–21; Mark 6:32–44; Luke 9:10–17. John’s account adds details (Philip, Andrew, the boy, barley loaves) and the discourse that follows.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Tiberias is another name for the Sea of Galilee, from the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore and named after the emperor Tiberius.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes up on the hillside and sits down there with his disciples.

The mountain. Perhaps an echo of Moses on Sinai: the new Moses will give bread from heaven. Sitting was the posture of a teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand. Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip, "Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jewish feast of Passover is near. Looking up and seeing a large crowd coming towards him, Jesus asks Philip where they can buy bread for these people to eat.

Passover. The feast of the exodus and the lamb, followed in the wilderness by manna. Jesus is about to explain himself as the true manna, and to speak of eating his flesh and drinking his blood, a year before his Passover death.

Why Philip? He came from nearby Bethsaida (1:44) and would know where to buy food.
verseByVerse.note: This is the second Passover John mentions; the Passover setting prepares for Jesus’ words about bread and his flesh and blood.

verseByVerse.quote: He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do. Philip answered him, "Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks this to test him, since he already knows what he is going to do. Philip answers that two hundred denarii’ worth of bread would not be enough for each person to have a little.

A test. Not to trap but to train: will Philip look to resources or to Jesus? (Compare Genesis 22:1.)

Two hundred denarii. About eight months’ wages for a labourer. Philip does the maths and concludes it is impossible.

On a Tuesday. When faced with a need far beyond your budget or ability, begin by asking what Jesus intends to do.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; two hundred denarii was most of a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: where am I to get meat?

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, said to him, "There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, tells Jesus there is a boy with five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they among so many?

Andrew again. Bringing someone to Jesus (1:41–42; 12:22).

A boy. Paidarion: a little boy, perhaps a servant. Only John mentions him.

Barley loaves. The bread of the poor. Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, with some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). A greater than Elisha is here.

Two fish. Probably small dried or pickled fish, eaten with bread.

On a Tuesday. Bring what little you have to Jesus: time, money, skills. In his hands it is enough.
verseByVerse.note: Barley loaves were the cheap bread of the poor.

parallels.desc: Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Have the people sit down." Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number. Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells them to have the people sit down. There is plenty of grass there. So the men sit down, about five thousand of them. Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks and distributes them to those seated, and the same with the fish, as much as they want.

Much grass. Spring, near Passover. Psalm 23:2: he makes me lie down in green pastures. The Shepherd feeds his flock (Mark 6:34).

Five thousand men. Plus women and children (Matthew 14:21).

Gave thanks. Eucharistēsas: the word from which “Eucharist” comes. John’s readers would think of the Lord’s Supper, though this is not the Supper.

As much as they wanted. Abundance, not rationing. Compare the wine at Cana (2:6).

Textual note. Later manuscripts add that he gave to the disciples, and the disciples to those seated (KJV), from the other Gospels. Verdict: not original in John.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples, "Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost." So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When everyone has eaten enough, he tells his disciples to gather the leftover pieces so that nothing is wasted. They gather them and fill twelve baskets with pieces of the five barley loaves left over by those who had eaten.

Nothing lost. The same phrase as verse 39: Jesus will lose nothing of what the Father gives him. A small instruction with a large echo.

Twelve baskets. One for each disciple, or for each tribe of Israel. More left over than they began with.

On a Tuesday. God’s abundance is no excuse for waste. Christians should be good stewards of food and resources.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said, "This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!" Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the people see the sign he has done, they say this is surely the Prophet who is to come into the world. Jesus, knowing they intend to come and seize him to make him king by force, withdraws again to the hills by himself.

The Prophet. Moses fed Israel with manna; the prophet like Moses would do the same (Deuteronomy 18:15). They are not wrong in title, but wrong in expectation.

By force. A crowd of thousands of Galilean men in the hills, at Passover, the feast of liberation, eager for a king who could feed armies: a revolt in the making.

Withdrew. Jesus refuses a political kingdom (18:36). He will be crowned, but with thorns.

What it does not mean. Jesus’ kingship is not indifferent to bodies and bread, but its throne is a cross, and its aim is eternal life.

On a Tuesday. Beware of wanting Jesus for what he can give you rather than for who he is.
verseByVerse.note: “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised. Many hoped for a Messiah who would lead a revolt against Rome.

parallels.desc: my kingdom is not of this world

verseByVerse.quote: When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea, got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When evening comes, his disciples go down to the lake, get into a boat and set off across it to Capernaum. By now it is dark, and Jesus has not yet joined them.

Dark. In John, darkness is often symbolic (1:5; 3:2). The disciples are alone, without Jesus, in the night.

On a Tuesday. There are nights when Jesus seems absent. He has not forgotten you (Mark 6:48: he saw them).

verseByVerse.quote: The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A strong wind is blowing, and the water grows rough.

Galilean storms. The lake lies about 700 feet below sea level, ringed by hills; cold air pouring down from the heights can whip up violent waves suddenly.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden strong winds are common.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened. But he said to them, "It is I; do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they have rowed three or four miles, they see Jesus walking on the lake and coming near the boat, and they are terrified. But he tells them, “It is I; do not be afraid.”

Walking on the sea. In the Old Testament, God alone treads on the waves (Job 9:8) and makes a path through the sea (Psalm 77:19; Isaiah 43:16).

It is I. Literally “I am” (egō eimi), the words God used of himself (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:10, 25). On the water, it is a self-revelation of God.

Do not be afraid. The word that accompanies God’s appearing throughout Scripture.

Where Christians differ: did it really happen? Some sceptical scholars suggest Jesus was walking on the shore or a sandbank. The Gospels plainly describe him on the water in the middle of the lake (three or four miles out). Verdict: a real miracle, consistent with the Creator having become flesh.

For worship. The one who walks on storms comes to you in yours, saying, “I am; do not be afraid.”
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is literally twenty-five or thirty stadia. “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they are glad to take him into the boat, and at once the boat reaches the shore they were heading for.

Glad. Fear turns to welcome.

Immediately at the land. A further wonder, or simply a vivid description of how quickly the rest of the journey seemed to pass. Psalm 107:29–30: he made the storm be still and brought them to their desired haven.

parallels.desc: he brought them to their desired haven

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–71 — The Bread of Life Discourse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The crowd follows Jesus to Capernaum, wanting more bread. He urges them to seek food that lasts, given by the Son of Man, and tells them the work God asks is faith in the one he sent. When they demand a sign like the manna, he declares that he is the true bread from heaven, the bread of life, who satisfies hunger and thirst for ever. All the Father gives him will come, none will be turned away or lost, and he will raise them on the last day. As they grumble at his claim, he teaches that no one comes unless the Father draws and teaches them. The bread he will give for the world is his own flesh; only those who eat his flesh and drink his blood have life and remain in him. Many disciples are offended and leave. Jesus says his words are Spirit and life, but some do not believe. When he asks the Twelve whether they will go, Peter replies that only Jesus has the words of eternal life; they know he is the Holy One of God. Jesus warns that one of the Twelve, Judas, will betray him.
verseByVerse.theology: The Bread of Life discourse is simultaneously eucharistic (the language of eating and drinking Jesus's flesh and blood points to the Lord's Supper) and spiritual (the key interpretive statement is 'it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all'). The flesh and blood Jesus speaks of is not a literal cannibalism but the reception of his atoning death: to eat his flesh and drink his blood is to appropriate by faith the benefits of his sacrifice. No one can come to Jesus unless the Father draws them; all who are given to the Son by the Father will come; all who come will be raised up on the last day. The sovereignty of grace and the necessity of faith are held together throughout.
verseByVerse.examples: The Bread of Life discourse sheds light on the Lord's Supper without being confined to it: feeding on Christ is spiritual, received by faith, not a physical re-sacrifice. The mass defection at the end of the discourse — 'many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him' — is the most important event in John 6: it reveals that the crowd's 'belief' was not genuine, and that the true disciples are known not by enthusiasm but by perseverance. Peter's confession — 'you have the words of eternal life' — is the greatest response to a hard teaching in the Gospels: when you cannot understand what Jesus is saying, you remain because of who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone. Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day the crowd still on the other side of the lake realises that only one boat had been there, and that Jesus had not got into it with his disciples, who had left alone. Other boats from Tiberias land near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord gave thanks.

A puzzle. How did Jesus get across? The crowd works it out slowly; John’s readers know.

After the Lord had given thanks. John stresses the thanksgiving again, perhaps with the Lord’s Supper in mind. Textual note. A few manuscripts omit this phrase. Verdict: probably original.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when the crowd sees that neither Jesus nor his disciples are there, they get into the boats and go to Capernaum to look for Jesus.

Seeking Jesus. Good in itself; but motives matter (v. 26).

verseByVerse.quote: When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, "Rabbi, when did you come here?" Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they find him on the other side of the lake, they ask him, as Rabbi, when he got there. Jesus tells them solemnly that they are looking for him not because they saw signs but because they ate the loaves and were filled.

When? A question of curiosity. Jesus ignores it and goes to the heart.

Not because of signs. They saw the miracle but missed what it pointed to. They want a meal ticket, not a Saviour.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly why you follow Jesus: for blessings, or for him?

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They should not work for food that spoils, but for food that lasts to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give them. For God the Father has set his seal on him.

Do not work. Not a ban on earning a living (2 Thessalonians 3:10), but a call to set priorities. Isaiah 55:2: why spend your labour on what does not satisfy?

Will give. Eternal life is a gift, even as they are told to “work” for it. The paradox is resolved in verse 29.

Sealed. Authenticated, as a document or a sacrifice was marked approved, perhaps at his baptism (1:32–33).
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity.

parallels.desc: why do you labour for that which does not satisfy?

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they said to him, 'What must we do, to be doing the works of God?' Jesus answered them, 'This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they ask what they must do to carry out the works God requires. Jesus answers that the work of God is this: to believe in the one he has sent.

What must we do? The natural religious question: give us a list of works.

The work of God. Singular. Not many works, but one: faith. And faith is not a meritorious work but the receiving of Christ (Romans 4:4–5). Augustine read “the work of God” as also meaning the work God does in us: faith is his gift (Ephesians 2:8).

For worship. Thank God that what he requires, he also gives.

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they ask what sign he will do, so that they may see and believe him. What work will he perform? Their ancestors ate manna in the wilderness; as Scripture says, he gave them bread from heaven to eat.

Another sign? Astonishing, the day after the feeding. But they want something greater: Moses fed Israel for forty years, Jesus only once.

Manna. Exodus 16; Psalm 78:24. Jewish hope held that the Messiah would bring back the manna.

parallels.desc: he gave them the grain of heaven
bread from heaven

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells them solemnly that it was not Moses who gave them bread from heaven, but his Father who now gives them the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.

Not Moses. God gave the manna; Moses only announced it.

True bread. Manna was real, but a shadow; Christ is the reality (1 Corinthians 10:3–4).

Comes down from heaven. The language of incarnation (3:13). Repeated seven times in the chapter.

To the world. Manna fed Israel; this bread is for all nations.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Sir, give us this bread always." Jesus said to them, "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask him to give them this bread always. Jesus tells them, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.”

Give us always. Like the Samaritan woman (4:15), they misunderstand, thinking of physical bread.

I am. The first of seven great “I am” sayings with a picture: bread (6:35), light (8:12), door (10:7), good shepherd (10:11), resurrection and life (11:25), way, truth and life (14:6), true vine (15:1). Each says something essential about Christ, and each echoes God’s name.

Bread of life. Bread was the staple: life depended on it. Christ is not a luxury or a supplement, but the necessity of the soul.

Comes and believes. Parallel phrases: to come to Jesus is to believe in him.

For worship. Feed on Christ today: read of him, trust him, rest in him.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first of Jesus’ seven “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: come, buy and eat

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus has told them that they have seen him and yet do not believe.

Seeing is not believing. They saw the sign and the man, and still did not believe (12:37). Faith is not produced by evidence alone.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that the Father gives him will come to him, and whoever comes to him he will never drive away. For he has come down from heaven not to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him.

All that the Father gives. Neuter singular in Greek: the whole people given to the Son as one gift (17:2, 6, 9, 24). Before anyone comes, the Father has given them to the Son.

Will come. Not “may come”: the Father’s gift guarantees their coming. This is effectual calling.

Never cast out. A double negative in Greek: certainly not. No one who comes, however sinful, will be refused. This is the free offer.

Where Christians differ: election. Arminians hold that God elects those he foresees will believe. Reformed theology holds that the Father’s giving comes first and causes the coming. Verdict: unconditional election, held with this verse’s own balance: God’s choice guarantees that his people will come, and Christ’s welcome guarantees that anyone who comes will be received. Both halves are to be preached.

For worship. If you have come, you were given. If you have not, come: he will not cast you out.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is the will of the one who sent him: that he should lose nothing of all that the Father has given him, but raise it up on the last day.

Lose nothing. Like the fragments (v. 12). The Son’s mission is to keep every one of the Father’s gift.

The last day. Repeated four times (vv. 39, 40, 44, 54). Salvation ends not at death but in bodily resurrection.

Where Christians differ: can a believer be lost? Arminians and others hold that a true believer may finally fall away (citing Hebrews 6:4–6). Reformed theology holds the perseverance of the saints: none whom the Father gave will be lost, because the Son does the Father’s will (10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). Verdict: perseverance of the saints: those truly given to Christ will be kept to the end, not because they are strong, but because he is faithful. Warning passages are means by which he keeps them.

verseByVerse.quote: "For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is his Father’s will: that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and Jesus will raise him up on the last day.

Everyone who looks. The human side of verse 39: those given are those who look and believe. Compare the bronze serpent (3:14–15).

I will raise. The personal promise of Jesus himself.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, "I am the bread that came down from heaven." They said, "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, 'I have come down from heaven'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jewish listeners begin to grumble about him because he said he is the bread that came down from heaven. They ask whether this is not Jesus, Joseph’s son, whose father and mother they know. How can he now say he came down from heaven?

Grumbled. The word used of Israel grumbling against Moses over the manna (Exodus 16:2, 7–8). History repeats itself.

We know his parents. Familiarity breeds unbelief. They know his origin, they think, but do not know his true origin.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do not grumble among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells them to stop grumbling among themselves. No one can come to him unless the Father who sent him draws him, and Jesus will raise him up on the last day.

No one can. Spiritual inability: by nature no one is able or willing to come to Christ (Romans 8:7–8; 1 Corinthians 2:14).

Draws. Helkō, used of dragging a net (21:6, 11) or a person (Acts 16:19). Not mere persuasion that may be refused, but effective drawing; yet not against the will, for the Father draws by teaching (v. 45).

Where Christians differ: drawing. Arminians speak of a prevenient grace drawing all people, which each may accept or resist, citing 12:32 (“will draw all people”). Reformed theology answers that those drawn in 6:44 are raised on the last day, so the drawing is effectual; and that “all people” in 12:32 means all kinds of people, Greeks as well as Jews (12:20–21). Verdict: effectual calling: everyone the Father draws comes, and everyone who comes is raised.

For worship. If you love Christ, it is because the Father drew you. Thank him.

parallels.desc: I will draw all people to myself

verseByVerse.quote: "It is written in the Prophets, 'And they will all be taught by God.' Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me — not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is written in the Prophets that they will all be taught by God. Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to Jesus, not that anyone has seen the Father except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.

Isaiah 54:13. In the new covenant all God’s people will be taught by him (Jeremiah 31:33–34).

Drawing is teaching. The Father draws by opening minds and hearts to the truth, so that people come gladly. The effect is a willing response.

Seen the Father. Only the Son has (1:18). We learn from the Father through the Son.

parallels.desc: all your children shall be taught by the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life. I am the bread of life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells them solemnly that whoever believes has eternal life. He is the bread of life.

Has. Again present possession.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “in me” after “believes” (KJV). Verdict: not original, but the meaning is clearly faith in Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their ancestors ate manna in the wilderness, and they died. But this is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat it and not die.

They died. Manna sustained physical life for a time. The generation that ate it died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:29–35).

Not die. Not that believers escape physical death, but that death no longer has the last word (11:25–26).

parallels.desc: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats this bread will live for ever. And the bread he will give for the life of the world is his flesh.

Living bread. Bread that is alive and gives life.

Will give. Future: on the cross. “For” (hyper) is sacrificial language (10:11; 11:51; 15:13).

My flesh. His real human body, given in death. The incarnation (1:14) leads to the cross.

For worship. Thank Christ that he gave his flesh, so that you might live.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" So Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jewish listeners argue sharply among themselves about how this man can give them his flesh to eat. Jesus tells them solemnly that unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, they have no life in them.

How can he? Taken literally, it sounds like cannibalism, a charge later made against Christians by pagans.

Drink his blood. Even more shocking: drinking blood was forbidden (Leviticus 17:10–14), because life is in the blood. Jesus says his life must be received.

Jesus does not soften it. He makes it stronger.
verseByVerse.note: Drinking blood was forbidden by the law, which made these words shocking.

parallels.desc: the life is in the blood

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever feeds on his flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life, and he will raise him up on the last day.

Feeds. A vivid, earthy verb (trōgō, chew, munch). There is no avoiding the physical picture.

Parallel to believing. Compare verse 40: whoever looks and believes has eternal life, and I will raise him. Eating and drinking are pictures of believing, receiving and depending on Christ’s death for life (v. 35).

Where Christians differ: is this the Lord’s Supper? Roman Catholic teaching reads these verses as about the Eucharist, in which the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood (transubstantiation). Lutherans hold Christ’s body is present in, with and under the elements. Zwinglians see a memorial and read John 6 as about faith, not the Supper. Calvin and the Reformed confessions hold that John 6 is first about faith feeding on Christ at all times, and that the Supper is a sign and seal of that same feeding, in which, by the Spirit, believers truly partake of Christ’s body and blood spiritually (Westminster Confession 29.7). Verdict: the app’s Calvinist view: this passage is about faith in Christ crucified, which the Supper later signifies; in the Supper believers really feed on Christ by faith through the Spirit, not by the mouth. Verse 63 guards against a crudely physical reading.

parallels.desc: a participation in the blood of Christ

verseByVerse.quote: "For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For his flesh is true food, and his blood is true drink. Whoever feeds on his flesh and drinks his blood remains in him, and he in them.

True. Real food, in the fullest sense: what bread is to the body, Christ is to the soul.

Abides. Mutual indwelling: believer in Christ, Christ in believer (15:4–7). Union with Christ is the heart of salvation.

On a Tuesday. Feeding is continual, not once in a lifetime. Keep feeding on Christ daily through his word and prayer.

parallels.desc: abide in me

verseByVerse.quote: "As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the living Father sent him, and he lives because of the Father, so whoever feeds on him will live because of him. This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the ancestors ate and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live for ever.

A chain of life. The Father is the source; the Son lives from the Father; believers live from the Son.

For worship. Your life is held in a chain that runs back to the living Father. Nothing can break it.

parallels.desc: Christ who lives in me

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum. When many of his disciples heard it, they said, "This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says these things while teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum. On hearing it, many of his disciples say this is a hard teaching: who can accept it?

The synagogue. The white limestone synagogue visible at Capernaum today dates from the fourth or fifth century, but it stands on the black basalt foundations of an earlier building, possibly the one where Jesus taught.

Disciples. Not the Twelve only, but a wider circle of followers.

Hard. Not difficult to understand but offensive to accept: a crucified Messiah whose death is life.

On a Tuesday. Some of Jesus’ words will offend you. That is when you discover whether you follow him or your preferences.
verseByVerse.note: The remains of a later synagogue at Capernaum stand on the foundations of an earlier one, perhaps the one where Jesus taught.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, "Do you take offense at this? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, aware that his disciples are grumbling about this, asks whether it offends them. What if they were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?

Offended. Skandalizō: tripped up.

Ascending. If they stumble at his descent from heaven and his giving his flesh, how much more at his return to heaven through the cross and resurrection? Or: when they see him ascend, they will understand that he did not mean physical eating.

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some of you who do not believe." (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is of no help at all. The words he has spoken to them are spirit and life. But some of them do not believe. For Jesus knew from the beginning who did not believe and who would betray him.

The Spirit gives life. The key to the discourse. Physical eating, even of Christ’s physical flesh, would profit nothing. Life comes through the Spirit, by faith in his words.

The flesh. Not Jesus’ flesh given for the world (v. 51), but human nature and a merely physical understanding.

Spirit and life. Christ’s words carry the life they describe (5:24).

Knew from the beginning. Jesus is never surprised by unbelief or betrayal (2:24–25; 13:11).
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature on its own, apart from the Spirit.

parallels.desc: the Spirit gives life

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He says that is why he told them that no one can come to him unless the Father has granted it.

Granted. Coming to Christ is a gift (v. 44; Philippians 1:29).

Why mention it now? To explain unbelief: it does not defeat God’s plan, and it is not a sign that the message is false.

On a Tuesday. When friends reject the gospel, keep praying: what is impossible for them God can grant.

verseByVerse.quote: After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. So Jesus said to the twelve, "Do you want to go away as well?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
From then on many of his disciples turn back and no longer go about with him. So Jesus asks the Twelve whether they want to leave too.

Many turned back. The crowd that wanted to crown him (v. 15) melts away when he will not be their kind of king. Popularity was never his goal.

Do you want to go? Expecting the answer no, but giving them freedom. Jesus does not chase the departing with a softer message.

On a Tuesday. Faithful teaching sometimes thins a church. Do not water down the truth to keep numbers.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter answered him, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter answers, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.”

To whom? Peter does not claim to understand everything Jesus has said. He knows only that there is no alternative.

Words of eternal life. Echoing verse 63. Peter has grasped the point: life is found in Jesus’ words.

For worship. When faith is hard and you are tempted to walk away, make Peter’s prayer your own.

parallels.desc: all the words of this Life

verseByVerse.quote: "and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God." Jesus answered them, "Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter adds that they have believed and have come to know that he is the Holy One of God. Jesus answers that he chose them, the Twelve, and yet one of them is a devil.

Believed and known. Perfect tenses: a settled conviction.

The Holy One of God. A title used by a demon in Mark 1:24, of one set apart and belonging to God.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “the Christ, the Son of the living God” (KJV), from Matthew 16:16. Verdict: “the Holy One of God” is original.

I chose you. Jesus’ choice, not theirs (15:16). Yet even Judas was chosen as one of the Twelve: chosen for apostleship, not for salvation (17:12).

A devil. Not literally a demon, but one who acts as Satan’s agent (13:2, 27; compare Peter in Mark 8:33).

parallels.desc: Peter’s confession

verseByVerse.quote: He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He means Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, who, though one of the Twelve, is going to betray him.

Iscariot. Perhaps “man of Kerioth”, a town in Judea, which would make Judas the only non-Galilean among the Twelve. Other suggestions link it to sicarius, dagger-man, or a word for “false one”. Uncertain.

One of the Twelve. The phrase rings with tragedy. Being close to Jesus, sharing his ministry and hearing his teaching do not guarantee a changed heart.

On a Tuesday. Do not rely on your church role or religious nearness. Examine whether you truly trust him (2 Corinthians 13:5).

For worship. Thank Jesus that he knew the betrayer, and went on to the cross anyway, for us.
verseByVerse.note: “Iscariot” is often taken to mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea, but that is uncertain.

6.title: The Bread of Life
6.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias.<sup>2</sup>And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.<sup>3</sup>Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.<sup>4</sup>Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.<sup>5</sup>Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?”<sup>6</sup>He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do.<sup>7</sup>Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little.”<sup>8</sup>One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,<sup>9</sup>“There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?”<sup>10</sup>Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number.<sup>11</sup>Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.<sup>12</sup>And when they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples, “Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost.”<sup>13</sup>So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.<sup>14</sup>When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said, “This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!”<sup>15</sup>Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.<sup>16</sup>When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea,<sup>17</sup>got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.<sup>18</sup>The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.<sup>19</sup>When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened.<sup>20</sup>But he said to them, “It is I; do not be afraid.”<sup>21</sup>Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.<sup>22</sup>On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone.<sup>23</sup>Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.<sup>24</sup>So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.<sup>25</sup>When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, “Rabbi, when did you come here?”<sup>26</sup>Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.<sup>27</sup>Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal.”<sup>28</sup>Then they said to him, “What must we do, to be doing the works of God?”<sup>29</sup>Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.”<sup>30</sup>So they said to him, “Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform?<sup>31</sup>Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, ’He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’”<sup>32</sup>Jesus then said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.<sup>33</sup>For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”<sup>34</sup>They said to him, “Sir, give us this bread always.”<sup>35</sup>Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.<sup>36</sup>But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe.<sup>37</sup>All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out.<sup>38</sup>For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.<sup>39</sup>And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.<sup>40</sup>For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.”<sup>41</sup>So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.”<sup>42</sup>They said, “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, ’I have come down from heaven’?”<sup>43</sup>Jesus answered them, “Do not grumble among yourselves.<sup>44</sup>No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day.<sup>45</sup>It is written in the Prophets, ’And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me—<sup>46</sup>not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father.<sup>47</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life.<sup>48</sup>I am the bread of life.<sup>49</sup>Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.<sup>50</sup>This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die.<sup>51</sup>I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”<sup>52</sup>The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”<sup>53</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.<sup>54</sup>Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.<sup>55</sup>For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.<sup>56</sup>Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.<sup>57</sup>As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me.<sup>58</sup>This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever.”<sup>59</sup>Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum.<sup>60</sup>When many of his disciples heard it, they said, “This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?”<sup>61</sup>But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, “Do you take offense at this?<sup>62</sup>Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?<sup>63</sup>It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.<sup>64</sup>But there are some of you who do not believe.” (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)<sup>65</sup>And he said, “This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father.”<sup>66</sup>After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him.<sup>67</sup>So Jesus said to the twelve, “Do you want to go away as well?”<sup>68</sup>Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life,<sup>69</sup>and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.”<sup>70</sup>Jesus answered them, “Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil.”<sup>71</sup>He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
6.overview:
The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, recorded in all four Gospels. John sets it near Passover and tells it so that it opens into one of Jesus’ longest discourses. On a hillside by the Sea of Galilee Jesus feeds a vast crowd from a boy’s five barley loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered. The crowd hails him as the Prophet like Moses and tries to force him to be their king, so he withdraws. That night, as his disciples row against a storm, he comes to them walking on the water and says, “It is I; do not be afraid,” words that echo the divine name.

Next day, in the synagogue at Capernaum, the crowd that ate the bread wants more. Jesus tells them to work for food that lasts, and that the work God requires is to believe in the one he has sent. They ask for a sign like the manna; he replies, “I am the bread of life.” All the Father gives him will come to him, and he will lose none of them but raise them up on the last day; no one can come unless the Father draws him. Then he says that the bread he will give is his flesh for the life of the world, and that unless they eat his flesh and drink his blood they have no life. Many disciples find this too hard and leave. When Jesus asks the Twelve whether they will go too, Peter answers for them all: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.” Yet even among the Twelve is one who will betray him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With his life in danger in Judea, Jesus stays in Galilee until the Feast of Booths. His unbelieving brothers press him to go and make himself known; he answers that his time is not yet, and goes up privately later. In Jerusalem the crowds argue about him in hushed tones. Midway through the feast he teaches in the temple, and the leaders marvel at his learning. He says his teaching is from God, recognisable to anyone who wants to do God’s will; their anger at his Sabbath healing is inconsistent, since they circumcise on the Sabbath. People debate whether he could be the Messiah, since they think they know his origins. Jesus declares that he comes from the true God, whom they do not know. Attempts to arrest him fail, for his hour has not come, though many believe. When officers are sent, he speaks of going where they cannot follow. On the great last day he invites the thirsty to come to him and drink, promising rivers of living water, meaning the Spirit, to be given after his glorification. The crowd divides over whether he is the Prophet or the Christ, or merely a Galilean. The officers return saying no one has ever spoken like him. The Pharisees scorn them and the crowd, and when Nicodemus pleads for a fair hearing, they mock him as a Galilean.
verseByVerse.theology: The controversy in John 7 turns on the question of Jesus's origins and authority. Where is he from? Did he come from God or from himself? The crowd is divided: some say he is a good man; others say he leads the people astray. Jesus's teaching in the temple provokes astonishment: 'How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?' His answer is theological: his teaching is not his own but the Father's, and the one who seeks to do God's will will recognize its divine origin. The authority question and the origin question are ultimately the same question: who sent him?
verseByVerse.examples: The Feast of Tabernacles is the most eschatological of the Jewish festivals — it looks forward to the final harvest, the ultimate ingathering. Jesus's claim at the climax of the feast ('out of his heart will flow rivers of living water') is the claim to be the fulfillment of Israel's end-times hope. The officers who were sent to arrest Jesus and returned saying 'no one ever spoke like this man' (v. 46) give one of the most powerful testimonies to the authority of Jesus's teaching in the entire Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Now the Jews' Feast of Booths was at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Jesus travels around Galilee. He avoids Judea because the Jewish leaders there are looking for a way to kill him. The Jewish Feast of Booths is near.

Six months. From Passover (6:4) to Booths, in September or October: a period John passes over in a sentence.

The Feast of Booths. Sukkot (Leviticus 23:33–43; Deuteronomy 16:13–15), the most joyful of the pilgrim feasts. For eight days people lived in shelters of branches, recalling the wilderness, and celebrated the harvest. Daily water was carried from the Pool of Siloam and poured at the altar with prayers for rain, and huge lamps lit the temple courts. Both rituals lie behind Jesus’ words in 7:37–39 and 8:12.

Not afraid but wise. Jesus avoids danger until his hour.
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) was the joyful autumn harvest festival. For a week people lived in shelters made of branches, remembering Israel’s years in the wilderness.

parallels.desc: the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: So his brothers said to him, "Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing. For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So his brothers tell him to leave Galilee and go to Judea, so that his disciples there can see the works he is doing. No one who wants to be known publicly acts in secret. If he does these things, he should show himself to the world.

His brothers. James, Joseph, Simon and Judas (Mark 6:3).

Show yourself. Their advice is worldly: maximise exposure, go to the capital at the busiest time. They want a celebrity, perhaps reflected glory for the family.

On a Tuesday. Not every good opportunity for publicity is God’s timing. Seek his will before others’ expectations.
verseByVerse.note: His brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon.

verseByVerse.quote: For not even his brothers believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For not even his brothers believe in him.

Family unbelief. Those who grew up with him did not believe (Mark 3:21). After the resurrection, they did: Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), the brothers prayed with the disciples (Acts 1:14), and James led the Jerusalem church and wrote a letter, as perhaps did Jude.

On a Tuesday. Keep praying for unbelieving family. Jesus’ own brothers took years, and a resurrection, to believe.
verseByVerse.note: James later led the church in Jerusalem, and the brothers were among the believers after the resurrection.

parallels.desc: with Mary and his brothers
he appeared to James

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "My time has not yet come, but your time is always here. The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells them that his time has not yet come, but for them any time is right. The world cannot hate them, but it hates him because he testifies that its works are evil.

My time. Kairos, the right moment, close to “my hour” (2:4). His movements are governed by the Father.

Your time is always here. Living by the world’s rules, they can come and go as they please.

The world hates me. Because he exposes it (3:19–20). The world loves its own (15:18–19).

On a Tuesday. If no one is ever uncomfortable with your faith, ask whether you are testifying to anything.

parallels.desc: if the world hates you

verseByVerse.quote: "You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come." After saying this, he remained in Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They should go up to the feast themselves. He is not going up to this feast, because his time has not yet fully come. Having said this, he stays in Galilee.

Did Jesus deceive them? He later goes (v. 10). Some see a change of plan; others say he refused to go up as they suggested, publicly, as a pilgrim seeking acclaim, or that he meant he would not go up in the sense of his final “going up” to the Father (20:17, the same verb). Textual note. Many manuscripts read “not yet going up” (ESV margin), probably a scribal attempt to remove the difficulty. Verdict: “not” is original; Jesus refused their agenda, not the feast itself, and went later in a different way.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “yet” — “I am not yet going up.”

verseByVerse.quote: But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private. The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, "Where is he?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But after his brothers have left for the feast, he too goes up, not publicly but privately. The Jewish leaders are looking for him at the feast and asking where he is.

In private. Not in a pilgrim caravan, and not as a celebrity.

Where is he? Everyone is talking about him: the authorities to arrest him, the crowds out of curiosity.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, "He is a good man," others said, "No, he is leading the people astray." Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among the crowds there is a lot of whispering about him. Some say he is a good man; others say no, he leads the people astray. But no one speaks about him openly, for fear of the Jewish leaders.

Good or a deceiver? The two poles of opinion. Leading the people astray was a capital charge (Deuteronomy 13:1–5), and later Jewish sources accused Jesus of it.

C. S. Lewis. “A good man” is the one option Jesus does not leave open: a man who claimed what he claimed is either a liar, a lunatic or Lord.

Fear. Fear of authority silences people (9:22; 12:42; 19:38).

parallels.desc: a prophet who leads you astray
that impostor

verseByVerse.quote: About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching. The Jews therefore marveled, saying, "How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
About halfway through the feast Jesus goes up to the temple and begins to teach. The Jewish leaders are amazed and ask how this man has such learning when he has never studied.

Never studied. He had not trained under a recognised rabbi, as Paul did under Gamaliel. Yet his knowledge of Scripture astonished them (Acts 4:13).

On a Tuesday. Formal qualifications are good, but they are not the measure of truth. Listen to faithful teachers whatever their credentials; and if you have credentials, do not trust them.
verseByVerse.note: “Never studied” means he had not been trained under a recognised rabbi.

parallels.desc: uneducated, common men

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus answered them, "My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers that his teaching is not his own but comes from the one who sent him. If anyone wants to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether Jesus speaks on his own authority.

Not mine. His authority is not a school but his Father.

Willing, then knowing. The obstacle to recognising truth is often moral, not intellectual. Those who sincerely want to do God’s will come to recognise Jesus’ voice (10:4, 27).

On a Tuesday. If you are unsure about Christ, ask yourself: am I willing to do God’s will if it is shown to me? Start there, and pray.

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood. Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but whoever seeks the glory of the one who sent him is truthful, and there is nothing false in him. Moses gave them the law, didn’t he? Yet none of them keeps the law. Why are they trying to kill him?

A test of teachers. Whose glory do they seek? (5:41–44.)

None of you keeps the law. Their plot to kill him breaks the sixth commandment while claiming to defend the fourth.

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd answered, "You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?" Jesus answered them, "I did one work, and you all marvel at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd answers that he has a demon: who is trying to kill him? Jesus replies that he did one work, and they are all amazed.

You have a demon. Perhaps meaning “you’re mad” or “paranoid”. The crowd, mostly pilgrims, may not know the leaders’ plans.

One work. The healing at Bethesda on the Sabbath (5:1–9), eighteen months earlier, still the talk of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.note: The “one work” is the healing at the pool on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses gave them circumcision (though it actually came from the patriarchs, not Moses), and they circumcise a man on the Sabbath.

From the fathers. Circumcision began with Abraham (Genesis 17:10–14), before Moses (Leviticus 12:3).

On the Sabbath. If the eighth day after birth fell on a Sabbath, rabbis ruled that circumcision overrode the Sabbath rest.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision on the eighth day went ahead even when that day was a Sabbath. It began with Abraham, before Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: "If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man's whole body well? Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a boy can receive circumcision on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses is not broken, why are they angry with Jesus for making a man’s whole body well on the Sabbath? They should stop judging by appearances and judge rightly.

From the lesser to the greater. A rabbinic style of argument. If one part of the body may be “perfected” on the Sabbath, how much more the whole man?

Judge rightly. Do not judge superficially (1 Samuel 16:7; Isaiah 11:3).

What it does not mean. “Judge not” (Matthew 7:1) does not forbid all moral judgment. Jesus commands right judgment here.

On a Tuesday. Before criticising, look beyond appearances to the heart of the matter.

parallels.desc: judge righteously

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, "Is not this the man whom they seek to kill? And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the people of Jerusalem ask whether this is not the man the leaders want to kill. Here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Could the authorities really have concluded that he is the Christ?

Jerusalem residents. Unlike pilgrims, they know of the plot.

Openly. The authorities’ silence puzzles them.

verseByVerse.quote: "But we know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears no one will know where he is from.

A hidden Messiah. Some Jewish traditions expected the Messiah to be hidden until he suddenly appeared (compare Malachi 3:1). Others, by contrast, knew he would come from Bethlehem (v. 42).

Irony. They think they know where Jesus is from, Nazareth, but do not know his true origin, from the Father.
verseByVerse.note: Some expected the Messiah to appear suddenly from hiding.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus proclaimed, as he taught in the temple, 'You know me, and you know where I come from. But I have not come of my own accord. He who sent me is true, and him you do not know. I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus, teaching in the temple, cries out that they know him and know where he comes from. Yet he has not come on his own. The one who sent him is true, and they do not know him. But Jesus knows him, because he comes from him, and he sent him.

Cried out. A loud, public proclamation.

You know … you do not know. Perhaps ironic: “So you know me, do you?” They know his earthly home but not his Father.

I know him. Jesus alone truly knows the Father (1:18; Matthew 11:27).

verseByVerse.quote: So they were seeking to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come. Yet many of the people believed in him. They said, "When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they try to seize him, but no one lays a hand on him, because his hour has not yet come. Yet many in the crowd believe in him, and ask whether the Christ, when he comes, will do more signs than this man has done.

His hour. God’s timetable governs events (8:20). Jesus is not a victim of circumstances.

Many believed. Faith of a sort, based on signs (2:23). But it is a beginning.

For worship. No one could touch Jesus before the Father’s time, and no one can touch you outside it (Psalm 31:15).

parallels.desc: his hour had come

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees hear the crowd whispering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees send temple officers to arrest him.

An alliance. Chief priests (Sadducees) and Pharisees, usually rivals, unite against Jesus.

Officers. The Levite temple guard.
verseByVerse.note: The officers were the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said, "I will be with you a little longer, and then I am going to him who sent me. You will seek me and you will not find me. Where I am you cannot come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says he will be with them only a little longer, then he is going to the one who sent him. They will look for him and not find him; where he is, they cannot come.

A little longer. About six months until the cross.

Going to him who sent me. His death, resurrection and ascension as a return to the Father (13:1; 16:28).

You cannot come. Not merely physically: unbelief cannot follow him to the Father (8:21). Contrast what he says to the disciples (13:36; 14:3).

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews said to one another, "Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? What does he mean by saying, 'You will seek me and you will not find me,' and, 'Where I am you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jewish leaders ask one another where he means to go that they will not find him. Will he go to the Jews scattered among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? What does he mean by saying they will look for him and not find him, and that where he is they cannot come?

The Dispersion. Jews living outside the land, across the Greek-speaking world.

Unconscious prophecy. They mock, but it came true: through his apostles, Jesus did teach the Greeks (12:20–24; Acts). Like Caiaphas (11:49–52), they spoke better than they knew.
verseByVerse.note: The Dispersion means the Jews living scattered outside the land among the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stands up and cries out that if anyone is thirsty, he should come to him and drink. Whoever believes in him, as Scripture has said, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.

The water ceremony. Each morning of the feast a priest drew water from the Pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher and poured it at the altar, while the choir sang Isaiah 12:3: with joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation. It recalled the water from the rock in the wilderness (Exodus 17:6) and prayed for rain and for the promised outpouring (Zechariah 14:8; Ezekiel 47:1–12).

Stood and cried out. Rabbis sat to teach; Jesus stands and shouts, at the climax of the festival.

Come to me. Not to the temple or the ritual, but to him (Isaiah 55:1).

Out of whose heart? The Greek can be punctuated two ways: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and let him who believes in me drink. As Scripture says, out of his heart…” (meaning Christ’s heart, the source of the water, as the rock was, 1 Corinthians 10:4; and from his pierced side, 19:34); or (ESV) “Whoever believes in me… out of his heart” (meaning the believer’s, who becomes a channel of the Spirit to others, 4:14). Verdict: both are ancient and true; the Christological reading fits the stress on Jesus as the source, and the Spirit flows from him through believers.

As the Scripture said. No single verse matches; probably a combination of Ezekiel 47, Zechariah 14:8 and the rock in the wilderness.

For worship. Are you thirsty, dry, empty? Come to Jesus and drink.
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish writings describe water being carried from the pool of Siloam and poured out at the altar each day of the feast. No single verse says these exact words; Jesus draws on several prophecies. The ESV notes a different punctuation that makes Jesus himself the source of the water.

parallels.desc: come to the waters
water flowing from the temple
living waters from Jerusalem

verseByVerse.quote: Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He says this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.

John explains. The living water is the Holy Spirit (compare 4:10, 14).

Not yet. Literally “the Spirit was not yet”. The Spirit existed and worked in the Old Testament (Psalm 51:11; Numbers 11:25), but his full outpouring on all God’s people awaited Jesus’ glorification through the cross and resurrection (20:22; Acts 2:33).

Textual note. Some manuscripts add “given” or “upon them” to clarify. Verdict: the shorter, harder reading is original; translations rightly add “given” for sense.

Where Christians differ: the Spirit in the Old Testament. Some hold that Old Testament believers were not indwelt by the Spirit; others that they were regenerated by the Spirit, but without the fullness of the new covenant. Verdict: the Spirit gave new life to believers in every age (3:5, which Nicodemus should have known), but the indwelling fullness and universal gift belong to the new covenant after Pentecost.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these words, some of the people said, "This really is the Prophet." Others said, "This is the Christ." But some said, "Is the Christ to come from Galilee?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they hear these words, some in the crowd say this really is the Prophet. Others say he is the Christ. But some ask whether the Christ is to come from Galilee.

The Prophet and the Christ. Some saw them as two figures (1:20–21). Jesus is both.

From Galilee? They know only his upbringing.
verseByVerse.note: “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was?" So there was a division among the people over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does not Scripture say that the Christ comes from David’s descendants and from Bethlehem, the village where David lived? So the crowd is divided because of him.

Bethlehem. Micah 5:2; 2 Samuel 7:12–16. John’s readers know that Jesus was born in Bethlehem and was of David’s line (Matthew 2:1–6; Luke 2:4). John lets the irony stand: the objection is true, and Jesus fulfils it.

Division. Schisma. Jesus divides people (9:16; 10:19; Luke 12:51).

On a Tuesday. When people dismiss Jesus on a point of fact, check the facts. The answer is often already known.
verseByVerse.note: They did not know that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem.

parallels.desc: from Bethlehem shall come a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some want to seize him, but no one lays hands on him.

Restrained. Again his hour has not come (v. 30).

verseByVerse.quote: The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, "Why did you not bring him?" The officers answered, "No one ever spoke like this man!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officers go back to the chief priests and Pharisees, who ask them why they did not bring him in. The officers answer that no one ever spoke like this man.

Disarmed by words. Sent to arrest him, they were arrested by him (Matthew 7:28–29).

For worship. No one ever spoke like Jesus. Read his words today and let them seize you.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees answered them, "Have you also been deceived? Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees reply by asking whether they too have been deceived. Have any of the rulers or the Pharisees believed in him?

Argument from authority. No expert believes, so it cannot be true. Ironically, one is about to speak up (v. 50), and others secretly believed (12:42).

On a Tuesday. “No serious scholar believes that” is not an argument. Truth is not decided by the elite.

parallels.desc: many even of the authorities believed

verseByVerse.quote: "But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed.

Contempt. Rabbinic writings sometimes used am ha’aretz, “people of the land”, with scorn for those ignorant of the finer points of the law.

Who is accursed? Those who reject Christ, not the ordinary people who hear him gladly (Mark 12:37; 1 Corinthians 1:26–29).
verseByVerse.note: Religious leaders despised ordinary people who did not know the finer points of the law.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them, "Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus, who had earlier visited Jesus and was one of their number, asks whether their law condemns a man without first hearing him and finding out what he is doing.

Nicodemus again. Cautiously, procedurally, he speaks up (Deuteronomy 1:16–17; 17:4). The leaders who boast of knowing the law are not keeping it.

Growing courage. At night in chapter 3, a procedural question here, openly at the burial in 19:39.

On a Tuesday. When colleagues gang up on someone, ask for fairness. A small act of courage may be the beginning of a bigger one.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: inquire diligently

verseByVerse.quote: They replied, "Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee." They went each to his own house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They reply by asking whether he is from Galilee too. He should look into it and see that no prophet comes from Galilee. Then each of them goes home.

Mockery. No answer to his point, only a sneer.
