Wrong on the facts. Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25), and possibly others. Textual note. One early papyrus (P66) reads “the Prophet”, which would mean the prophet like Moses. Verdict: “a prophet” is better attested; their sweeping claim is simply false.

Each to his own house. The end of 7:52 runs into 7:53, which begins the passage about the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11). The earliest manuscripts do not contain it; see the notes on chapter 8.
verseByVerse.note: They were wrong: the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee. The ESV notes that the earliest manuscripts do not include 7:53–8:11 and brackets the passage.

parallels.desc: Jonah son of Amittai, of Gath-hepher
Galilee of the nations

7.title: Rivers of Living Water
7.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.<sup>2</sup>Now the Jews’ Feast of Booths was at hand.<sup>3</sup>So his brothers said to him, “Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing.<sup>4</sup>For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world.”<sup>5</sup>For not even his brothers believed in him.<sup>6</sup>Jesus said to them, “My time has not yet come, but your time is always here.<sup>7</sup>The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil.<sup>8</sup>You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come.”<sup>9</sup>After saying this, he remained in Galilee.<sup>10</sup>But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private.<sup>11</sup>The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, “Where is he?”<sup>12</sup>And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, “He is a good man,” others said, “No, he is leading the people astray.”<sup>13</sup>Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.<sup>14</sup>About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching.<sup>15</sup>The Jews therefore marveled, saying, “How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?”<sup>16</sup>So Jesus answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.<sup>17</sup>If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority.<sup>18</sup>The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood.<sup>19</sup>Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?”<sup>20</sup>The crowd answered, “You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?”<sup>21</sup>Jesus answered them, “I did one work, and you all marvel at it.<sup>22</sup>Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath.<sup>23</sup>If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man’s whole body well?<sup>24</sup>Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.”<sup>25</sup>Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, “Is not this the man whom they seek to kill?<sup>26</sup>And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks?<sup>36</sup>What does he mean by saying, ’You will seek me and you will not find me,’ and, ’Where I am you cannot come’?”<sup>37</sup>On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.<sup>38</sup>Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ’Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.’”<sup>39</sup>Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.<sup>40</sup>When they heard these words, some of the people said, “This really is the Prophet.”<sup>41</sup>Others said, “This is the Christ.” But some said, “Is the Christ to come from Galilee?<sup>42</sup>Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was?”<sup>43</sup>So there was a division among the people over him.<sup>44</sup>Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.<sup>45</sup>The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, “Why did you not bring him?”<sup>46</sup>The officers answered, “No one ever spoke like this man!”<sup>47</sup>The Pharisees answered them, “Have you also been deceived?<sup>48</sup>Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?<sup>49</sup>But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed.”<sup>50</sup>Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them,<sup>51</sup>“Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?”<sup>52</sup>They replied, “Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.”<sup>53</sup>[[They went each to his own house,
7.overview:
Six months after the feeding of the five thousand, the Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) arrives: the joyful autumn festival when Israel lived in shelters of branches to remember the wilderness, and prayed for rain. Jesus’ unbelieving brothers urge him to go to Jerusalem and show himself; he refuses to move on their timetable, then goes up privately. Halfway through the feast he teaches openly in the temple, and the chapter becomes a swirl of opinions: he is a good man; he deceives the people; he has a demon; he is the Prophet; he is the Christ; he cannot be, because the Christ comes from Bethlehem. Jesus answers that his teaching comes from God, that anyone willing to do God’s will can recognise it, and that their anger at his Sabbath healing is hypocrisy, since they circumcise on the Sabbath. The authorities send officers to arrest him.

On the last and greatest day of the feast, when water from the Pool of Siloam was poured out at the altar, Jesus stands and cries out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” and promises rivers of living water flowing from within. John explains that he meant the Spirit, who would be given once Jesus was glorified. The officers return without him, saying, “No one ever spoke like this man!” The Pharisees scorn them and the ignorant crowd, until Nicodemus, one of their own, asks whether the law condemns a man without a hearing, and is mocked for it. The chapter shows a people divided by Jesus, as every generation has been.

8.title: The Light of the World

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — Light in the Darkness: The Second I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus spends the night on the Mount of Olives and returns to the temple at dawn, where crowds gather and he sits to teach. The scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery, stand her before everyone, and ask him whether she should be stoned as Moses commanded, hoping to trap him. Jesus bends down and writes on the ground with his finger. When they keep pressing, he straightens up and tells whoever among them is without sin to throw the first stone, then stoops and writes again. One by one, the oldest first, they leave, until only Jesus and the woman remain. He asks where her accusers are: has no one condemned her? No one, she says. Neither does he; she may go, and must leave her sin behind. Then Jesus declares that he is the light of the world: his followers will not walk in darkness but have the light of life. The Pharisees object that his self-testimony is invalid. He replies that his testimony is true because he knows where he came from and where he is going, and the Father who sent him also testifies; they do not know the Father, because they do not know him. He says this in the treasury, and no one seizes him, for his hour has not come. He warns that he is going away, and they will die in their sin, unable to follow; unless they believe that he is who he claims, they will die in their sins. When they have lifted up the Son of Man, they will realise who he is and that he speaks as the Father taught him, the Father who is always with him because he always pleases him. Many believe.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is saturated with the language of witness and judgment (a courtroom), light and darkness (the ceremonial torch-lighting of Tabernacles still in view), and the 'I AM' sayings that claim identity with the God who spoke to Moses. Jesus simultaneously judges (he is the one who judges truly, v. 16) and refuses to judge (he did not come to condemn, v. 15). This paradox is resolved in the cross: all judgment was poured out on him so that those who come to him face no condemnation.
verseByVerse.examples: The woman caught in adultery: the accusers depart one by one, beginning with the oldest (the most self-aware of their own sin). Only two are left: the woman and the one who could have condemned her. She goes free not because the law is set aside but because Jesus will shortly bear its full penalty. Every Christian stands where she stood: condemned by the law, set free by the one who alone can say 'neither do I condemn you,' because he bore the condemnation himself.

verseByVerse.quote: but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Early in the morning he came again to the temple. All the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes to the Mount of Olives. At dawn he comes back to the temple, and all the people gather round him; he sits down and teaches them.

Textual note: the woman caught in adultery. The story (7:53–8:11) is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts (P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus), from early translations and from the commentaries of the early Greek fathers. It first appears in Codex Bezae (fifth century), and in other manuscripts it is placed after 7:36, 7:44, 21:25 or Luke 21:38. Its vocabulary is more like Luke’s than John’s. Yet it was known early (perhaps by Papias, about AD 125) and has every mark of a true story about Jesus.

Where Christians differ. Some (especially those who follow the Byzantine text) defend it as part of John. Most evangelical scholars hold that it was not in the original Gospel but is a reliable early tradition. Verdict: it is probably not part of inspired Scripture as John wrote it, so no doctrine should rest on it alone; but it agrees fully with Jesus’ character in the Gospels and may be read and taught with that caution.

The Mount of Olives. Jesus lodged at Bethany or camped on the hillside during festivals (Luke 21:37).
verseByVerse.note: Jesus spent nights on the Mount of Olives during his time in Jerusalem. Teachers sat to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman who had been caught in adultery, and placing her in the midst they said to him, "Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The teachers of the law and the Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery. They make her stand in front of everyone and tell Jesus, as Teacher, that this woman has been caught in the very act of adultery.

Where is the man? Caught in the act means two were involved; the law required both to die (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). His absence exposes the injustice.

In the midst. Publicly shamed, used as bait.

On a Tuesday. Beware of using someone’s sin as a weapon in an argument. People are not exhibits.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now in the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. So what do you say?" This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him. Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They point out that in the law Moses commanded them to stone such women, and ask what he says. They are testing him, to find grounds to accuse him. Jesus bends down and writes on the ground with his finger.

The trap. If Jesus says “stone her”, he defies Rome, which reserved capital punishment (18:31), and loses his reputation for mercy. If he says “let her go”, he defies Moses.

Writing on the ground. What he wrote is not recorded. Suggestions: their sins; Jeremiah 17:13 (those who turn away will be written in the earth); the law, as God wrote it with his finger (Exodus 31:18); or simply a refusal to be hurried. Verdict: unknown, and the silence is part of the point.
verseByVerse.note: The law required both the man and the woman caught in adultery to be put to death; the man is missing. Rome did not allow the Jewish authorities to carry out executions, so the question was a trap either way.

parallels.desc: both of them shall die

verseByVerse.quote: And as they continued to ask him, he stood up and said to them, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her." And once more he bent down and wrote on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they keep questioning him, he straightens up and tells them that whoever among them is without sin should be the first to throw a stone at her. Again he bends down and writes on the ground.

The first stone. The law required witnesses to throw first (Deuteronomy 17:7). Jesus upholds the law but applies it to the accusers’ consciences.

What it does not mean. Not that sin should never be named or justice never done, or that only the sinless may judge. Jesus exposes hypocrisy and misuse of the law, not the rightness of courts (Romans 13:4).

On a Tuesday. Before you condemn someone, look in the mirror (Matthew 7:3–5; Galatians 6:1).
verseByVerse.note: Under the law the witnesses were to throw the first stones.

parallels.desc: the hand of the witnesses first against him

verseByVerse.quote: But when they heard it, they went away one by one, beginning with the older ones, and Jesus was left alone with the woman standing before him. Jesus stood up and said to her, "Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?" She said, "No one, Lord." And Jesus said, "Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they hear this, they leave one by one, beginning with the oldest, until Jesus is left alone with the woman standing there. He straightens up and asks her where they are: has no one condemned her? No one, she says. Then neither does he condemn her. She is to go, and from now on sin no more.

The oldest first. Perhaps the most self-aware, or the ones with the longest record.

Alone. Augustine: “Two were left, misery and mercy.”

Neither do I condemn you. The only sinless one, who could have thrown the stone, does not. Not because sin does not matter, but because he will bear its condemnation himself (Romans 8:1–3).

Go and sin no more. Forgiveness and repentance go together. Grace does not excuse sin; it frees from it (Titus 2:11–12). The order matters: first no condemnation, then a new life.

For worship. Thank Jesus that when your accusers have their case, he says, “Neither do I condemn you.”

parallels.desc: no condemnation

verseByVerse.quote: Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." So the Pharisees said to him, "You are bearing witness about yourself; your testimony is not true." Jesus answered, "Even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from and where I am going, but you do not know where I come from or where I am going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus speaks to them again: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” The Pharisees object that he is testifying about himself, so his testimony is not valid. Jesus answers that even if he testifies about himself, his testimony is true, because he knows where he came from and where he is going, but they do not.

The lamps of the feast. On the first night of Booths, four great golden lamps were lit in the Court of the Women, near the treasury (v. 20), so that it was said every courtyard in Jerusalem was lit. Against that background Jesus claims to be the true light, not for one city but for the world (1:4–9; Isaiah 49:6).

Follows. As Israel followed the pillar of fire in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21).

The light of life. Light that gives life, and life lived in the light.

Self-testimony. In 5:31 Jesus conceded the legal point. Here he adds that his testimony is in fact true, because he alone knows his origin and destiny.

For worship. Follow the light today, one step at a time (Psalm 119:105).
verseByVerse.note: At the Feast of Booths great lamps were lit in the temple courts. This is the second of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: a pillar of fire to give them light
a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They judge by human standards; he judges no one. Yet even if he does judge, his judgment is true, because he is not alone: it is he and the Father who sent him.

According to the flesh. By appearances (7:24).

I judge no one. His purpose in coming was to save, not condemn (3:17). Yet he will judge (5:22, 27), and his judgment is perfectly just.

verseByVerse.quote: "In your Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In their own law it is written that the testimony of two witnesses is valid. He testifies about himself, and the Father who sent him testifies about him.

Your law. Not disowning the law, but pressing them on their own ground (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15).

Two witnesses. The Son and the Father: a claim that only God could make.

parallels.desc: two or three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him therefore, "Where is your Father?" Jesus answered, "You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also." These words he spoke in the treasury, as he taught in the temple; but no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask where his Father is. Jesus answers that they know neither him nor his Father; if they knew him, they would know his Father too. He says this in the treasury, while teaching in the temple, but no one seizes him, because his hour has not yet come.

Where is your Father? Perhaps a sneer about his birth (v. 41).

Know me, know the Father. The Son is the only way to know God (14:7–9).

The treasury. Probably the area in the Court of the Women where thirteen trumpet-shaped offering chests stood (Mark 12:41), close to the great lamps, and next to the chamber where the Sanhedrin met. He speaks almost under their noses.
verseByVerse.note: The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, where the offering chests stood.

verseByVerse.quote: So he said to them again, "I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come." So the Jews said, "Will he kill himself, since he says, 'Where I am going, you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He tells them again that he is going away. They will look for him and die in their sin; where he is going, they cannot come. The Jewish leaders wonder whether he will kill himself, since he says they cannot come where he is going.

Die in your sin. The most solemn warning: to die unforgiven, with sin unremoved.

Kill himself? Mockery: suicide was thought to lead to the depths of Hades, where they would certainly not go. Irony again: he will lay down his life, though not by his own hand (10:17–18).

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. I told you that you would die in your sins, for unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He tells them that they are from below, but he is from above; they belong to this world, but he does not. That is why he said they will die in their sins: unless they believe that “I am he”, they will die in their sins.

From below, from above. Two origins, two kingdoms (3:31; 18:36).

I am he. Literally “I am”, with no predicate. In Isaiah 43:10–13 God says, “that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he.” Jesus claims the divine self-identification.

Where Christians differ: must people believe Jesus is God? Some say it is enough to follow Jesus’ teaching. Jesus says faith in who he is, is necessary for salvation. Verdict: saving faith trusts Jesus as the one he says he is: the I AM, God the Son, come in the flesh (1 John 4:2–3; 5:20).
verseByVerse.note: “That I am he” is literally “that I am” — the divine name.

parallels.desc: that you may know and believe me, that I am he

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you?" Jesus said to them, "Just what I have been telling you from the beginning. I have much to say about you and much to judge, but he who sent me is true, and I declare to the world what I have heard from him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask who he is. Jesus says he is what he has been telling them from the beginning. He has much to say about them and much to judge, but the one who sent him is truthful, and he tells the world what he has heard from him.

A difficult phrase. The Greek of Jesus’ reply is notoriously obscure. It may mean “What I have told you from the beginning”, or “Why do I speak to you at all?” Verdict: the ESV’s reading fits the context: he has been consistent from the start.

verseByVerse.quote: They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father. So Jesus said to them, "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They do not understand that he is speaking to them about the Father. So Jesus says that when they have lifted up the Son of Man, then they will know that “I am he”, and that he does nothing on his own but speaks just as the Father taught him.

When you have lifted up. They will crucify him (3:14; 12:32–33). The cross will reveal who he is (Mark 15:39).

Then you will know. Not that all will believe, but that the truth will become plain: some will know to their salvation (Acts 2:36–41), others to their judgment.

For worship. At the cross we see who Jesus is: the great I AM, lifted up for sinners.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: he shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: "And he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him." As he was saying these things, many believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who sent him is with him and has not left him alone, because he always does what pleases him. As he says these things, many believe in him.

Not alone. Even facing hostility, Jesus has the Father’s presence (16:32). On the cross he will cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34), bearing our forsakenness.

Always. A claim of sinlessness (v. 46; Hebrews 4:15).

Many believed. But their faith is about to be tested (vv. 31–59).

parallels.desc: I am not alone, for the Father is with me

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–59 — The Children of Abraham and the Great I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus tells Jews who had believed him that if they hold to his teaching, they are truly his disciples; they will know the truth, and it will free them. They protest that as Abraham’s descendants they have never been anyone’s slaves. Jesus answers that whoever sins is a slave to sin; a slave has no permanent place in the household, but a son does, so if the Son frees them, they will be truly free. They are Abraham’s descendants, yet they want to kill him because his word finds no room in them. If they were Abraham’s children, they would act as Abraham did. They insist God is their only Father; Jesus says that if he were, they would love him, since he came from God. They cannot hear his word because they belong to their father the devil, a murderer from the start and the father of lies. They do not believe him precisely because he tells the truth; none of them can prove him guilty of sin. They accuse him of being a Samaritan with a demon. He denies it: he honours his Father, who will vindicate him. Whoever keeps his word will never see death. They scoff: Abraham and the prophets died; is he greater than they? Jesus answers that his Father glorifies him, and that Abraham rejoiced to see his day. They object that he is not yet fifty, and Jesus replies that before Abraham came into being, he is. They pick up stones, but he slips away from the temple.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage presents two competing genealogies: Abraham's children versus the devil's children. The distinguishing mark is not ethnic lineage but moral resemblance — you are of your father the devil if you do his works (lying and murder). This is not ethnic polemic but spiritual diagnosis: the unregenerate heart, whatever its ancestry, is in bondage to the father of lies. The truth that sets free (v. 32) is not philosophical insight but the person of Christ himself (v. 36). Freedom is not the absence of constraint but the liberation of the will from slavery to sin, accomplished by the Son who is himself free.
verseByVerse.examples: The stoning attempt at chapter's end is the authorities' answer to 'Before Abraham was, I am.' They understand perfectly: this is a claim to be the eternal God, the I AM of Exodus 3. They reach for stones because they reject the claim as blasphemy. For the Christian, reading this from the other side of the resurrection, this is the moment where the curtain is drawn back and the eternal Word stands visible in human flesh, claiming what was always true. The authorities stone the wrong person for the right reason — he is exactly who he says he is.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, "If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says to the Jews who had believed him that if they remain in his word, they are truly his disciples. They will know the truth, and the truth will set them free.

Abide. Continuing in Jesus’ word is the mark of true discipleship (15:7). Initial belief must become settled faith.

The truth. Not truth in general, but the truth revealed in Jesus, who is the truth (14:6).

Free. From sin (v. 34), not merely from ignorance.

What it does not mean. Often quoted on university buildings to mean that education liberates. Jesus means that knowing him frees from slavery to sin.

For worship. Thank Christ for the freedom that only he can give.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "We are offspring of Abraham and have never been enslaved to anyone. How is it that you say, 'You will become free'?" Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answer that they are Abraham’s descendants and have never been slaves to anyone. How can he say they will be set free? Jesus answers solemnly that everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.

Never enslaved? A remarkable claim from a people who had been slaves in Egypt and Babylon and were under Roman rule. They mean they have never been inwardly enslaved, as children of Abraham.

A slave to sin. Sin is not just an act but a master (Romans 6:16–20).

Where Christians differ: free will. Pelagians and many moderns hold that humans have a natural freedom to choose good. Augustine, Luther (“The Bondage of the Will”), Calvin and the Reformed confessions teach that fallen people freely choose what they want, but cannot by nature want God; their will is enslaved to sin until Christ sets it free (Westminster Confession 9.3–4). Verdict: bondage of the will: we are free to do what we love, but by nature we do not love God; only the Son makes us free indeed.
verseByVerse.note: Israel had been in bondage to Egypt, Babylon and now Rome; they meant they had never inwardly accepted slavery.

parallels.desc: slaves of sin

verseByVerse.quote: "The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A slave does not have a permanent place in the household, but a son belongs there for ever. So if the Son sets them free, they will be free indeed.

Slave and son. Ishmael and Isaac (Genesis 21:10; Galatians 4:21–31). A slave could be sold; a son is heir.

The Son. Only the Son of the house can free slaves and adopt them as sons.

Free indeed. Real freedom: not doing whatever we want, but being made able to do what God made us for.

On a Tuesday. What habit still enslaves you? Bring it to the Son, who sets free.
verseByVerse.note: A slave had no permanent place in a household; a son did.

parallels.desc: cast out this slave woman and her son

verseByVerse.quote: "I know that you are offspring of Abraham; yet you seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you. I speak of what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have heard from your father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus knows they are Abraham’s descendants, yet they are trying to kill him, because his word has no place in them. He speaks of what he has seen in his Father’s presence, and they do what they have heard from their father.

Descendants, but not children. Physical descent is not spiritual kinship (Romans 9:6–8; Galatians 3:7).

No place. His word makes no headway in them.

Your father. Not yet named, but soon (v. 44).

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Abraham is our father." Jesus said to them, "If you were Abraham's children, you would be doing the works Abraham did, but now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. This is not what Abraham did."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answer that Abraham is their father. Jesus says that if they were Abraham’s children, they would do what Abraham did. But now they are trying to kill a man who has told them the truth he heard from God. Abraham did not do this.

The works of Abraham. Abraham believed God (Genesis 15:6) and welcomed God’s messengers (Genesis 18). Children resemble their father.

A man. Jesus speaks of himself as fully human.

On a Tuesday. Religious heritage is a gift, but not a substitute for personal faith. Being raised in a Christian home does not make you a Christian.

parallels.desc: Abraham welcomes the LORD’s messengers

verseByVerse.quote: "You are doing the works your father did." They said to him, "We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father — even God." Jesus said to them, "If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came from God and I am here. I came not of my own accord, but he sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are doing what their father does. They reply that they were not born of sexual immorality; they have one Father, God himself. Jesus answers that if God were their Father, they would love him, for he came from God and is here. He did not come on his own; God sent him.

Not born of immorality. Perhaps a jibe at Jesus’ birth, rumoured to be illegitimate (compare later Jewish polemic). Or a claim that they are not idolaters, spiritual adulterers (Hosea 2:4).

If God were your Father. Love for God shows itself in love for his Son (1 John 5:1).
verseByVerse.note: Their retort may hint at rumours about Jesus’ own birth.

parallels.desc: have we not all one Father?

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word. You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks out of his own character, for he is a liar and the father of lies."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do they not understand what he says? Because they cannot bear to hear his word. They belong to their father, the devil, and they want to carry out his desires. He was a murderer from the beginning and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks his native language, for he is a liar and the father of lies.

Cannot hear. Moral inability: they do not want to hear.

Your father the devil. The strongest words in the Gospels. Jesus addresses particular opponents who are seeking to kill him (v. 40), not the Jewish people as a whole; he himself was a Jew, as were all his first disciples. The same charge applies to anyone, Gentile or Jew, who resists the truth and seeks to destroy (1 John 3:8–10).

What it does not mean. This verse has been abused to justify centuries of Christian persecution of Jews, an evil the church must repent of. Jesus’ words diagnose the spiritual state of his enemies; they give no licence for hatred (Romans 9:1–5; 10:1).

A murderer from the beginning. Through the lie in Eden he brought death (Genesis 3:4; Romans 5:12); Cain followed his example (1 John 3:12).

The father of lies. All deception ultimately originates with him (2 Corinthians 11:3; Revelation 12:9).
verseByVerse.note: The devil’s lie led to death in Eden; the first murder followed.

parallels.desc: “You will not surely die”

verseByVerse.quote: "But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me. Which one of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But because he tells the truth, they do not believe him. Which of them can convict him of sin? If he tells the truth, why do they not believe him?

Because I tell the truth. Those committed to a lie are repelled by truth.

Which of you convicts me? No one could answer. Jesus’ challenge is a claim of sinlessness that no prophet or apostle ever made (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:22).

For worship. Praise the sinless Son, whose perfect life is credited to all who believe.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason why you do not hear them is that you are not of God." The Jews answered him, "Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever belongs to God hears God’s words. The reason they do not hear is that they do not belong to God. The Jewish leaders reply that they are surely right to say he is a Samaritan and has a demon.

Of God. Belonging precedes hearing (10:26–27). Those born of God hear his voice.

A Samaritan. The worst insult they can think of: a heretic and half-breed. Perhaps also because he criticises Jews as Samaritans did.

A demon. When argument fails, insult remains.
verseByVerse.note: Calling a Jew a Samaritan was an insult.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. Yet I do not seek my own glory; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers that he does not have a demon; he honours his Father, and they dishonour him. He does not seek his own glory; there is one who seeks it, and he is the judge.

Calm reply. He ignores the insult “Samaritan”.

Not my own glory. He leaves vindication to the Father (1 Peter 2:23).

On a Tuesday. When insulted, you need not defend your reputation. Entrust it to God, who judges justly.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.' The Jews said to him, 'Now we know that you have a demon! Abraham died, as did the prophets, yet you say, 'If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says solemnly that if anyone keeps his word, he will never see death. The Jewish leaders say that now they know he has a demon. Abraham died, and so did the prophets, yet he says that whoever keeps his word will never taste death.

Never see death. Not that believers will not die physically, but that death will not be death for them: it has lost its sting (11:25–26; 1 Corinthians 15:55).

Taste death. They misquote him slightly, but the meaning is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: "Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died! Who do you make yourself out to be?" Jesus answered, "If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, 'He is our God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is he greater than their father Abraham, who died? The prophets died too. Who does he make himself out to be? Jesus answers that if he glorifies himself, his glory is nothing. It is his Father who glorifies him, the one they claim as their God.

Greater than Abraham? As with Jacob (4:12), the answer is yes.

Who do you make yourself? The question of the whole Gospel.

My Father glorifies me. In the resurrection and exaltation (17:1, 5).

verseByVerse.quote: "But you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you. But I do know him and I keep his word. Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they do not know him. Jesus knows him. If he said he did not know him, he would be a liar like them. But he does know him and keeps his word. Their father Abraham rejoiced that he would see Jesus’ day; he saw it and was glad.

A liar like you. False modesty would be a lie.

Abraham rejoiced. When? Perhaps at the promise of a seed in whom all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18), or at Isaac’s birth (Genesis 21:6), or the ram provided on Moriah (Genesis 22:8, 13–14), or by faith looking forward (Hebrews 11:13). Jewish tradition held that God showed Abraham the future.

For worship. Abraham longed to see Christ’s day. We live in it. Rejoice.

parallels.desc: having seen them and greeted them from afar

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to him, "You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?" Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jewish leaders object that he is not yet fifty years old; has he seen Abraham? Jesus tells them solemnly, “Before Abraham was, I am.”

Not yet fifty. A round number for the age when a man was past his prime (Numbers 4:3). Jesus was in his early thirties (Luke 3:23).

Textual note. Some early manuscripts read “has Abraham seen you?”. Verdict: “have you seen Abraham?” is better attested; the sense is the same.

Before Abraham was, I am. Not “I was”: Abraham “came into being” (genesthai), but Jesus simply “is” (egō eimi). He claims eternal existence and the very name of God from the burning bush (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:13; 48:12).

Where Christians differ. Jehovah’s Witnesses translate “I have been”, as a statement of pre-existence only. The contrast of tenses and the hearers’ response (v. 59) show that Jesus claimed more. Verdict: the historic Christian reading: Jesus claims to be the eternal God.

For worship. Bow before the I AM, who was before Abraham and is now and ever shall be.
verseByVerse.note: “I am” without anything added echoes the name God gave himself at the burning bush.

parallels.desc: “I AM WHO I AM”
from everlasting to everlasting

verseByVerse.quote: So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they pick up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hides himself and goes out of the temple.

Stones. The penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16). They understood his claim exactly. Building work on the temple meant stones were close at hand.

Hid himself. Not yet his hour. Perhaps a miraculous escape, perhaps slipping away in the crowd.

Leaving the temple. Symbolic: the glory of God departs from the temple, as in Ezekiel 10.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is not a safe, tame teacher. Either he is the I AM, or he is a blasphemer. There is no middle ground.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy.

He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him.”<sup>30</sup>As he was saying these things, many believed in him.<sup>31</sup>So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, “If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples,<sup>32</sup>and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.”<sup>33</sup>They answered him, “We are offspring of Abraham and have never been enslaved to anyone. How is it that you say, ’You will become free’?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin.<sup>35</sup>The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever.<sup>36</sup>So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.<sup>37</sup>I know that you are offspring of Abraham; yet you seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you.<sup>38</sup>I speak of what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have heard from your father.”<sup>39</sup>They answered him, “Abraham is our father.” Jesus said to them, “If you were Abraham’s children, you would be doing the works Abraham did,<sup>40</sup>but now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. This is not what Abraham did.<sup>41</sup>You are doing the works your father did.“ They said to him, ”We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father—even God.”<sup>42</sup>Jesus said to them, “If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came from God and I am here. I came not of my own accord, but he sent me.<sup>43</sup>Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word.<sup>44</sup>You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks out of his own character, for he is a liar and the father of lies.<sup>45</sup>But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me.<sup>46</sup>Which one of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?<sup>47</sup>Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason why you do not hear them is that you are not of God.”<sup>48</sup>The Jews answered him, “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?”<sup>49</sup>Jesus answered, “I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me.<sup>50</sup>Yet I do not seek my own glory; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge.<sup>51</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.”<sup>52</sup>The Jews said to him, “Now we know that you have a demon! Abraham died, as did the prophets, yet you say, ’If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.’<sup>53</sup>Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died! Who do you make yourself out to be?”<sup>54</sup>Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, ’He is our God.’<sup>55</sup>But you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you, but I do know him and I keep his word.<sup>56</sup>Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad.”<sup>57</sup>So the Jews said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?”<sup>58</sup>Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.”<sup>59</sup>So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
8.overview:
The chapter opens with the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11), which the earliest manuscripts of John do not contain; it appears in later manuscripts in various places, sometimes after Luke 21:38. Most scholars, conservative ones included, conclude that it was not part of John’s original Gospel but preserves a genuine memory of Jesus. Its message is unforgettable: the accusers, convicted by Jesus’ words, leave one by one; Jesus does not condemn the woman, and tells her to go and sin no more.

The rest of the chapter continues Jesus’ teaching at the Feast of Booths, where great lamps lit the temple courts. “I am the light of the world,” he says. The Pharisees challenge his self-testimony; he answers that the Father testifies with him, and that unless they believe that “I am he” they will die in their sins; when they have lifted up the Son of Man they will know. To Jews who had believed him he promises that if they abide in his word, the truth will set them free, which offends them as Abraham’s descendants who have never been slaves. Jesus answers that everyone who commits sin is a slave, and that their murderous intent shows that their true father is not Abraham, nor God, but the devil, the father of lies. The argument climaxes in the most explicit claim to deity in the Gospels: “Before Abraham was, I am.” They take up stones, and Jesus leaves the temple. Because the chapter has been used to fuel hatred of Jews, it must be read with care: Jesus speaks as a Jew to particular opponents who were seeking to kill him, and his words warn every religious person, not one people.

9.title: The Man Born Blind

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–41 — Sight and Blindness: The Light of the World at Work
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus sees a man blind from birth, and the disciples ask whose sin caused it. Jesus answers that it is not a matter of blame: it happened so that God’s work could be shown. As the world’s light, he spreads mud made with saliva on the man’s eyes and sends him to wash in Siloam, and the man returns seeing. Neighbours dispute whether he is the same beggar. Because it is the Sabbath, the Pharisees question him; some say a Sabbath-breaker cannot be from God, others that a sinner could not do such signs. The man calls Jesus a prophet. His frightened parents, fearing expulsion from the synagogue, confirm only that he is their son and was born blind. Pressed again to condemn Jesus, the man says he knows only that he was blind and now sees, and teasingly asks if they want to become disciples. They abuse him as a follower of Jesus, while they follow Moses. He argues that God would not answer a sinner, and no one has ever opened eyes born blind, so Jesus must be from God. They expel him. Jesus seeks him out and reveals himself as the Son of Man, and the man believes and worships. Jesus says he came so that the blind might see and those who think they see might become blind; the Pharisees who claim sight remain guilty.
verseByVerse.theology: Physical sight and spiritual sight run in parallel throughout the chapter. The man born blind is a picture of humanity in its natural state — unable to see the Light from birth, requiring an external, sovereign act to receive vision. The Pharisees, who see perfectly with physical eyes, are spiritually blind precisely because they are confident they see (v. 41). This is the paradox of total depravity and spiritual pride: the one who knows he cannot see is the one who can be given sight; the one who insists he sees will remain blind. Spiritual humility is the precondition of illumination.
verseByVerse.examples: The progression of the healed man's confession is a model of growing faith: 'the man called Jesus' (v. 11), 'a prophet' (v. 17), 'from God' (v. 33), 'Lord, I believe' and worship (v. 38). Every encounter with Jesus under pressure produces clearer confession. The Pharisees' investigation — a hostile inquisition — inadvertently drives the man deeper into faith. Opposition to the gospel, when it cannot overcome the testimony of experience, ends by casting out the witness (v. 34) — and Jesus finds the cast-out (v. 35).

verseByVerse.quote: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. And his disciples asked him, "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus walks along, he sees a man who has been blind from birth. His disciples ask him, as Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind.

He saw. The man does not ask; Jesus notices him (5:6).

Blind from birth. Incurable then; and congenital blindness made healing unheard of (v. 32).

Who sinned? The common assumption that suffering is punishment for specific sin (Job’s friends; Exodus 20:5 misapplied). Some rabbis even speculated that a baby could sin in the womb (compare Genesis 25:22).

On a Tuesday. Do we look at people with disabilities as problems to be explained? Jesus saw a person.
verseByVerse.note: Many assumed that disability was punishment for a particular sin, even a parent’s.

parallels.desc: the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers that it was not that this man or his parents sinned, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. We must do the works of the one who sent him while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work.

Not this man. Jesus does not deny that they were sinners, but denies that his blindness was punishment for a particular sin.

That God’s works might be displayed. The purpose, not the cause. God brings good even out of suffering (11:4; Romans 8:28).

Where Christians differ: why does God allow disability? Some read this as meaning God directly caused the blindness for this purpose; others that God permitted a fallen world’s brokenness and redeemed it. Verdict: God is sovereign over all things, including disability (Exodus 4:11), and never acts without purpose; yet suffering belongs to a fallen world, and God’s aim is always mercy and glory. Disabled people are not punished or less valuable; often God’s works are displayed through them in ways the strong miss (2 Corinthians 12:9).

We must work. Jesus includes the disciples. Textual note. Some manuscripts read “I must work”. Verdict: “we” is better attested and harder.

Night is coming. His time is short (12:35).

verseByVerse.quote: "As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world." Having said these things, he spit on the ground and made mud with the saliva. Then he anointed the man's eyes with the mud
verseByVerse.commentary:
As long as he is in the world, he is the light of the world. Having said this, he spits on the ground, makes mud with the saliva and spreads the mud on the man’s eyes.

The light of the world. Repeated from 8:12; now acted out.

Saliva and mud. Saliva was thought to have healing power in the ancient world (Mark 7:33; 8:23). The mud may recall God forming Adam from the dust (Genesis 2:7): the Creator re-creating eyes. Irenaeus made this point in the second century.

Kneading. Making mud was one of the thirty-nine kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath in later rabbinic law; so was anointing eyes for healing when life was not at risk. Jesus seems to provoke the confrontation deliberately.
verseByVerse.note: Saliva was widely believed to have healing power. Kneading mud counted as work on the Sabbath under the traditions.

parallels.desc: the LORD God formed the man of dust

verseByVerse.quote: and said to him, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam" (which means Sent). So he went and washed and came back seeing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He tells him to go and wash in the pool of Siloam, which means Sent. So the man goes, washes and comes back seeing.

Siloam. The pool at the south end of the city, fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel (2 Kings 20:20). In 2004 a large stepped pool from the time of Jesus was uncovered there. Water for the Feast of Booths was drawn from it (7:37).

Sent. John explains the name because Jesus is the one Sent from the Father (vv. 4, 7; 3:17). Washing in “Sent” is a picture of finding light in the Sent One.

Obedience. Like Naaman (2 Kings 5:10–14), he must go and wash. He walks across the city, blind, with mud on his face, trusting Jesus’ word.

For worship. Praise Jesus who opens blind eyes, physical and spiritual (2 Corinthians 4:6).
verseByVerse.note: The pool of Siloam lay at the south end of the city, fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel.

parallels.desc: Hezekiah brought water into the city
the waters of Shiloah

verseByVerse.quote: The neighbors and those who had seen him before as a beggar were saying, "Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?" Some said, "It is he." Others said, "No, but he is like him." He kept saying, "I am the man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His neighbours and those who used to see him begging ask whether this is not the man who used to sit and beg. Some say it is; others say no, he just looks like him. He keeps saying, “I am the man.”

A beggar. Disability meant begging; there was no other living.

Is it he? Conversion makes people unrecognisable.

I am the man. Literally “I am” (egō eimi), an everyday use of the phrase Jesus uses for himself; here simply “It’s me”.

parallels.desc: they recognized him as the one who sat begging

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Then how were your eyes opened?" He answered, "The man called Jesus made mud and anointed my eyes and said to me, 'Go to Siloam and wash.' So I went and washed and received my sight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they ask how his eyes were opened. He answers that the man called Jesus made mud, anointed his eyes and told him to go to Siloam and wash; so he went, washed and received his sight.

The man called Jesus. His first, simple view of Jesus. It will grow (vv. 17, 33, 38).

Simple testimony. He tells what happened, no more, no less.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Where is he?" He said, "I do not know." They brought to the Pharisees the man who had formerly been blind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask where Jesus is. He says he does not know. They bring the man who had been blind to the Pharisees.

I do not know. He has never seen Jesus. He went to Siloam blind.

To the Pharisees. Perhaps from concern about the Sabbath, perhaps just because something extraordinary needs official comment.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was a Sabbath day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. So the Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. And he said to them, "He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was a Sabbath when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. So the Pharisees also ask him how he received his sight. He tells them that Jesus put mud on his eyes, he washed, and now he sees.

The Sabbath. Again (5:9). Jesus could have waited a day; he chose the Sabbath to show that he is Lord of it and that the Sabbath is for mercy (Mark 2:27–28; 3:4).

Shorter each time. His account gets briefer as he grows tired of repeating it.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the Pharisees said, "This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath." But others said, "How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?" And there was a division among them. So they said again to the blind man, "What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes?" He said, "He is a prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the Pharisees say this man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath. Others ask how a sinner could perform such signs. So they are divided. Then they ask the blind man again what he has to say about him, since it was his eyes he opened. He says, “He is a prophet.”

Two arguments. One from the law as they interpret it (Deuteronomy 13:1–5: a sign-worker who leads people astray), one from the evidence. Theology that ignores facts, or facts that ignore theology, both go wrong.

Division. Again (7:43; 10:19).

A prophet. Like Elijah and Elisha, who did miracles. His understanding grows (4:19).

parallels.desc: a prophet who gives a sign

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received his sight and asked them, "Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jewish leaders do not believe he had been blind and received his sight until they call his parents. They ask whether this is their son, who they say was born blind, and how he now sees.

Unbelief seeks a loophole. If the man was not really blind, there is no miracle.

On a Tuesday. When evidence is unwelcome, people often attack the witness. Be patient with sceptics, and honest yourself about evidence you do not like.

verseByVerse.quote: His parents answered, "We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His parents answer that they know he is their son and that he was born blind. But they do not know how he now sees or who opened his eyes. They tell them to ask him; he is of age and can speak for himself.

Careful answers. They confirm the facts, which proves the miracle, but say nothing about Jesus.

Of age. Over thirteen, able to give legal testimony.
verseByVerse.note: A son was regarded as of age at about thirteen.

verseByVerse.quote: (His parents said these things because they feared the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess Jesus to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue. Therefore his parents said, "He is of age; ask him.")
verseByVerse.commentary:
His parents say this because they are afraid of the Jewish leaders, who had already agreed that anyone who confessed Jesus to be the Christ would be put out of the synagogue. That is why his parents say that he is of age and they should ask him.

Put out of the synagogue. Aposynagōgos (also 12:42; 16:2). Expulsion meant social and religious exclusion: no worship, community, perhaps work or marriage.

Where Christians differ: an anachronism? Some scholars argue that formal expulsion of Christians dates from the 80s AD (a synagogue prayer cursing “heretics”), and that John reads his own day back into Jesus’ time. Others note that synagogues could discipline members long before, and that local action against Jesus’ followers is entirely plausible (Luke 6:22). Verdict: there is no good reason to doubt that local synagogue leaders threatened exclusion during Jesus’ ministry.

Fear. The parents choose safety over gratitude. Fear of exclusion still silences believers.

On a Tuesday. What would it cost you to confess Christ openly at work, at school or in your family? Ask God for courage.
verseByVerse.note: Being put out of the synagogue meant exclusion from the community’s worship and social life.

parallels.desc: they will put you out of the synagogues

verseByVerse.quote: So for the second time they called the man who had been blind and said to him, "Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner." He answered, "Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the second time they summon the man who had been blind and tell him to give glory to God: they know this man is a sinner. He answers that whether he is a sinner he does not know. One thing he does know: he was blind, and now he sees.

Give glory to God. An oath formula, as Joshua used it with Achan (Joshua 7:19): tell the truth before God. They want him to confess that he lied, or to credit God and not Jesus.

We know. Their minds are made up.

One thing I know. He will not be drawn into theological debate; he sticks to his experience. John Newton echoed him in “Amazing Grace”: “was blind, but now I see.”

On a Tuesday. You may not be able to answer every argument, but you can say what Christ has done for you.
verseByVerse.note: “Give glory to God” was a solemn call to tell the truth.

parallels.desc: give glory to the LORD and tell me now what you have done

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?" He answered them, "I have told you already, and you would not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask what Jesus did to him: how did he open his eyes? He answers that he has told them already, and they would not listen. Why do they want to hear it again? Do they want to become his disciples too?

Growing bold. The once-dependent beggar now teases the religious elite.

Also. “You too?”: he implies that he is already a disciple.

On a Tuesday. A little humour in witness can disarm hostility, as long as it is not cruel.

verseByVerse.quote: And they reviled him, saying, "You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They abuse him and say that he is that man’s disciple, but they are disciples of Moses. They know God spoke to Moses, but as for this man, they do not know where he comes from.

Disciples of Moses. As if Moses and Jesus were rivals. Moses wrote of Jesus (5:46).

We do not know where he comes from. Ironic: earlier they claimed to know (7:27). And the man who knows where Jesus comes from has his eyes opened.

verseByVerse.quote: The man answered, "Why, this is an amazing thing! You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man answers that this is astonishing! They do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened his eyes. We know that God does not listen to sinners, but he listens to anyone who worships him and does his will.

Amazing. The experts do not know; the beggar does.

God does not listen to sinners. A common Old Testament principle (Psalm 66:18; Proverbs 15:29; Isaiah 1:15): God does not answer the prayers of the impenitent.

Where Christians differ: does God hear the prayers of unbelievers? Some have used this verse to say God hears no prayer from an unbeliever. But the man is not stating doctrine; he is arguing from accepted wisdom. Scripture shows God hearing a sinner’s cry for mercy (Luke 18:13–14) and answering pagans’ prayers (Jonah 1:14–16; Acts 10:4). Verdict: God does not reward the prayers of those who hold on to sin, but he always hears the cry of a sinner turning to him.

parallels.desc: if I had cherished iniquity, the Lord would not have listened

verseByVerse.quote: "Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Never since the world began has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.

Never. No such healing is recorded in the Old Testament. Isaiah connects opening the eyes of the blind with the coming of God himself (Isaiah 29:18; 35:5; 42:7).

From God. The man’s logic is sound: what Jesus did shows where he is from (3:2).

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind shall be opened

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?" And they cast him out. Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, "Do you believe in the Son of Man?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answer that he was born steeped in sin; is he trying to teach them? And they throw him out. Jesus hears that they have thrown him out, and when he finds him, he asks whether he believes in the Son of Man.

Born in utter sin. They contradict themselves: they now admit he was born blind, and blame his birth on sin (v. 2).

Cast him out. Probably both from the meeting and from the synagogue (v. 22).

Jesus found him. Rejected by the religious community, he is sought by the Shepherd (10:3–4, 16). The church may cast out; Christ never casts out those who come (6:37).

The Son of Man. Textual note. Later manuscripts read “Son of God” (KJV). Verdict: “Son of Man” is original, the figure of judgment (v. 39; 5:27).

For worship. If you have been rejected for Christ’s sake, he will find you.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: brought forth in iniquity

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?" Jesus said to him, "You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He replies, calling him Sir, by asking who that is, so that he may believe in him. Jesus tells him that he has seen him: the one speaking with him is he.

Ready to believe. His heart is open.

You have seen him. With the eyes Jesus gave him. The first face this man ever saw clearly may have been that of the Son of Man.

The one speaking. As with the Samaritan woman (4:26).

parallels.desc: I who speak to you am he

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Lord, I believe," and he worshiped him. Jesus said, "For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He says, “Lord, I believe,” and worships him. Jesus says he came into this world for judgment, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.

He worshipped. Proskyneō, used in John for worship of God (4:20–24). Jesus accepts it. Contrast Peter (Acts 10:25–26) and the angel (Revelation 22:8–9), who refuse it.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts omit “He said, Lord, I believe, and he worshipped him. Jesus said”. Verdict: most scholars keep it; the omission is probably accidental, and the climax fits the story.

For judgment. Not his purpose (3:17) but the inevitable effect: the light reveals and divides.

For worship. Say it with him: “Lord, I believe,” and worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, "Are we also blind?" Jesus said to them, "If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, 'We see,' your guilt remains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the Pharisees who are with him hear this and ask whether they are blind too. Jesus tells them that if they were blind, they would not be guilty; but now that they claim to see, their guilt remains.

Are we blind? Expecting the answer no.

If you were blind. Those who know they are blind can be healed. Those who claim to see refuse the light, and their guilt stays (Revelation 3:17–18).

The most dangerous blindness. Not ignorance but self-confidence.

On a Tuesday. Pray daily, “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18).

parallels.desc: a guide to the blind
