One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.”<sup>26</sup>They said to him, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”<sup>27</sup>He answered them, “I have told you already, and you would not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?”<sup>28</sup>And they reviled him, saying, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.<sup>29</sup>We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from.”<sup>30</sup>The man answered, “Why, this is an amazing thing! You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes.<sup>31</sup>We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him.<sup>32</sup>Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind.<sup>33</sup>If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”<sup>34</sup>They answered him, “You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?” And they cast him out.<sup>35</sup>Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”<sup>36</sup>He answered, “And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?”<sup>37</sup>Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you.”<sup>38</sup>He said, “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped him.<sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”<sup>40</sup>Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?”<sup>41</sup>Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, ’We see,’ your guilt remains.
9.overview:
Jesus has just called himself the light of the world (8:12); now he gives sight to a man blind from birth, the sixth sign in John. The disciples ask whose sin caused the blindness; Jesus answers that it happened so that God’s works might be displayed in him. He makes mud with saliva, spreads it on the man’s eyes and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam, “Sent”, and the man comes back seeing. Then follows one of the most dramatic and humorous scenes in the Gospels, a series of interrogations. The neighbours cannot agree it is the same man. The Pharisees are split, because the healing happened on a Sabbath. The parents, afraid of being expelled from the synagogue, refuse to say more than that he is their son and was born blind. Questioned again, the man refuses to call Jesus a sinner: “One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.” When he asks, with an edge, whether they want to become disciples too, they insult him and throw him out.

Meanwhile his understanding of Jesus grows: “the man called Jesus”, then “a prophet”, then a man “from God”, and finally, when Jesus finds him after his expulsion, “Lord, I believe”, as he worships him. The Pharisees go the other way, from confident sight to blindness. Jesus says he came so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind; because they claim to see, their guilt remains. The chapter is a parable of conversion and of religious self-deception.

10.title: The Good Shepherd

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Good Shepherd Lays Down His Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus contrasts the true shepherd with thieves who climb into the sheepfold another way. The shepherd comes through the gate; the sheep recognise his voice as he calls each by name and leads them out, but they run from strangers. When his hearers miss the meaning, Jesus says plainly that he is the door: whoever enters through him will be saved and find pasture. Thieves come to steal and destroy; he came to give life to the full. He is the good shepherd, who gives his life for the sheep, unlike the hired hand who abandons them to the wolf. He knows his sheep and they know him, as he and the Father know each other. He has other sheep outside this fold, whom he will gather into one flock under one shepherd. The Father loves him because he lays down his life freely, with authority to take it up again. Some in the crowd say he is mad and possessed; others reply that no demon could open blind eyes.
verseByVerse.theology: The shepherd imagery draws on the entire Old Testament tradition: God as shepherd (Ps. 23; Ezek. 34), the coming Davidic shepherd-king (Ezek. 34:23-24; Jer. 23:4), and the contrast between true and false shepherds throughout the prophets. Jesus claims all of these simultaneously: he is the door (the only legitimate access to God), the good shepherd (who gives rather than takes), and the one who lays down his life voluntarily (the self-giving that no hired hand would perform). The death is central: the shepherd metaphor cannot be understood apart from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The sheep hear his voice: the recognition of Christ by the elect is not achievement but gift. The sheep do not learn to recognize the shepherd's voice; they already know it because they are his sheep. This is Calvinist soteriology rendered in pastoral imagery: election precedes hearing, calling brings the elect home, and not one of the Father's sheep is lost. The Pharisees cannot hear because they are not sheep (v. 26); the church hears because she has been given ears by the Shepherd himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber. But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says solemnly that anyone who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in another way is a thief and a robber. The one who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.

Context. Spoken to the Pharisees who had just cast out the healed man (9:34–41). They are the false shepherds.

The sheepfold. A walled enclosure, often of stone, where several flocks were kept at night, with one entrance watched by a gatekeeper.

Ezekiel 34. God condemns Israel’s shepherds who fed themselves and scattered the flock, and promises to shepherd his sheep himself and set over them one shepherd, his servant David. Jesus claims to fulfil it.

On a Tuesday. If you lead others in a church, a family or a team, ask whether you are a shepherd or a thief: do you feed them or use them?
verseByVerse.note: A sheepfold was a walled enclosure where several flocks might be kept overnight, with a single doorway.

parallels.desc: the false shepherds of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: "To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gatekeeper opens the door for him, and the sheep hear his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. When he has brought out all his own, he walks ahead of them, and the sheep follow him because they know his voice.

The gatekeeper. Probably just a detail of the picture, though some see John the Baptist or the Father.

By name. Middle Eastern shepherds still name their sheep and call them, and the sheep respond only to their own shepherd. Jesus knows each of his people personally (Isaiah 43:1).

Leads them out. Out of the fold of Judaism that has rejected him, as the blind man was put out (9:34).

He goes before them. Eastern shepherds lead from the front rather than driving from behind. Jesus never asks his people to go where he has not gone.

For worship. The Shepherd calls you by name. Listen for his voice in his word.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds in the East led their flocks rather than drove them, and named their sheep; the sheep knew their shepherd’s call.

parallels.desc: who shall go out before them and bring them in

verseByVerse.quote: "A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers." This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will not follow a stranger but will run away from him, because they do not recognise a stranger’s voice. Jesus uses this illustration, but they do not understand what he is telling them.

Discernment. Sheep that know the shepherd’s voice recognise false voices. The blind man would not follow the Pharisees.

Figure of speech. Paroimia: an extended picture, a parable.

On a Tuesday. The best protection against false teaching is knowing Christ’s voice in Scripture so well that a false voice sounds wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus again said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus tells them again solemnly that he is the door of the sheep. All who came before him are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them.

The door. The third “I am”. Some shepherds slept across the entrance of the fold, so that the shepherd himself was the door.

Before me. Not the prophets, but false messiahs and leaders who claimed to bring salvation (Acts 5:36–37). Textual note. Some manuscripts omit “before me”, perhaps to avoid seeming to condemn the prophets. Verdict: probably original.
verseByVerse.note: This is the third of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the door. Whoever enters through him will be saved and will come in and go out and find pasture. The thief comes only to steal, kill and destroy. Jesus has come so that they may have life and have it abundantly.

The only door. “If anyone”: open to all; “by me”: through him alone (14:6; Acts 4:12).

In and out. A Hebrew phrase for living in safety and freedom (Deuteronomy 28:6; Psalm 121:8).

Abundantly. Life overflowing: eternal life now, full of God.

What it does not mean. Not health and wealth. The prosperity gospel misuses this verse. Abundant life may include suffering (16:33); its abundance is Christ himself (Philippians 4:11–13).

For worship. Thank Christ for the door he opened, and for the pasture beyond it (Psalm 23).
verseByVerse.note: “Go in and out” is a Hebrew expression for living in safety.

parallels.desc: this is the gate of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. The hired man, who is not the shepherd and does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep and runs away, and the wolf seizes and scatters them.

Good. Kalos: noble, beautiful, true, not merely competent.

Lays down his life. Shepherds sometimes risked their lives (1 Samuel 17:34–35), but rarely died. Jesus will die, deliberately, for the sheep. “For” (hyper) means on behalf of, in place of.

Where Christians differ: for whom did he die? Arminians say Christ died for all people equally. Reformed theology sees in this chapter a particular, effective death “for the sheep”, those the Father gave him (vv. 15, 26–29), who will certainly be saved. Verdict: definite atonement: the Shepherd died to save his sheep, and none of them will be lost; yet the call to come to him goes to all, and none who come are refused (6:37).

The hired hand. Paid, but not committed. Leaders who serve for wages or status abandon people in danger (Zechariah 11:17).
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds risked their lives against wild animals and thieves.

parallels.desc: David rescues a lamb from a lion

verseByVerse.quote: "He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He runs away because he is a hired hand and does not care about the sheep. Jesus is the good shepherd. He knows his own, and his own know him.

Cares nothing. The real difference between shepherd and hireling is love.

Knows. Personal, intimate, saving knowledge (Matthew 7:23; 2 Timothy 2:19).

On a Tuesday. Pastors, elders and leaders: do you know your people? Members: do you let yourselves be known?

parallels.desc: woe to my worthless shepherd
the Lord knows those who are his

verseByVerse.quote: "just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep. And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as the Father knows him and he knows the Father; and he lays down his life for the sheep. He has other sheep that are not of this fold. He must bring them too, and they will listen to his voice, so there will be one flock, one shepherd.

As the Father knows me. Our relationship with Christ is modelled on the love within the Trinity (17:21–23).

Other sheep. Gentiles who will believe (11:52; Ephesians 2:11–22). Not people on other planets, nor (as Latter-day Saints teach) ancient inhabitants of America. Verdict: the Gentile mission, as the rest of John and the New Testament confirm.

Must. Divine necessity: Christ will gather all his sheep through the preaching of the gospel (Romans 10:14–17).

One flock. Not one fold (the Latin Vulgate wrongly had “one fold”, used to argue for one visible institution). One flock may have many folds, but one shepherd.

For worship. Thank Christ for bringing you, perhaps a Gentile, into his flock.
verseByVerse.note: The “other sheep” are Gentiles who would believe.

parallels.desc: I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David

verseByVerse.quote: "For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father loves him because he lays down his life in order to take it up again. No one takes it from him, but he lays it down of his own accord. He has authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again. This command he received from his Father.

Voluntary. Jesus is not a victim. He chose the cross (18:4–11; 19:11, 30).

To take it up. The resurrection is in view from the start; Jesus himself rises (2:19), though elsewhere the Father raises him (Acts 2:24). The persons of the Trinity act together.

The command. His death is obedience (Philippians 2:8).

verseByVerse.quote: There was again a division among the Jews because of these words. Many of them said, "He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again the Jews are divided because of these words. Many say he has a demon and is out of his mind: why listen to him?

Insane. The same verdict his family once reached (Mark 3:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Others said, "These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Others say these are not the words of someone demon-possessed. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?

The evidence speaks. His words are sane and his works are good (9:32–33).

On a Tuesday. Jesus still divides opinion. Make sure your verdict rests on his words and works, not on others’ opinion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–42 — I and the Father Are One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the winter Feast of Dedication, the leaders corner Jesus in Solomon’s Colonnade and demand that he say plainly whether he is the Christ. He replies that his works already testify, but they do not believe because they are not his sheep. His sheep hear his voice and follow; he gives them eternal life, and neither he nor the Father will let anyone snatch them away. He and the Father are one. They reach for stones, accusing him of making himself God. He answers from the psalm in which God’s word calls human judges “gods”: since Scripture cannot be overturned, how can they call it blasphemy when the one the Father consecrated and sent calls himself God’s Son? At least they should believe his works, and see that the Father is in him and he in the Father. Escaping arrest, he withdraws beyond the Jordan, where many believe in him, saying that everything John said about him has proved true.
verseByVerse.theology: The climactic declaration — I and the Father are one — is the theological summit of the Good Shepherd discourse and of John's presentation of Jesus' identity in the public ministry. The unity is not merely unity of purpose (though it includes that) but ontological unity — the unity of shared divine nature that the Jews correctly understand as a claim to deity (v. 33). Jesus defends the claim not by retreating from it but by appealing to the greater logic: if Scripture can call judges 'gods,' how much more can the one the Father consecrated and sent be called the Son of God? The defense is not a reduction of the claim but an escalation of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Beyond the Jordan, many believe on the basis of John's testimony confirmed by Jesus' works. This is the pattern of fruitful ministry: the faithful witness of the forerunner, confirmed by the reality of the one the forerunner announced, produces lasting faith. The chapter ends not in Jerusalem with hostility but in the wilderness with harvest — a reminder that the gospel often bears its richest fruit outside the centers of established religion.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then comes the Feast of Dedication in Jerusalem. It is winter, and Jesus is walking in the temple, in Solomon’s Colonnade.

The Feast of Dedication. Hanukkah, in December, celebrating the rededication of the temple by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC after the Syrian king Antiochus IV had defiled it with pagan sacrifice (1 Maccabees 4:36–59). It was also called the Feast of Lights. Hopes of a new liberator ran high.

Winter. Cold and wet; Jesus walks in the shelter of the covered colonnade on the east side of the temple court, later a meeting place of the church (Acts 3:11; 5:12).

The true temple. At a feast of temple dedication, Jesus is the one “consecrated” by the Father (v. 36), the true temple (2:21).
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) celebrated the re-dedication of the temple in 164 BC, after Antiochus IV had defiled it. It fell in December. Solomon’s colonnade ran along the east side of the temple courts.

parallels.desc: Solomon’s Portico

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, "How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly." Jesus answered them, "I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father's name bear witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jewish leaders gather round him and ask how long he will keep them in suspense. If he is the Christ, he should tell them plainly. Jesus answers that he has told them, and they do not believe. The works he does in his Father’s name testify about him.

Surrounded. Hemmed in, perhaps threateningly.

Tell us plainly. They want a political claim they can act on, or use against him.

I told you. Not in the word “Messiah”, which they would misunderstand, but in his words and works.

verseByVerse.quote: "but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they do not believe, because they are not his sheep. His sheep hear his voice; he knows them, and they follow him.

The order. Not “you are not my sheep because you do not believe”, but “you do not believe because you are not my sheep”. Belonging to Christ by the Father’s gift comes before faith and explains it (6:37, 44; 8:47).

Three marks of the sheep. They hear, he knows, they follow.

verseByVerse.quote: "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He gives them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of his hand. His Father, who has given them to him, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand.

Never perish. A double negative in Greek: they will certainly not.

Two hands. The Son’s and the Father’s. The believer’s security does not rest on the grip of the sheep but on the grip of God.

Where Christians differ: can a believer be lost? Some say no one can snatch the sheep, but the sheep may walk away by their own choice. Reformed theology answers that “no one” includes the sheep themselves, and that Christ’s promise is that they “will never perish”. Verdict: perseverance of the saints: those who are truly Christ’s will be kept to the end by God’s power (1 Peter 1:5; Romans 8:38–39).

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “What my Father has given me is greater than all.” Verdict: a difficult variant; the usual reading makes good sense, and the promise stands either way.

For worship. Rest in the two hands that hold you.

parallels.desc: there is none that can deliver out of my hand

verseByVerse.quote: "I and the Father are one." The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says, “I and the Father are one.” The Jewish leaders pick up stones again to stone him.

One. Neuter (hen): one thing, not one person. Against modalism (that the Father and Son are the same person), Jesus says “I and the Father”, two; against Arianism (that the Son is a lesser being), he says “are one”: one in nature, power and work. Augustine: “are” refutes Sabellius; “one” refutes Arius.

In context. One in power to keep the sheep (vv. 28–29), but the hearers rightly take it as a claim to deity (v. 33).

For worship. Worship the Father and the Son as one God, with the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: “One” is neuter in Greek — one in nature and purpose, not one person.

parallels.desc: the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?" The Jews answered him, "It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers that he has shown them many good works from the Father; for which of these do they want to stone him? They reply that they are not stoning him for any good work but for blasphemy, because he, a man, makes himself God.

Good works. Beautiful works (kala), like the good shepherd (kalos).

Making yourself God. They understood him exactly (5:18). Their error is not in understanding but in denying it is true. He did not make himself God; he is God who made himself man (1:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Is it not written in your Law, 'I said, you are gods'? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came — and Scripture cannot be broken —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers by asking whether it is not written in their law, “I said, you are gods”. If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken…

Psalm 82:6. God rebukes unjust judges, calling them “gods” because they acted as his representatives in judgment, yet they will die like men. “Law” here means the whole Old Testament.

The argument. From the lesser to the greater: if Scripture can call humans “gods” because they received God’s word, it cannot be blasphemy for the one who is the Word to call himself God’s Son.

What it does not mean. Not that humans are or can become gods, as some Word-of-Faith teachers, Mormons and New Age writers claim. The psalm is ironic and ends in their death.

Scripture cannot be broken. A passing phrase about an obscure verse, showing Jesus’ view of the whole Bible: it cannot be annulled or set aside. The basis of the doctrine of inerrancy (Matthew 5:18). Where Christians differ. Some today hold that Scripture contains errors in history or science though it is reliable in faith. Verdict: Jesus’ own view: Scripture is God’s word and true in all it affirms.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm calls Israel’s judges “gods” because they represented God’s authority. “Your Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole.

parallels.desc: “I said, ‘You are gods’”

verseByVerse.quote: "do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then how can they say that the one the Father consecrated and sent into the world is blaspheming because he said he is the Son of God?

Consecrated. Set apart, at the feast celebrating the temple’s consecration. Jesus is the holy one, the true temple.

Sent. Pre-existence: he was the Son before he came.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: "If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If he is not doing his Father’s works, they need not believe him. But if he does them, even if they do not believe him, they should believe the works, so that they may know and keep knowing that the Father is in him and he is in the Father.

Believe the works. Evidence can lead to faith. Jesus invites investigation.

Mutual indwelling. The Father in the Son, the Son in the Father (14:10–11; 17:21): the doctrine later called perichoresis.

On a Tuesday. For sceptical friends, start with the evidence: the works and words of Jesus in the Gospels.

verseByVerse.quote: Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands. He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again they try to seize him, but he escapes from their grasp. He goes back across the Jordan to the place where John had baptised at first, and stays there.

Escaped. Not yet his hour.

Back to the beginning. Bethany beyond the Jordan (1:28), where it all began. A period of retreat before the final weeks.
verseByVerse.note: “Across the Jordan” is Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John had baptized.

verseByVerse.quote: And many came to him. And they said, "John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true." And many believed in him there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many people come to him, saying that John did no sign, but everything John said about this man was true. And many believe in him there.

John did no sign. The Baptist worked no miracles; his greatness lay in his faithful witness (5:35).

All true. The best epitaph a witness could have.

On a Tuesday. You may never do anything spectacular. Aim that what you say about Jesus proves true in people’s lives.

For worship. Many believed there. Thank God that where Christ is faithfully pointed to, people still come to him.

It was winter,<sup>23</sup>and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.<sup>24</sup>So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”<sup>25</sup>Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me,<sup>26</sup>but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep.<sup>27</sup>My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.<sup>28</sup>I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.<sup>29</sup>My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand.<sup>30</sup>I and the Father are one.”<sup>31</sup>The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.<sup>32</sup>Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?”<sup>33</sup>The Jews answered him, “It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God.”<sup>34</sup>Jesus answered them, “Is it not written in your Law, ’I said, you are gods’?<sup>35</sup>If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—<sup>36</sup>do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ’You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ’I am the Son of God’?<sup>37</sup>If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me;<sup>38</sup>but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”<sup>39</sup>Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands.<sup>40</sup>He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.<sup>41</sup>And many came to him. And they said, “John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true.”<sup>42</sup>And many believed in him there.
10.overview:
Chapter 10 follows straight on from the healing of the blind man, whom the Pharisees had thrown out and Jesus had found. Against those false shepherds Jesus describes himself in two pictures from village life. He is the door of the sheepfold: those who enter through him are saved, and find pasture and abundant life. And he is the good shepherd, who knows his sheep by name, leads them out, and lays down his life for them, unlike hired hands who run from the wolf. The background is Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel’s selfish shepherds and promises to shepherd his flock himself through his servant David. Jesus has other sheep, not of this fold, whom he must also bring, so that there will be one flock and one shepherd. He lays down his life of his own accord and has authority to take it up again.

Two months later, at the winter Feast of Dedication, which celebrated the cleansing of the temple by the Maccabees, the leaders surround Jesus in Solomon’s Colonnade and demand that he tell them plainly whether he is the Messiah. He answers that his works testify, but they do not believe because they are not his sheep. His sheep hear his voice and follow him; he gives them eternal life, they will never perish, and no one can snatch them from his hand or from the Father’s. “I and the Father are one.” They take up stones for blasphemy. Jesus answers from Psalm 82, where human judges are called “gods”, arguing that Scripture cannot be broken and that the one the Father consecrated and sent is rightly called the Son of God. Escaping, he withdraws across the Jordan, where many believe in him.

11.title: The Resurrection and the Life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–44 — Lazarus Raised: The Sign That Decides
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Lazarus of Bethany falls ill, his sisters Martha and Mary send word to Jesus, whom they know loves him. Jesus says this sickness will end in God’s glory, not death, and deliberately waits two more days before returning to Judea despite the danger. He tells the disciples that Lazarus has fallen asleep and he will wake him; when they misunderstand, he tells them plainly that Lazarus has died, and Thomas resolves that they will go and die with him. Lazarus has been entombed four days when they arrive. Martha meets Jesus, grieving that he came too late yet trusting him still. He promises that her brother will rise and declares that he himself is the resurrection and the life; she confesses him as the Christ, the Son of God. Mary comes and falls weeping at his feet, and Jesus, deeply stirred and troubled, weeps with them. At the tomb he orders the stone moved despite Martha’s fear of the stench, prays aloud to the Father so that the crowd may believe, and calls Lazarus out. The dead man emerges, still wrapped, and Jesus tells them to free him.
verseByVerse.theology: The miracle is a preview of Jesus' own resurrection and, through his, the resurrection of all who are in him. I am the resurrection and the life (v. 25) is not merely a claim about what Jesus can do but about what he is: the source and substance of resurrection-life, the one in whom the age-to-come has already broken into the present. Those who believe in him will never die — not because they avoid physical death but because they have already passed from death to life (5:24). Lazarus' resurrection is the bodily demonstration of what Jesus gives spiritually to every believer.
verseByVerse.examples: The weeping of Jesus (vv. 33-35) is one of the most theologically dense moments in the gospel: the one who knows he is about to raise Lazarus weeps with those who grieve. His tears are not ignorance of the outcome but solidarity with human grief, genuine compassion that does not remove itself from suffering even when it is about to overcome suffering. This is the incarnation at its most moving: God in the flesh does not observe human sorrow from a distance; he enters it, feels it, and weeps in it — before he conquers it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man named Lazarus is ill. He is from Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. This Mary is the one who anointed the Lord with perfume and wiped his feet with her hair; it is her brother Lazarus who is ill.

Lazarus. A form of Eleazar, “God helps”. Not the beggar in Jesus’ parable (Luke 16:19–31), though that story ends with a warning that people would not believe even if someone rose from the dead.

Bethany. On the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from Jerusalem (v. 18): not the Bethany beyond the Jordan (1:28; 10:40).

Mary and Martha. Known from Luke 10:38–42. John assumes his readers know of the anointing, which he narrates in 12:1–8.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was a village on the Mount of Olives, about two miles east of Jerusalem. John mentions Mary’s anointing ahead of time; it comes in chapter 12.

parallels.desc: Martha and Mary

verseByVerse.quote: So the sisters sent to him, saying, "Lord, he whom you love is ill." But when Jesus heard it he said, "This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the sisters send a message to Jesus: “Lord, he whom you love is ill.” When Jesus hears it, he says that this illness will not end in death; it is for God’s glory, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.

A model prayer. They state the need and appeal to his love, without telling him what to do (compare Mary at Cana, 2:3).

Not to death. Lazarus will die, but death will not be the end of the story.

The glory of God. As with the blind man (9:3). And the Son will be glorified through it in a double sense: the miracle reveals his glory, and it leads to his death, which John calls his glorification (12:23; 13:31).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus loves Martha, her sister and Lazarus. So when he hears that Lazarus is ill, he stays where he is two more days.

Loved … so stayed. The shocking “so”. His delay is not neglect but love: he intends something greater than a healing.

Two days. Lazarus was probably already dead when the message arrived (four days in the tomb, v. 17: a day for the messenger, two days’ delay, a day’s journey).

Where Christians differ: why does God delay? Some conclude that unanswered prayer means lack of faith or lack of love from God. This passage shows that God’s delays can be acts of love with purposes we cannot yet see (2 Peter 3:9). Verdict: trust his love when you cannot trace his timing.

On a Tuesday. If you are waiting for an answer, remember Bethany: delay is not denial, and silence is not indifference.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after this he said to the disciples, "Let us go to Judea again." The disciples said to him, "Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he tells his disciples that they should go back to Judea. The disciples object, calling him Rabbi: the Jewish leaders were just trying to stone him, and he is going back there?

Courage. Going to Lazarus means going towards death (10:31, 39).

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers that there are twelve hours of daylight. Anyone who walks in the day does not stumble, because he sees by this world’s light. But anyone who walks at night stumbles, because the light is not in him.

Twelve hours. His working day is fixed by the Father. Until it ends, no one can cut it short (9:4).

Light in him. Those who walk with Jesus, the light, walk safely. Without him people stumble in the dark (12:35–36).
verseByVerse.note: The daylight hours were counted as twelve, from sunrise to sunset.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, he said to them, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him." The disciples said to him, "Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this he tells them that their friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, and he is going to wake him up. The disciples say that if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.

Our friend. Lazarus is the friend of all the disciples.

Asleep. A common biblical picture for the death of believers (Daniel 12:2; Matthew 9:24; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14): death is temporary, and waking will follow.

Where Christians differ: soul sleep. Seventh-day Adventists and some others teach that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. Most Christians hold that “sleep” describes the body, while the soul of the believer is consciously with Christ (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). Verdict: the intermediate state is conscious rest with Christ; sleep is a picture of the body awaiting resurrection (Westminster Confession 32.1).
verseByVerse.note: Sleep was a common picture of death for believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep. Then Jesus told them plainly, "Lazarus has died,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought he meant ordinary sleep. So Jesus tells them plainly that Lazarus has died.

Misunderstanding again. A pattern in John: people take Jesus literally when he speaks figuratively, and figuratively when he speaks literally.

Plainly. Death is not to be denied with euphemisms.

verseByVerse.quote: "and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him." So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, "Let us also go, that we may die with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For their sake he is glad he was not there, so that they may believe. But let them go to him. Thomas, called the Twin, says to his fellow disciples that they should go too, so that they may die with him.

Glad. Not glad at Lazarus’s death, but at the faith that will come from what he is about to do.

That you may believe. Even disciples need their faith to grow.

Thomas. Aramaic for twin, as Didymus is Greek. Known for his doubt (20:24–29), but here for loyal courage, if gloomy. Better to follow Jesus pessimistically than not at all.
verseByVerse.note: Thomas’s name means “twin” in Aramaic; Didymus is the Greek equivalent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus arrives, he finds that Lazarus has already been in the tomb four days. Bethany is near Jerusalem, about two miles away.

Four days. Burial took place the same day as death in that climate. A Jewish belief held that the soul lingered near the body for three days; after that, death was irreversible and decomposition began. No one could say Lazarus was merely unconscious.

Two miles. Literally fifteen stadia. Close enough for many Jerusalem mourners to come, and for the news to reach the authorities.
verseByVerse.note: After four days there could be no doubt that he was dead. The ESV notes that the distance is literally fifteen stadia.

verseByVerse.quote: and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many of the Jewish people have come to Martha and Mary to comfort them about their brother. When Martha hears that Jesus is coming, she goes out to meet him, but Mary stays at home.

Mourning. Seven days of intense mourning, with friends, neighbours and sometimes hired mourners. A wealthy, well-known family.

Martha and Mary. Characteristic: Martha active, Mary still (Luke 10:38–42). Perhaps Mary is too grief-stricken, or sitting in mourning custom.
verseByVerse.note: Mourning for a close relative lasted seven days, with friends coming to console the family.

verseByVerse.quote: Martha said to Jesus, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Martha says to Jesus that if he had been there, her brother would not have died. But even now she knows that God will give him whatever he asks.

If only. Not an accusation but a lament, honest grief. Mary will say the same (v. 32).

Even now. Faith that has not given up, though it does not dare say what it hopes.

On a Tuesday. You can bring Jesus your “if only”. Honest lament is part of faith (Psalms 13; 88).

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Your brother will rise again." Martha said to him, "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells her that her brother will rise again. Martha replies that she knows he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.

Orthodox faith. Martha believes, with the Pharisees and against the Sadducees, in the resurrection at the end (Daniel 12:2).

But distant. A doctrine about the future, not much comfort today.
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees and most Jews believed in a resurrection at the end of the age.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die.” He asks whether she believes this.

I am. The fifth “I am” saying. Resurrection is not merely an event at the end; it is a person, present now.

Though he die, yet shall he live. Believers will die physically but rise.

Shall never die. Believers will never die the real death, separation from God (5:24; 8:51). Death becomes a door.

Textual note. One early papyrus (P45) and a few others omit “and the life”. Verdict: the longer reading is well attested and original.

Do you believe this? Jesus turns doctrine into a personal question. Read at Christian funerals for centuries, it asks every mourner the same.

For worship. Thank Christ that because he lives, death is not the end for those who trust him.
verseByVerse.note: This is the fifth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

verseByVerse.quote: She said to him, "Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world." When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, "The Teacher is here and is calling for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She tells him, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.” Having said this, she goes back and calls her sister Mary aside, telling her that the Teacher is here and is calling for her.

A great confession. Matching the purpose of the Gospel (20:31): Christ, Son of God. Martha’s confession stands beside Peter’s (Matthew 16:16).

The Teacher. A tender title from a woman whom Jesus taught (Luke 10:39).

Calling for you. Jesus asks for Mary personally.

verseByVerse.quote: And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Mary hears this, she gets up quickly and goes to him. Jesus has not yet entered the village but is still where Martha met him.

Quickly. His call brings her out of her grief.

Outside the village. Perhaps so that he could meet the sisters privately, or because the tomb lay outside.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there. Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews who were with Mary in the house comforting her see her get up quickly and go out, and they follow her, thinking she is going to the tomb to weep there. When Mary reaches the place where Jesus is and sees him, she falls at his feet and says that if he had been there, her brother would not have died.

At his feet. Where Mary is always found (Luke 10:39; John 12:3).

The same words. The sisters had probably said it to each other many times in those four days.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. And he said, "Where have you laid him?" They said to him, "Lord, come and see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus sees her weeping, and the Jews who came with her weeping too, he is deeply moved in spirit and greatly troubled. He asks where they have laid him. They tell him, as Lord, to come and see.

Deeply moved. Embrimaomai, a word that usually means to snort with anger (Mark 1:43; 14:5). Jesus is indignant, probably at death itself and the devastation it brings, the enemy he has come to destroy (1 Corinthians 15:26; Hebrews 2:14–15).

Troubled. Stirred to the depths (12:27; 13:21).

Where Christians differ: does God feel? The doctrine of divine impassibility holds that God is not subject to changing passions as we are. Jesus, being truly human as well as divine, truly feels grief and anger in his human nature. Verdict: the Chalcedonian view: one person in two natures; in his humanity the Son of God weeps and burns with anger at death, and this reveals the heart of God towards suffering.

Come and see. The words Jesus once used as invitation (1:39) now lead him to the grave.
verseByVerse.note: The words behind “deeply moved” carry a sense of anger or indignation — at death itself and the grief it brings.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus wept. So the Jews said, "See how he loved him!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus wept. So the Jews say, “See how he loved him!”

Wept. A different word from the loud wailing of the mourners (v. 33): quiet tears. Though he knows he will raise Lazarus in minutes, he weeps with those who weep (Romans 12:15).

The shortest verse. In English Bibles; one of the most precious.

What it does not mean. Not that grief is a lack of faith. Christians grieve, but not as those without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

For worship. The Saviour who weeps at the grave of his friend weeps with you in yours. “We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).
verseByVerse.note: This is the shortest verse in the English Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: But some of them said, "Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?" Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But some of them ask whether the one who opened the blind man’s eyes could not have kept this man from dying. Then Jesus, again deeply moved, comes to the tomb. It is a cave, with a stone lying across the entrance.

A sneer or a question? Perhaps both: the familiar question of suffering, why did God not prevent this?

Moved again. Indignation again (v. 33).

The tomb. A cave, natural or cut in the rock, with a large disc-shaped or rough stone across the entrance. Wealthy families had such tombs.
verseByVerse.note: Tombs were caves or rock chambers, with a large stone across the entrance.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Take away the stone." Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, "Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days." Jesus said to her, "Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells them to take away the stone. Martha, the dead man’s sister, warns him, calling him Lord, that by now there will be a smell, for he has been dead four days. Jesus asks whether he did not tell her that if she believed, she would see the glory of God.

Martha’s realism. Her faith (v. 27) and her fear sit together. She believes in Jesus but cannot imagine what he is about to do.

See the glory of God. Recalling verses 4 and 25–26.

On a Tuesday. Jesus sometimes asks us to roll away a stone, to do something that makes no sense, before he acts.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were not embalmed; after four days decay was well under way.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, "Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they remove the stone. Jesus lifts his eyes and says, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.”

Thanks before the miracle. He has already prayed, and gives thanks for the answer before he sees it.

Always hear me. The perfect communion of Father and Son.

For the people. His prayer is aloud so that the miracle will be understood as the Father’s work, confirming the Son’s mission.
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed looking upward.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out." The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, "Unbind him, and let him go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he has said this, he calls out in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.” The dead man comes out, his hands and feet bound with strips of linen and his face wrapped in a cloth. Jesus tells them to unbind him and let him go.

A loud voice. The voice of the Son of God that the dead will hear (5:25, 28–29). Augustine remarked that if Jesus had not named Lazarus, all the dead would have come out.

Came out. Bound, but walking or shuffling. Restored to mortal life; he would die again (12:10). Jesus’ own resurrection will be different: he leaves the grave-clothes behind (20:6–7) and never dies again.

Unbind him. Jesus gives life; the community helps remove what still binds. A picture of the church’s ministry to new believers.

For worship. The voice that called Lazarus will one day call you from the grave. Rejoice in the resurrection and the life.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were wrapped in strips of linen, with a separate cloth over the face.

parallels.desc: all who are in the tombs will hear his voice

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–57 — The Decision to Kill Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Many who saw the miracle believe in Jesus, but some report it to the Pharisees. The chief priests and Pharisees convene the council in alarm: if this man keeps doing signs, everyone will follow him and the Romans will destroy their temple and nation. Caiaphas, high priest that year, tells them they understand nothing: better that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish. John explains that he was unwittingly prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation, and also to gather God’s scattered children into one. From then on they plot his death, so Jesus withdraws from public view to Ephraim, near the desert, with his disciples. As Passover approaches and pilgrims arrive early to purify themselves, people look for Jesus in the temple, wondering if he will come, while the authorities order anyone who knows his whereabouts to report it so they can arrest him.
verseByVerse.theology: Caiaphas' political calculation — sacrifice one man to save the nation — is simultaneously cynical expediency and unconscious prophecy. John explicitly identifies it as prophecy (v. 51): the high priest, by virtue of his office, spoke better than he knew. The death he plots as preservation of institutional power is the death that will actually accomplish the salvation of God's people — and not only of the Jewish nation, but of the scattered children of God throughout the world (v. 52). The cross is always more than its perpetrators intend and exactly what God intends.
verseByVerse.examples: The decision of the Sanhedrin is the human side of the decree that was made in eternity: Christ was the Lamb slain before the foundation of the world (Rev. 13:8). Human hatred and divine love converge on the same event. The leaders plot what God has purposed; the victim goes willingly to what they intend as murder and he intends as sacrifice. The sovereign grace that works through human wickedness without being compromised by it is most visible at Calvary.

verseByVerse.quote: Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him, but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many of the Jews who had come with Mary and had seen what Jesus did believe in him. But some of them go to the Pharisees and tell them what Jesus has done.

Two responses. The same miracle produces faith in some and hostility in others (Luke 16:31).

On a Tuesday. Even overwhelming evidence does not compel faith. Pray for hearts, not only for arguments.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, "What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the chief priests and the Pharisees call a meeting of the council. They ask what they are to do, for this man is performing many signs. If they let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both their place and their nation.

The council. The Sanhedrin.

Many signs. They do not deny the miracles.

Our place. The temple, and their position. Their fear is political: a messianic movement would bring Roman reprisal and cost them their power. In AD 70 the Romans did destroy the temple and the nation, after they had rejected Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: “Our place” means the temple. The leaders feared a messianic movement would bring Roman retaliation — as happened in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, "You know nothing at all. Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, tells them they know nothing at all. They do not realise that it is better for them that one man should die for the people than that the whole nation should perish.

Caiaphas. High priest AD 18–36, son-in-law of Annas (18:13). An ossuary inscribed with his family name was found in Jerusalem in 1990.

That year. That fateful year, rather than meaning the office changed annually.

Political calculation. Sacrifice one man to save the nation. Cynical expediency.
verseByVerse.note: Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36; “that year” means that fateful year.

verseByVerse.quote: He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He did not say this on his own; as high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God scattered abroad.

An unwitting prophet. God can speak through unworthy people (Balaam, Numbers 22–24). Caiaphas meant expediency; God meant substitution.

For the nation. Substitution: one dies instead of many (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

The children of God scattered. Gentiles who will believe, already called God’s children before they are gathered, as the “other sheep” (10:16). God’s people are known to him before they come. The Reformed doctrine of election finds support here (Acts 18:10).

Gather into one. The goal of the cross is a united people, Jews and Gentiles in one body (Ephesians 2:14–16).

For worship. Thank God that Christ died to gather you, perhaps scattered far away, into his family.

parallels.desc: I will gather yet others

verseByVerse.quote: So from that day on they made plans to put him to death. Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So from that day on they plan to put him to death. Jesus therefore no longer moves about openly among the Jewish people, but goes away to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and stays there with his disciples.

The decision. The death sentence is passed, in effect, before any trial.

Irony. Jesus gives Lazarus life, and it costs him his own. The one who raises the dead must die.

Ephraim. Probably et-Taiyibeh, about twelve miles north-east of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness. Textual note. Some manuscripts add “Sapphurim”. Verdict: “Ephraim” alone is better attested.
verseByVerse.note: The town of Ephraim was probably north-east of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, "What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jewish Passover is near, and many people go up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. They look for Jesus and ask one another in the temple what they think: will he not come to the feast?

Purification. Pilgrims who had contracted ritual impurity had to purify themselves, sometimes for a week, before eating Passover (Numbers 9:6–12; 2 Chronicles 30:17–18).

The third Passover. The last of Jesus’ ministry (2:13; 6:4). He will become the Passover Lamb (1:29; 19:36).
verseByVerse.note: Pilgrims came early to undergo purification rites so they would be ritually clean for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests and Pharisees have ordered that anyone who knows where Jesus is should report it, so that they can arrest him.

A wanted man. The scene is set for Judas (12:4; 18:2–3).

On a Tuesday. Jesus will go to Jerusalem anyway (12:12). He knew the cost, and came for us.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha.<sup>2</sup>It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.<sup>3</sup>So the sisters sent to him, saying, “Lord, he whom you love is ill.”<sup>4</sup>But when Jesus heard it he said, “This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”<sup>5</sup>Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.<sup>6</sup>So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.<sup>7</sup>Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.”<sup>8</sup>The disciples said to him, “Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?”<sup>9</sup>Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world.<sup>10</sup>But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”<sup>11</sup>After saying these things, he said to them, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him.”<sup>12</sup>The disciples said to him, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”<sup>13</sup>Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep.<sup>14</sup>Then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died,<sup>15</sup>and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.”<sup>16</sup>So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”<sup>17</sup>Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.<sup>18</sup>Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off,<sup>19</sup>and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother.<sup>20</sup>So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.<sup>21</sup>Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.<sup>22</sup>But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.”<sup>23</sup>Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.”<sup>24</sup>Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”<sup>25</sup>Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live,<sup>26</sup>and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?”<sup>27</sup>She said to him, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.”<sup>28</sup>When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”<sup>29</sup>And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him.<sup>30</sup>Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.<sup>31</sup>When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there.<sup>32</sup>Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”<sup>33</sup>When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled.<sup>34</sup>And he said, “Where have you laid him?” They said to him, “Lord, come and see.”<sup>35</sup>Jesus wept.<sup>36</sup>So the Jews said, “See how he loved him!”<sup>37</sup>But some of them said, “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?”<sup>38</sup>Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.<sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, “Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.”<sup>40</sup>Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?”<sup>41</sup>So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.<sup>42</sup>I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.”<sup>43</sup>When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.”<sup>44</sup>The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Unbind him, and let him go.”<sup>45</sup>Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him,<sup>46</sup>but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.<sup>47</sup>So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs.<sup>48</sup>If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”<sup>49</sup>But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all.<sup>50</sup>Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.”<sup>51</sup>He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation,<sup>52</sup>and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.<sup>53</sup>So from that day on they made plans to put him to death.<sup>54</sup>Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.<sup>55</sup>Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves.<sup>56</sup>They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?”<sup>57</sup>Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
11.overview:
The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and greatest sign in John, and the event that leads directly to the cross. Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, falls ill, and the sisters send word to Jesus: “Lord, he whom you love is ill.” Because he loves them, Jesus waits two more days, then returns to Judea despite the danger, telling the disciples that Lazarus has fallen asleep and he is going to wake him. Thomas gloomily urges the others to go and die with him. By the time they arrive, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Martha meets Jesus with grief and faith mixed; he tells her, “I am the resurrection and the life,” and she confesses him the Christ, the Son of God. Mary falls at his feet weeping, and Jesus, deeply moved and troubled, weeps too. At the tomb he orders the stone removed, prays aloud to his Father, and cries, “Lazarus, come out.” The dead man walks out still bound in grave-clothes.

Many believe, but some report to the Pharisees, and the Sanhedrin meets in alarm: if Jesus goes on like this, the Romans will destroy the temple and the nation. The high priest Caiaphas declares that it is better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish. John comments that, without knowing it, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and to gather into one the scattered children of God. From that day they plan to kill him. Jesus withdraws to Ephraim, and as Passover approaches the crowds wonder whether he will dare to come to the feast. The one who gives life will give his own life, so that the dead may live.

12.title: The Hour Has Come

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Anointing and the Entry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Jesus’ honour in Bethany, with Martha serving and Lazarus at table, Mary anoints Jesus’ feet with a pound of expensive nard and wipes them with her hair, filling the house with fragrance. Judas, the future betrayer and a thief who pilfers from the common purse, protests that it could have been sold for the poor. Jesus defends her: she has kept it for his burial, and they will always have the poor, but not always him. Crowds come to see Jesus and the risen Lazarus, and the chief priests resolve to kill Lazarus too. Next day festival crowds carry palm branches out to meet Jesus, hailing him as the blessed King of Israel, and he rides in on a young donkey as the prophet foretold, though the disciples grasp this only later. Witnesses of Lazarus’s raising spread the news, drawing more people, and the Pharisees despair that the whole world is following him.
verseByVerse.theology: Mary's extravagance is the gospel's aesthetic: 'she has done a beautiful thing' (Matt. 26:10). The ointment worth a year's wages poured out on Jesus is the only appropriate response to the one who will pour out his life for the world. Judas' objection — it should have been sold and given to the poor — sounds pious but is calculated. He uses the language of charity to mask the language of control. The contrast between Mary's love and Judas' calculation is the contrast between authentic discipleship and the discipleship that has never really left the world's economy.
verseByVerse.examples: The triumphal entry is at once a royal procession and a misunderstood one. The crowd hails Jesus as king; they are right about the title and wrong about what it means. They expect a Davidic warrior-king who will restore national sovereignty; Jesus enters on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9, the prophecy of the humble king of peace. The disciples do not understand this until after the resurrection (v. 16) — another instance of John's pattern where events are incomprehensible until the Spirit illuminates them in the light of the cross and resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six days before the Passover, Jesus comes to Bethany, where Lazarus lives, the man he raised from the dead. They give a dinner for him there; Martha serves, and Lazarus is among those reclining at table with him.

Six days. Probably the Saturday before Passover week. John’s chronology moves day by day towards the cross.

A dinner in his honour. Mark 14:3 places it at the house of Simon the leper, perhaps a friend or relative of the family.

Lazarus at table. A living testimony, eating with the one who raised him.

verseByVerse.quote: Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary takes a pound of expensive perfume made of pure nard, pours it on Jesus’ feet and wipes his feet with her hair. The house is filled with the fragrance of the perfume.

Nard. An aromatic oil from a plant of the Himalayas, imported at great cost. A Roman pound (about 11 ounces, 325 grams) was a huge quantity.

The feet. Mark and Matthew say the head (Mark 14:3); probably both. John stresses the feet: the most humble act, and a foreshadowing of Jesus washing his disciples’ feet (13:5).

Her hair. A respectable woman did not let her hair down in public. Mary disregards propriety in devotion.

Where Christians differ: one anointing or two? Luke 7:36–50 describes a “sinful woman” anointing Jesus in Galilee, and medieval tradition merged Mary of Bethany, the sinful woman and Mary Magdalene. Verdict: Luke’s is a different, earlier event; Mark, Matthew and John describe the same anointing at Bethany. Mary of Bethany is not Mary Magdalene.

The fragrance. Love for Christ fills a house (2 Corinthians 2:14–16). Mark 14:9 says it would be told wherever the gospel is preached.

For worship. What costly thing could you pour out for Jesus?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the pound was a Roman pound, about 11½ ounces. Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. A respectable woman did not normally let down her hair in public.

parallels.desc: a different woman in Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?" He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples, the one who was about to betray him, asks why this perfume was not sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor. He says this not because he cares about the poor, but because he is a thief; he keeps the money bag and helps himself to what is put in it.

Three hundred denarii. About a year’s wages for a labourer.

A pious objection. Concern for the poor can be a mask for other motives. The other Gospels say several disciples complained (Matthew 26:8); Judas led them.

A thief. John alone tells us. Greed opened the door to betrayal (Matthew 26:14–15).

On a Tuesday. If you handle money for a church or charity, be scrupulously accountable (2 Corinthians 8:20–21). And beware of criticising others’ generosity.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: Judas had the moneybag

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells him to leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of his burial. They will always have the poor with them, but they will not always have him.

Keep it for my burial. Perhaps she had kept it for this; perhaps she sensed his death was near. Jesus interprets her act as an anointing for burial in advance.

The poor always with you. Deuteronomy 15:11, which continues: therefore open your hand to your brother, the needy and the poor. Jesus is not dismissing the poor.

What it does not mean. Not a reason to ignore poverty. Jesus’ point is that this moment of devotion to him, before his death, is unique.

Where Christians differ: worship or social action? Some set costly worship (beautiful buildings, music) against care for the poor; others the reverse. Verdict: both flow from love for Christ, and each needs the other; Judas cared for neither.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A large crowd of the Jewish people learns that Jesus is there and comes, not only because of Jesus but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. So the chief priests plan to kill Lazarus as well, because on account of him many of the Jews are going away and believing in Jesus.

Curiosity. A man raised from the dead was a sensation.

Kill Lazarus too. Evil compounds itself. If you cannot deny the evidence, destroy it.

Going away. Leaving the authorities’ side.

On a Tuesday. A changed life is powerful testimony, and may attract opposition.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!" And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day the great crowd that has come for the festival hears that Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem. They take palm branches and go out to meet him, shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!” Jesus finds a young donkey and sits on it, as it is written.

The triumphal entry. Recorded in all four Gospels (Mark 11:1–10).

Palm branches. A symbol of Jewish nationalism since the Maccabees, who entered Jerusalem with palms after freeing it (1 Maccabees 13:51). The crowd hails a liberator king.

Hosanna. Hebrew for “save us, we pray” (Psalm 118:25–26), a pilgrim psalm sung at feasts, by now a shout of praise.

The King of Israel. Nathanael’s confession (1:49).

A donkey. Jesus responds to their nationalist hopes by choosing a humble mount, not a war horse.
verseByVerse.note: Palm branches had become a symbol of national victory and celebration. “Hosanna” means “save, we pray.”

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
branches of palm trees at the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: "Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey's colt!" His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture says, “Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt!” His disciples do not understand these things at first, but when Jesus is glorified, they remember that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.

Zechariah 9:9. The king who comes humble and riding on a donkey, bringing peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:10). “Fear not” may come from Isaiah 40:9 or Zephaniah 3:16.

Understood later. After the resurrection and the giving of the Spirit (2:22; 14:26).

For worship. Welcome your King, who comes not to conquer by force but to make peace by his blood.
verseByVerse.note: A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey
fear not, O Zion

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness. The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
