Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”<sup>38</sup>Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, “I find no guilt in him.<sup>39</sup>But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”<sup>40</sup>They cried out again, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.
18.overview:
John’s account of the arrest and trials shows Jesus not as a victim but as the one in control. In the garden across the Kidron, when soldiers and temple police come with Judas, Jesus steps forward and asks whom they seek; at his “I am he” they fall to the ground. He protects his disciples, rebukes Peter’s sword, and goes willingly to drink the cup his Father has given him. Bound, he is taken first to Annas, the former high priest and power behind the office, and questioned about his teaching, while outside in the courtyard Peter, warming himself at a charcoal fire, denies three times that he is a disciple, and the rooster crows.

At dawn he is brought to Pilate, the Roman governor. The Jewish leaders will not enter the praetorium, lest they be defiled before Passover, while they hand over the true Passover Lamb to be killed. Pilate moves in and out between the accusers outside and the prisoner inside. To his question, “Are you the King of the Jews?”, Jesus answers that his kingdom is not of this world; he came to bear witness to the truth, and everyone who is of the truth listens to his voice. Pilate replies, “What is truth?”, declares Jesus innocent, and offers to release him for Passover; the crowd demands Barabbas instead. The judge is on trial before the truth, and fails.

19.title: The Crucifixion and Burial of Jesus

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Crown of Thorns and the Cross
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pilate has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him as king with a crown of thorns and a purple cloak, striking him. Pilate brings him out to the crowd to show he finds no fault, and presents him: “Behold the man!” The chief priests demand crucifixion. When they add that he claimed to be God’s Son, Pilate becomes more afraid and questions Jesus, who first stays silent, then tells him that his authority comes from above, and the one who delivered Jesus bears greater guilt. Pilate seeks to free him, but the leaders threaten that this would make him no friend of Caesar. At noon on the day of Preparation, seated on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement, Pilate offers them their king; they cry for his death and declare Caesar their only king, and Pilate gives him up. Jesus carries his cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others, beneath Pilate’s trilingual notice, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews”, which Pilate refuses to alter.
verseByVerse.theology: Behold the man (v. 5) and Behold your King (v. 14) are Pilate's two presentations of Jesus to the crowd — each one a deeper truth than Pilate knows. Ecce Homo is the great statement of the incarnation: here is humanity in its representative, here is the man who is also the king. Pilate intends mockery and irony; the Spirit intends revelation. The crown of thorns (the curse of Gen. 3:18 placed on the head of the one who came to bear the curse), the purple robe (borrowed royalty that will soon be stripped), and the reed scepter — all are parodies of kingship that are simultaneously truths about the king who reigns from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: They crucified him, and with him two others — one on either side (v. 18): the king flanked by his 'court,' the condemned alongside the condemned, the innocent among the guilty. The inscription in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek — the languages of religion, law, and culture — makes the proclamation universal: in every language, beside a road just outside the city, in the full light of Passover day, the truth is declared. The chief priests want it changed to 'he said he was king'; Pilate refuses: What I have written, I have written.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him. And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The King is crowned with thorns: the curse of the ground (Genesis 3:18) pressed onto the head of the one who came to remove it.

Flogged. Roman scourging used whips with pieces of bone or metal, and could tear flesh to the bone; some victims died of it. Pilate perhaps hoped a severe flogging would satisfy the crowd (Luke 23:16, 22). Isaiah 53:5: with his wounds we are healed.

Crown of thorns. A mock crown, perhaps of acanthus or date-palm spines, imitating the radiate crowns on emperors’ coins.

Purple robe. Probably a faded soldier’s cloak, the colour of royalty.
verseByVerse.note: Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal. Purple was the colour of royalty.

verseByVerse.quote: They came up to him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" and struck him with their hands. Pilate went out again and said to them, "See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers mock Jesus as king without knowing that he is the King, and Pilate brings him out to declare him innocent again.

Hail, King of the Jews. A parody of “Hail, Caesar!” Every insult is unknowingly true.

No guilt. The second declaration (18:38).

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, "Behold the man!" When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, "Crucify him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate presents a beaten, mocked man, perhaps hoping for pity, and the leaders demand his death; John wants us to look and see true humanity, and true God, in that bleeding figure.

Behold the man! Ecce homo. Pilate means “Look at this pathetic figure: is he a threat?” John may hear more: here is the true Man, the Son of Man, the second Adam (Zechariah 6:12; 1 Corinthians 15:45).

Crucify! The first time the word is used in John.

Take him yourselves. Sarcastic; they cannot legally. The third declaration of innocence.

For worship. Behold the man who was wounded for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5).

parallels.desc: no beauty that we should desire him

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews answered him, "We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God." When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The real charge comes out at last: Jesus claimed to be the Son of God, and Pilate, superstitious and uneasy, becomes afraid.

We have a law. Leviticus 24:16: blasphemy deserves death. They do not see that his claim might be true.

Son of God. To a Roman, a “son of the gods” was a divine man, a frightening figure. Pilate’s wife had already warned him (Matthew 27:19).

parallels.desc: whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death

verseByVerse.quote: He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, "Where are you from?" But Jesus gave him no answer. So Pilate said to him, "You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate asks the deepest question of John’s Gospel, “Where are you from?”, but asks too late and with the wrong motive, so Jesus is silent.

Where are you from? The question running through the Gospel (7:27–28; 8:14; 9:29–30). Jesus is from the Father above.

Silence. Like the lamb before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7).

I have authority. Pilate boasts of power he is about to show he does not really have: he cannot even do what he believes is right.

parallels.desc: he opened not his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin." From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, "If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the Roman governor acts only under authority granted by God, so that the cross is both a human crime and a divine plan.

From above. From God (Romans 13:1). Pilate is responsible, but not sovereign.

The greater sin. Caiaphas, or Judas, who handed him over with fuller knowledge. Sin has degrees (Luke 12:47–48).

Where Christians differ: who killed Jesus? For centuries some Christians blamed “the Jews” collectively, with terrible consequences. Scripture names Jewish leaders, Pilate, Herod, Gentiles and the people of Israel together (Acts 4:27–28), and above all says that Christ died for our sins: we all put him there, and the Father gave him up (Romans 8:32; Isaiah 53:10). Verdict: no people bears collective guilt; every sinner shares in it, and God ordained it for our salvation (Acts 2:23).

Friend of Caesar. An official title for trusted associates. Releasing a would-be king could be reported to the suspicious emperor Tiberius as treason. Pilate’s career was at stake.
verseByVerse.note: “Friend of Caesar” was an honorary title for loyal officials; the threat was that Pilate would be reported to the emperor.

parallels.desc: there is no authority except from God

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha. Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, "Behold your king!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate sits as judge, but John lets us see that the real Judge stands before him, and the hour is the hour of the Passover lambs.

The judgment seat. The bēma. The Greek could mean that Pilate sat Jesus on the judgment seat in mockery; some ancient writers took it so. Verdict: more likely Pilate sat; but John’s irony is clear either way.

The Stone Pavement, Gabbatha. A paved area outside the governor’s residence; its location is uncertain.

The day of Preparation of the Passover. The day the Passover lambs were slaughtered, from noon onward. Jesus dies as the true Lamb (1:29; 1 Corinthians 5:7).

The sixth hour. About noon. Mark says Jesus was crucified at the third hour, 9 a.m. (Mark 15:25). Where Christians differ. Explanations include different time reckonings, approximate times in an age without clocks (the “third” and “sixth” hours being blocks of the morning), and a copying error. Verdict: both writers give approximate times for a morning of events; there is no real contradiction.

Behold your King! Pilate mocks them; John proclaims it.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave judgment. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon; Mark gives the third hour for the crucifixion — times were approximate and may be reckoned differently.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Shall I crucify your King?" The chief priests answered, "We have no king but Caesar." So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders of God’s people renounce their true King and declare loyalty to Caesar, the climax of rejection in John’s Gospel.

Away with him. As the crowd cried at Paul’s arrest (Acts 21:36).

We have no king but Caesar. An astonishing betrayal of Israel’s faith that God alone is king (Judges 8:23; 1 Samuel 8:7). Every Passover they sang of God as King.

Delivered him over. Pilate hands him to them, that is, to their wishes, though Roman soldiers carry out the crucifixion.

On a Tuesday. Ask what “Caesar” claims your loyalty instead of Christ: money, nation, career, approval.

parallels.desc: they have rejected me from being king over them

verseByVerse.quote: And he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha. There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus carries the instrument of his own death outside the city, as the sin offering was taken outside the camp (Hebrews 13:11–13), and is crucified between criminals.

Bearing his own cross. The crossbeam. The other Gospels record that Simon of Cyrene was forced to carry it, probably after Jesus collapsed (Mark 15:21). John stresses that Jesus carries it himself, as Isaac carried the wood (Genesis 22:6).

Golgotha. Aramaic for skull; Latin calvaria (Calvary). Probably a rocky outcrop outside the city walls near a road. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre marks the traditional site, which archaeology supports as outside the walls at the time; Gordon’s Calvary is a later suggestion.

Crucified. The most shameful and painful Roman execution, reserved for slaves and rebels. Death came slowly by exhaustion and asphyxiation. Isaiah 53:12: numbered with the transgressors.

For worship. “When I survey the wondrous cross on which the Prince of glory died” (Isaac Watts).
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution; Simon of Cyrene was later made to carry it. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.”

parallels.desc: Isaac carries the wood

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews." Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate’s notice, written to insult, proclaims the truth to the whole world in its three great languages.

The titulus. A placard naming the crime. Here, the crime is being king.

Aramaic, Latin, Greek. The languages of religion, government and culture. The King of the Jews is announced to the nations.

Near the city. Crucifixions were placed by busy roads as a warning.
verseByVerse.note: Aramaic was the local language, Latin the language of Roman government, Greek the common language of the eastern empire.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, "Do not write, 'The King of the Jews,' but rather, 'This man said, I am King of the Jews.'" Pilate answered, "What I have written, I have written."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests want the claim disowned, but Pilate refuses: what God intended to be written stays written.

What I have written. A final act of spite against the leaders, but also, without knowing it, the last word of a pagan governor on Jesus’ identity.

On a Tuesday. God can use even the stubbornness of unbelievers to proclaim his truth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–42 — The Death and Burial of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The soldiers divide Jesus’ clothes in four and cast lots for his seamless tunic, fulfilling the psalm. Near the cross stand his mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene; Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, who takes her into his home. Knowing his work is complete, Jesus says he is thirsty, to fulfil Scripture, and is given sour wine on a hyssop branch. Then he says, “It is finished,” bows his head and gives up his spirit. Because the Sabbath of Passover week is near, the leaders ask Pilate to have the legs of the crucified broken and the bodies removed. The soldiers break the legs of the two others, but finding Jesus already dead, one pierces his side with a spear, and blood and water flow out. The eyewitness testifies truthfully so that readers may believe; these things fulfilled the Scriptures that none of his bones would be broken and that they would look on the one they pierced. Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple, gets Pilate’s permission to take the body, and Nicodemus brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes. They wrap the body with the spices in linen, as Jews bury, and, because it is the day of Preparation and the tomb is near, lay him in a new tomb in a garden by the place of crucifixion.
verseByVerse.theology: It is finished is the single most important word of the gospel. It announces a completed action whose effects are permanent: the work of redemption is done, accomplished, complete — it does not require addition, continuation, or supplement. Every subsequent act of piety, every religious effort, every moral striving — none adds to what is finished on the cross. Salvation is received, not achieved; accepted, not earned.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple who stood at the cross (with Mary, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the wife of Clopas) is the model of discipleship under pressure: present where the cost is highest, faithful where the others fled. He sees the blood and water from the soldier's spear — the sign that Jesus is truly dead, truly human, truly sacrificed — and testifies that what he saw is true. His testimony is the foundation of the gospel that will go to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, so they said to one another, "Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be." This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, "They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." So the soldiers did these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the soldiers’ gambling fulfils Scripture: Jesus is stripped of everything, as the righteous sufferer of Psalm 22 foretold.

Four parts. A squad of four soldiers (Acts 12:4) took the condemned man’s clothes as perquisites: probably sandals, belt, head covering and outer garment.

The seamless tunic. Woven in one piece, like the high priest’s robe (Exodus 28:31–32; Josephus). Some see a hint that Jesus dies as High Priest; others a symbol of the church’s unity. John does not explain.

Psalm 22:18. The psalm of the forsaken righteous one, whose opening words Jesus cries from the cross (Mark 15:34). Its details of mockery, thirst and pierced hands and feet fit the crucifixion strikingly.

For worship. He was stripped so that we might be clothed with his righteousness (Isaiah 61:10).
verseByVerse.note: The four shares suggest a squad of four soldiers; the clothes of the condemned went to them.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, "Woman, behold, your son!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
While soldiers gamble, the women who love Jesus stay near him, and in his agony he provides for his mother.

The women. Probably four: his mother; her sister (perhaps Salome, the mother of James and John, Mark 15:40; Matthew 27:56, which would make John Jesus’ cousin); Mary the wife of Clopas; and Mary Magdalene. The men, except John, have fled.

Woman. As at Cana (2:4), a respectful address. Now his hour has come.

Behold your son. Jesus’ brothers did not yet believe (7:5). He entrusts Mary to a believing disciple.

Where Christians differ: Mary, mother of the church? Roman Catholic teaching reads this as giving Mary to all believers as their spiritual mother. Protestants see a son’s care for his widowed mother, fulfilling the fifth commandment. Verdict: a tender act of filial duty, and a picture of the new family of faith (Mark 3:35); it gives no basis for devotion to Mary as mediator.

parallels.desc: a sword will pierce your own soul

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the disciple, "Behold, your mother!" And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), "I thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus completes his care for his mother, and then, knowing all is finished, fulfils the Scripture of his thirst.

To his own home. John cared for Mary. Tradition says later at Ephesus.

Knowing that all was finished. Even in death he is in full awareness and control.

I thirst. Psalm 69:21; 22:15. The one who offered living water (4:14; 7:37) thirsts. A sign of his real humanity and real suffering.

parallels.desc: my tongue sticks to my jaws

verseByVerse.quote: A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, "It is finished," and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ last word in John is a cry of triumph: the work the Father gave him to do is fully accomplished.

Sour wine. Cheap vinegar wine, the drink of soldiers and labourers.

Hyssop. A small, bushy plant, too flimsy, some say, to lift a sponge; a stalk or bundle could. Hyssop was used to daub the Passover lamb’s blood on the doorposts (Exodus 12:22). Textual note. One late manuscript reads hyssō, javelin, and some scholars have adopted this conjecture. Verdict: “hyssop” is in virtually all manuscripts, and its Passover echo is surely deliberate.

It is finished. Tetelestai: completed, accomplished, paid in full. The word appeared on receipts in the papyri. The work of redemption is done (17:4; Hebrews 10:12–14).

Where Christians differ: a finished sacrifice? Roman Catholic teaching holds that the Mass re-presents Christ’s sacrifice, offered for the living and the dead. The Reformers insisted that Christ’s sacrifice was once for all, complete and unrepeatable (Hebrews 7:27; 9:25–28); the Supper remembers and receives its benefits (Westminster Confession 29.2). Verdict: “It is finished” means nothing remains to be added, by priest, Mass or merit.

Gave up his spirit. Literally “handed over”. He did not have his life taken; he gave it (10:18).

For worship. Rest your whole weight on his finished work.
verseByVerse.note: Hyssop was the plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb. “It is finished” is a cry of completion, not defeat.

parallels.desc: a bunch of hyssop

verseByVerse.quote: Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away. So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders, careful about the holiness of the Sabbath, ask for death to be hastened, and God uses even this to fulfil his word.

The day of Preparation. Friday.

A high day. The Sabbath of Passover week was especially holy.

Not remain on the cross. Deuteronomy 21:22–23: a hanged body must be buried the same day.

Broken legs. Crurifragium: breaking the legs with a mallet so that the victim could not push himself up to breathe, and died quickly. The skeleton of a crucified man found at Giv’at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem (1968), with a nail through the heel, confirms details of the practice.
verseByVerse.note: The law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight; the coming Sabbath made it more urgent. Breaking the legs stopped a crucified man pushing up to breathe and hastened death.

parallels.desc: his body shall not remain all night on the tree

verseByVerse.quote: But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is truly dead, and from his pierced side flow blood and water, signs of the cleansing and life his death brings.

Already dead. No need to break his legs. Against later theories that he only fainted on the cross (the “swoon theory”), the soldiers, experts in death, confirm it, and the spear makes certain.

Blood and water. Physicians have suggested fluid from around the heart or lungs after trauma. John sees more: the blood of atonement and the water of the Spirit and cleansing (7:38–39; 1 John 5:6–8; Zechariah 13:1). Where Christians differ. Many church fathers saw the two sacraments, baptism and the Supper, flowing from Christ’s side. Verdict: the primary point is the reality of his death and the life that flows from it; a sacramental application is possible but secondary.

For worship. “Rock of Ages, cleft for me, let me hide myself in thee; let the water and the blood, from thy riven side which flowed, be of sin the double cure” (Augustus Toplady).

parallels.desc: the water and the blood
a fountain opened for sin

verseByVerse.quote: He who saw it has borne witness — his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth — that you also may believe. For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "Not one of his bones will be broken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eyewitness solemnly testifies so that we may believe, and shows that Jesus died as the true Passover Lamb.

He who saw it. The beloved disciple, the author (21:24). Testimony from someone at the foot of the cross.

That you also may believe. The purpose of the Gospel (20:31).

Not a bone broken. Exodus 12:46 and Numbers 9:12, of the Passover lamb; Psalm 34:20, of the righteous man.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover lamb’s bones were not to be broken.

parallels.desc: he keeps all his bones

verseByVerse.quote: And again another Scripture says, "They will look on him whom they have pierced." After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pierced one will be looked upon, in mourning and in faith, and two secret disciples come out into the open to bury him.

Zechariah 12:10. God says that his people will look on “me, on him whom they have pierced”, and mourn, and a fountain will be opened for cleansing (13:1). Revelation 1:7 applies it to Christ’s return.

Joseph of Arimathea. A rich member of the council who had not agreed to the verdict (Luke 23:50–51; Matthew 27:57). Fear had kept him secret (12:42); now, at the worst moment, he takes a public stand.

Asked Pilate. Bodies of crucified criminals were often left for scavengers or thrown into a common grave. Joseph’s request was risky.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: they look on me, on him whom they have pierced

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight. So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus, who first came by night, brings a royal quantity of spices: the King is buried like a king.

Nicodemus. His journey from darkness to light is complete (3:1–2; 7:50–51).

About seventy-five pounds. One hundred Roman pounds, about 33 kg: an enormous amount, fit for royalty (2 Chronicles 16:14).

Myrrh and aloes. Aromatic resin and powdered wood, sprinkled among the linen strips to counter decay; not embalming.

As is the burial custom. Jews did not embalm or cremate.

On a Tuesday. Courage sometimes comes late. If you have been a secret disciple, step out now.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the weight is literally a hundred Roman pounds — a quantity fit for a royal burial. Myrrh and aloes were aromatic spices laid with the linen wrappings.

parallels.desc: King Asa laid on a bier filled with spices
myrrh at his birth

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is laid in a new tomb in a garden, where the new creation will begin on the first day of the week.

A garden. Where Adam fell, the last Adam is buried and will rise (1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45).

A new tomb. No one else had been laid there, so there could be no confusion about whose body was missing. Isaiah 53:9: with a rich man in his death.

Close at hand. Time was short before the Sabbath began at sunset.

For worship. He went down into death for us. Wait with the women for the morning.

parallels.desc: with a rich man in his death

19.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him.<sup>2</sup>And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.<sup>3</sup>They came up to him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and struck him with their hands.<sup>4</sup>Pilate went out again and said to them, “See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him.”<sup>5</sup>So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, “Behold the man!”<sup>6</sup>When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him.”<sup>7</sup>The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God.”<sup>8</sup>When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.<sup>9</sup>He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.<sup>10</sup>So Pilate said to him, “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?”<sup>11</sup>Jesus answered him, “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin.”<sup>12</sup>From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.”<sup>13</sup>So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha.<sup>14</sup>Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, “Behold your King!”<sup>15</sup>They cried out, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your King?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar.”<sup>16</sup>So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,<sup>17</sup>and he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha.<sup>18</sup>There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.<sup>19</sup>Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”<sup>20</sup>Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.<sup>21</sup>So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ’The King of the Jews,’ but rather, ’This man said, I am King of the Jews.’”<sup>22</sup>Pilate answered, “What I have written I have written.”<sup>23</sup>When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom,<sup>24</sup>so they said to one another, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be.” This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, “They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.” So the soldiers did these things,<sup>25</sup>but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.<sup>26</sup>When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”<sup>27</sup>Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home.<sup>28</sup>After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said
