had received the sour wine, he said, “It is finished,” and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.<sup>31</sup>Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away.<sup>32</sup>So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.<sup>33</sup>But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.<sup>34</sup>But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.<sup>35</sup>He who saw it has borne witness— his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth— that you also may believe.<sup>36</sup>For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “Not one of his bones will be broken.”<sup>37</sup>And again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they have pierced.”<sup>38</sup>After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.<sup>39</sup>Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight.<sup>40</sup>So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.<sup>41</sup>Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.<sup>42</sup>So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.
19.overview:
John tells the crucifixion as the hour of Jesus’ glory and the fulfilment of Scripture. Pilate has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him with a crown of thorns and a purple robe. Pilate presents him to the crowd, “Behold the man!”, three times declares him innocent, and tries to release him; but when the leaders accuse Jesus of claiming to be Son of God, and threaten Pilate that releasing a rival king is disloyalty to Caesar, the governor gives way. At noon on the day of Preparation for the Passover, when the lambs were being slaughtered, Pilate hands him over, and the chief priests declare, “We have no king but Caesar.” Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others under a sign in Aramaic, Latin and Greek: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”

From the cross Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple. Knowing that all was now finished, he says, “I thirst,” and receiving sour wine, says, “It is finished,” bows his head and gives up his spirit. To hasten death before the Sabbath, the soldiers break the legs of the others, but finding Jesus already dead they pierce his side, and blood and water flow out. John, the eyewitness, insists that his testimony is true, and that these things fulfilled Scripture: not a bone of the Passover lamb was broken, and they will look on the one they pierced. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, secret disciples until now, bury him with a king’s quantity of spices in a new tomb in a garden. The work God gave him to do is complete.

20.title: The Resurrection

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Empty Tomb and Mary's Encounter with the Risen Lord
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before dawn on Sunday Mary Magdalene finds the stone moved and runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, fearing the body has been stolen. Racing to the tomb, they find the grave-clothes lying in place and the head cloth folded apart; the beloved disciple sees and believes, though they do not yet understand the Scriptures. Mary stays weeping, sees two angels, and then Jesus, whom she mistakes for the gardener until he speaks her name. He tells her not to cling to him but to tell his brothers that he is ascending to his Father and theirs, his God and theirs. She brings the disciples the news: she has seen the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology: The resurrection appearances in John are structured around recognition: the beloved disciple sees and believes from the evidence of the linen cloths; Mary recognizes Jesus when he calls her name (the Good Shepherd and the sheep who knows his voice, 10:3); Thomas recognizes Jesus when invited to touch the wounds. Each recognition is different, calibrated to each person's need and capacity. This is the risen Lord — the same person, now transformed, who meets each disciple where they are.
verseByVerse.examples: Mary Magdalene is the first witness to the resurrection, commissioned by the risen Lord to tell the disciples: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. The announcement is simultaneously personal (my Father) and covenantal (your Father) — the resurrection makes the disciples' relationship to the Father the same as Jesus' own. The first gospel proclamation after the resurrection is spoken by a woman who was weeping at a tomb and heard her name called by the one she thought was dead. This is how the gospel always comes: to those who have not ceased to love the crucified Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb. So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The resurrection begins in darkness and with grief: Mary comes expecting a corpse and finds an open tomb, but can only imagine theft.

The first day of the week. Sunday, the day of new creation, and from then on the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10).

Mary Magdalene. From Magdala on the Sea of Galilee, freed from seven demons (Luke 8:2). Not the sinful woman of Luke 7, despite later tradition. John focuses on her, though other women were with her (“we do not know”, v. 2).

The stone removed. Not to let Jesus out, but to let witnesses in.

They have taken. Her first thought is grave robbery, a known crime. No one expected resurrection.

Women as witnesses. In that culture women’s testimony counted for little in court. Inventors of a story would not have chosen them as first witnesses: a strong mark of historical authenticity.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb. Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two leading disciples run to investigate, and John records the race as only an eyewitness would.

Running. Urgency and love.

The other disciple outran Peter. Perhaps younger. A small, honest, slightly humorous detail.

parallels.desc: Peter runs to the tomb

verseByVerse.quote: And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grave-clothes are still there: whoever removed the body did not take the wrappings, which robbers would have done.

Stooping. Rock tombs had low entrances.

Did not go in. Out of reverence, or hesitation.

Peter went in. Characteristically impulsive.

verseByVerse.quote: and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus' head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself. Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The orderly grave-clothes are evidence that something extraordinary has happened, and the beloved disciple becomes the first to believe.

The face cloth. Folded or rolled up in a place by itself. Not the scene of a hurried theft. Contrast Lazarus, who came out still bound (11:44).

He saw and believed. He believed that Jesus had risen, without yet seeing him: the first of those blessed who believe without seeing (v. 29).

Where Christians differ: the Shroud of Turin. Some regard the Shroud as Jesus’ burial cloth; radiocarbon tests in 1988 dated it to the Middle Ages, though the results are disputed. Verdict: faith does not rest on relics but on the apostolic testimony (v. 31).
verseByVerse.note: Grave robbers would not have unwrapped the body and left the cloths neatly behind.

verseByVerse.quote: for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. Then the disciples went back to their homes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before they understood the Scriptures, the disciples were convinced by the empty tomb; afterwards they saw that it had been foretold all along.

The Scripture. Perhaps Psalm 16:10 (Acts 2:25–31), Isaiah 53:10–12, Hosea 6:2. The resurrection fulfils God’s word (1 Corinthians 15:4).

Must. Divine necessity.

Went home. Faith had begun, but they did not yet know what to do.

parallels.desc: you will not let your holy one see corruption

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb. And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grief keeps Mary at the tomb, and the one who stays weeping is the first to see the risen Lord.

Two angels. One at the head and one at the feet, like the cherubim at either end of the mercy seat (Exodus 25:18–22). The place where the body lay is the new place of atonement.

In white. Heavenly messengers (Mark 16:5; Acts 1:10).

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping?" She said to them, "They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him." Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary is so absorbed in grief that even angels do not move her, and she turns away from them to look for her Lord.

Woman, why are you weeping? A gentle question: there is no need to weep.

My Lord. Personal love, even for a body.

She did not know it was Jesus. Perhaps through tears and the dim light; perhaps because the risen body was changed (Luke 24:16; 21:4). He is recognised when he chooses to reveal himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?" Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, "Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away." Jesus said to her, "Mary." She turned and said to him in Aramaic, "Rabboni!" (which means Teacher).
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Good Shepherd calls his sheep by name, and she knows his voice at once.

Whom are you seeking? His first question in the Gospel (1:38).

The gardener. Unwittingly right: the second Adam in the garden of the new creation.

Mary. One word. 10:3: he calls his own sheep by name. Recognition comes not through argument but through his personal word.

Rabboni. “My teacher”, an intensified form of Rabbi.

For worship. The risen Lord knows your name.
verseByVerse.note: “Rabboni” is Aramaic for “my teacher,” a warm and respectful address.

parallels.desc: he calls his own sheep by name

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.'" Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord" — and that he had said these things to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary must not cling to the old relationship but go and announce the new one: through the risen Jesus, his Father is now his brothers’ Father.

Do not cling. Not “do not touch” (KJV), since Thomas is invited to touch (v. 27), but “stop holding on to me”. The old physical companionship is ending; a new, permanent presence through the Spirit is coming (16:7).

Not yet ascended. His going to the Father is in progress.

My brothers. The first time Jesus calls the disciples brothers (Hebrews 2:11–12). After the cross they are family.

My Father and your Father. Not “our Father”: he is Son by nature, they by grace. But the same Father.

I have seen the Lord. A woman is the first preacher of the resurrection, “apostle to the apostles”, as some fathers called her. Where Christians differ. Egalitarians cite this for women’s ordination. Verdict: the app’s complementarian view, held gladly: Mary’s witness is honoured and essential, and every believer, man or woman, is sent to tell that Christ is risen; the teaching office of elder is a separate question (1 Timothy 2:12).
verseByVerse.note: “Do not cling to me” means the old relationship cannot simply resume; he is going to the Father.

parallels.desc: not ashamed to call them brothers

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — Appearances to the Disciples and to Thomas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: That Sunday evening, with the doors locked for fear of the authorities, Jesus comes and stands among the disciples, greets them with peace, and shows them his hands and side, and they rejoice. He sends them as the Father sent him, breathes on them and tells them to receive the Holy Spirit; whoever’s sins they forgive are forgiven, and whoever’s they retain are retained. Thomas, absent, refuses to believe unless he touches the wounds. Eight days later Jesus comes again through locked doors and invites Thomas to touch and believe. Thomas responds, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus calls blessed those who believe without seeing. Jesus did many other signs, John says, but these are written so that readers may believe he is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name.
verseByVerse.theology: Peace be with you (vv. 19, 21, 26): three times in this section Jesus speaks this word. The resurrection peace is not the absence of the disciples' fear but the presence of the risen Lord. He shows them his hands and his side — the wounds are still present, the marks of the passion carried into the resurrection body. The resurrection does not erase the cross; it vindicates it, glorifies it, makes it permanently the ground of peace. The scars of Jesus in his resurrection body are the permanent declaration that the atonement is real and its benefits are everlasting.
verseByVerse.examples: Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (v. 29): the beatitude of all post-apostolic faith. Every Christian since the first generation believes on the basis of testimony rather than sight — on the word of those who were there, preserved in the Scripture the Spirit inspired, applied by the Spirit who illuminates. Thomas's faith required the visible wounds; blessed are those who trust the testimony about the wounds. This is where the fourth gospel places us: in the company of the blessed who believe without seeing.

verseByVerse.quote: On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, "Peace be with you." When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Jesus comes to frightened disciples behind locked doors, brings them peace, and shows them the wounds that prove it is really he.

Doors locked. Fear of the authorities. The risen body is not limited by walls, yet is physical and wounded (Luke 24:39–43).

Peace be with you. The usual greeting, now filled with meaning: peace with God won at the cross (14:27; Romans 5:1). He does not rebuke them for deserting him.

Hands and side. The risen Christ bears his scars for ever (Revelation 5:6). His glory includes his wounds.

Glad. 16:20–22 fulfilled.

Where Christians differ: the resurrection body. Some say Jesus rose only spiritually, or in the disciples’ faith. The Gospels insist on a bodily resurrection: an empty tomb, wounds, eating (21:13). Verdict: a real, physical, transformed body, the firstfruits of ours (1 Corinthians 15:20, 42–44).
verseByVerse.note: “Peace be with you” was the ordinary Hebrew greeting, shalom — now full of meaning.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them again, "Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you." And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, "Receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Christ commissions his church and gives it the Spirit for its mission.

As the Father sent me. 17:18. The church continues Christ’s mission, in his way: in humility, love and truth.

Breathed on them. As God breathed life into Adam (Genesis 2:7) and the breath brought the dry bones to life (Ezekiel 37:9–10). The new creation begins.

Receive the Holy Spirit. Where Christians differ: John’s Pentecost? Some see this as John’s version of Pentecost; others as a symbolic promise fulfilled at Pentecost; others as a real but preliminary giving, with the full outpouring for mission at Pentecost (Acts 2). Verdict: a real gift of the Spirit’s life to the disciples, anticipating the public outpouring at Pentecost; the two are complementary.
verseByVerse.note: Breathing on them recalls God breathing life into Adam.

parallels.desc: the breath of life
come, O breath

verseByVerse.quote: "If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld." Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church, sent with the gospel, declares forgiveness to those who believe and warns of sins retained to those who refuse.

Forgive and withhold. The Greek perfect tenses suggest “they have already been forgiven”: the disciples declare what God has done (Matthew 16:19; 18:18).

Where Christians differ: priestly absolution. Roman Catholic teaching sees here the institution of the sacrament of penance, in which a priest absolves sins in confession. Protestants hold that the authority is given to the church as a whole, exercised through the preaching of the gospel and church discipline: those who believe the gospel are assured of forgiveness; those who reject it are warned. Verdict: the “keys” are the gospel itself (Westminster Confession 30.2); ministers declare forgiveness on Christ’s authority, but only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7).

Thomas, not with them. Missing the gathering, he missed the Lord. Do not neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25).

verseByVerse.quote: So the other disciples told him, "We have seen the Lord." But he said to them, "Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe." Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, "Peace be with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thomas demands hard evidence, and the risen Lord will graciously give it.

We have seen the Lord. The same testimony as Mary’s (v. 18).

Unless. Thomas is not merely sceptical but grieving, and refuses to be hurt again. He wants to touch the same wounds he saw.

Eight days later. The following Sunday: the disciples meet again on the first day of the week.

On a Tuesday. Doubt is not the opposite of faith; unbelief is. Bring your doubts honestly to Christ, among his people.
verseByVerse.note: Nails were driven through the hands (or wrists) and feet.

parallels.desc: they have pierced my hands and feet

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Thomas, "Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe." Thomas answered him, "My Lord and my God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Lord knows what Thomas said, meets him exactly at his point of doubt, and draws from him the Gospel’s greatest confession.

Put your finger here. Jesus repeats Thomas’s own words. He heard them, though absent.

Do not disbelieve, but believe. Literally “do not become faithless but faithful”.

My Lord and my God! The climax of John’s Christology, matching 1:1: the Word was God. A monotheistic Jew addresses Jesus as God, and Jesus accepts it. Emperor Domitian later demanded the title “our Lord and God”; Christians gave it to Jesus alone.

Did he touch? John does not say so; seeing and hearing Jesus was enough.

For worship. Say it with Thomas today: my Lord and my God.

parallels.desc: my God and my Lord

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus blesses every future believer who trusts the apostolic testimony without seeing, and John tells us that his book is a selection.

Blessed are those who have not seen. A beatitude for us (1 Peter 1:8). We are not second-class believers.

Many other signs. John has selected (21:25).

In the presence of the disciples. Eyewitness testimony.

parallels.desc: though you do not now see him, you believe in him

verseByVerse.quote: but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole Gospel exists for one purpose: that readers may believe in Jesus as the Christ and Son of God, and so have life.

These are written. The signs, words and witnesses of the book.

That you may believe. Textual note. Manuscripts vary between a present tense (“go on believing”) and an aorist (“come to believe”). Where Christians differ. Some therefore see John written mainly for believers, to strengthen faith; others mainly for unbelievers, to bring them to faith. Verdict: the evidence is evenly balanced; John serves both purposes, and its Christ is for all.

The Christ, the Son of God. Messiah of Israel and eternal Son (1:41, 49; 11:27).

Life in his name. Eternal life (3:16; 17:3).

On a Tuesday. Give someone a copy of John’s Gospel, and pray that what it was written for would happen.

For worship. Thank God for this Gospel, and for the life it brings.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “may continue to believe.”

20.text: <sup>1</sup>Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.<sup>2</sup>So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.”<sup>3</sup>So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb.<sup>4</sup>Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.<sup>5</sup>And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.<sup>6</sup>Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,<sup>7</sup>and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus’ head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself.<sup>8</sup>Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;<sup>9</sup>for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.<sup>10</sup>Then the disciples went back to their homes.<sup>11</sup>But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb.<sup>12</sup>And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.<sup>13</sup>They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.”<sup>14</sup>Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.<sup>15</sup>Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”<sup>16</sup>Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!” (which means Teacher).<sup>17</sup>Jesus said to her, “Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, ’I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’”<sup>18</sup>Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”—and that he had said these things to her.<sup>19</sup>On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”<sup>20</sup>When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.<sup>21</sup>Jesus said to them again, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you.”<sup>22</sup>And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.<sup>23</sup>If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld.”<sup>24</sup>Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.<sup>25</sup>So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe.”<sup>26</sup>Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”<sup>27</sup>Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe.”<sup>28</sup>Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”<sup>29</sup>Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”<sup>30</sup>Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;<sup>31</sup>but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
20.overview:
On the first day of the week, while it is still dark, Mary Magdalene finds the stone rolled away and runs to tell Peter and the beloved disciple that the body has been taken. The two run to the tomb; the beloved disciple arrives first, looks in, and sees the linen cloths lying there; Peter goes in and sees the head cloth folded by itself. The beloved disciple goes in, sees, and believes. Mary stays weeping outside, sees two angels, then turns and sees Jesus, whom she takes for the gardener, until he calls her by name. He sends her to tell his brothers that he is ascending to his Father and their Father, to his God and their God. A woman becomes the first witness of the resurrection.

That evening Jesus stands among the disciples behind locked doors, shows them his hands and side, and gives them peace. As the Father sent him, so he sends them; he breathes on them and says, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” and gives them authority to declare sins forgiven or retained. Thomas is absent and refuses to believe without touching the wounds. A week later Jesus appears again and invites him to do so; Thomas answers with the highest confession in the Gospels, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus pronounces a blessing on all who will believe without seeing. John then states the purpose of his book: these signs are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name.

21.title: The Restoration of Peter and the Beloved Disciple

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Breakfast on the Shore: Restoration and Commission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By the Sea of Tiberias, Peter and six other disciples spend a fruitless night fishing. At dawn a stranger on the shore tells them to cast the net on the right side, and the catch is too great to haul in. The beloved disciple realises it is the Lord; Peter plunges into the water to reach him. On the shore Jesus has a fire of coals with fish and bread; the net, holding 153 large fish, is unbroken, and Jesus serves them breakfast. Afterwards he asks Peter three times whether he loves him, and each time, as Peter affirms his love, commissions him to feed and care for his flock. He foretells that in old age Peter will be bound and led where he would not choose, the death by which he would glorify God, and calls him to follow. When Peter asks about the beloved disciple, Jesus says that even if he wills him to remain until he returns, that is not Peter’s concern: Peter must follow. John corrects the rumour this started, identifies the beloved disciple as the author whose testimony is true, and closes by saying that the world could not hold the books needed to record all that Jesus did.
verseByVerse.theology: The threefold restoration of Peter — Do you love me? / Feed my sheep — is the most pastoral moment in the gospel. Three questions match three denials; three commissions match three failures. The charcoal fire (the same as 18:18) brings the smell of the denial back to Peter's senses; the same kind of fire is now the fire of restoration. Jesus does not ignore the failure or pretend it did not happen; he names it by re-enacting the scene in reverse. The gospel's answer to failure is not silence but renewed commission — the broken shepherd is restored to shepherd the flock.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple as the witness who wrote these things (v. 24): the gospel stakes its authority on eyewitness testimony. This is not mythology or legend but the account of one who was there — who saw the water turned to wine, stood at the cross, ran to the empty tomb, and watched Jesus break bread on the shore. The testimony is true because the witness is trustworthy; the witness is trustworthy because the one he testifies to is the resurrection and the life. The gospel ends not with a doctrine but with a person: if everything were written, the world itself could not contain the books. The Word is larger than any book.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way. Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Lord shows himself again, this time in ordinary Galilee, among men who have gone back to their old work.

An epilogue. Chapter 20 ended like a conclusion. Where Christians differ. Some scholars think chapter 21 was added later by the author’s circle. No manuscript of John lacks it, and its style matches the Gospel. Verdict: an integral epilogue, probably by the same author, perhaps added before the Gospel was circulated; it is fully Scripture.

The Sea of Tiberias. The Sea of Galilee (6:1), where Jesus had called them to fish for people (Luke 5:1–11).

Seven disciples. Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, James and John (the sons of Zebedee, named only here in John), and two unnamed, one of them the beloved disciple.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee. Nathanael came from Cana; the sons of Zebedee are James and John.

parallels.desc: he is going before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to them, "I am going fishing." They said to him, "We will go with you." They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing. Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without Jesus’ word, even experienced fishermen catch nothing.

I am going fishing. Not necessarily backsliding; they had to eat, and Jesus had told them to go to Galilee (Mark 16:7). But it echoes the time before their call.

That night nothing. Night was the best time for fishing. Apart from me you can do nothing (15:5).

They did not know. As with Mary (20:14). Recognition is his gift.
verseByVerse.note: Fishing on the lake was done at night.

parallels.desc: we toiled all night and took nothing

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Children, do you have any fish?" They answered him, "No." He said to them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obedience to Jesus’ word turns futile labour into overflowing fruitfulness.

Children. A familiar, affectionate address, perhaps like “lads”.

The right side. No magic in the side; the point is his word.

Not able to haul it. Abundance, as at Cana (2:6) and the feeding (6:13).

On a Tuesday. In your work and ministry, listen for Christ’s word before you labour harder.
verseByVerse.note: “Children” was a friendly way of addressing men.

parallels.desc: the first great catch

verseByVerse.quote: That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, "It is the Lord!" When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love recognises the Lord first, and impetuous love cannot wait to reach him.

It is the Lord! The beloved disciple sees first, as at the tomb (20:8). Perhaps the miracle reminded him of Luke 5.

Put on his outer garment. He had been working stripped for work; out of respect he dresses before going to meet the Lord, then jumps in.

About a hundred yards. Literally two hundred cubits.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is literally two hundred cubits.

verseByVerse.quote: When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread. Jesus said to them, "Bring some of the fish that you have just caught."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord who could make breakfast from nothing invites his disciples to contribute what he enabled them to catch.

A charcoal fire. Anthrakia, the same word as in 18:18, the fire where Peter denied him. Jesus sets the scene for Peter’s restoration.

Fish and bread. The food of the feeding of the five thousand (6:9–11).

Bring some. Jesus does not need their fish, but includes them in his provision.
verseByVerse.note: John mentions a charcoal fire only here and at Peter’s denial.

verseByVerse.quote: So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn. Jesus said to them, "Come and have breakfast." Now none of the disciples dared ask him, "Who are you?" They knew it was the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great catch is a picture of the mission to which Jesus sends them: a full net that does not break.

153. Only an eyewitness would count. Many have looked for symbolism: Jerome reported that Greek zoologists counted 153 species of fish (representing all nations); 153 is the triangular number of 17; others use number-codes. Verdict: probably simply the remembered count of a memorable catch; if it has a symbol, it is the fullness of the gospel harvest from every nation.

Not torn. Contrast Luke 5:6. Perhaps a hint that the church will hold all the nations without breaking (10:16; 17:21).

Come and have breakfast. The risen Lord serves a meal.

None dared ask. They knew, but were awed.
verseByVerse.note: Many symbolic meanings have been proposed for 153; the plainest point is that someone counted — a detail from an eyewitness.

parallels.desc: their nets were breaking

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish. This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Jesus is host and servant, feeding his friends with his own hands.

Took the bread and gave it. The words of the feeding and the Supper (6:11). A real meal: the risen Lord is no ghost.

The third time. To the disciples as a group (20:19, 26).

For worship. He still feeds his people, at his table and by his word.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, "Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Feed my lambs." He said to him a second time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Tend my sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not ignore Peter’s denial but heals it, giving him the chance to affirm his love and entrusting him with the care of the flock.

Simon, son of John. His old name, as when Jesus first met him (1:42). Not “Peter, the rock”, yet.

More than these. More than the other disciples love me? Peter had boasted that he would never fall away even if all others did (Mark 14:29). Or more than these things, the boats and nets? Verdict: probably the first: a gentle probe of his earlier boast. Peter now makes no comparison.

Two words for love. Jesus uses agapaō twice, Peter replies with phileō, and the third time Jesus uses phileō. Where Christians differ. Some preachers make much of the difference, as if Peter could only claim a lesser love. Most scholars note that John uses the two verbs interchangeably (3:35 and 5:20; 11:3, 5), and varies vocabulary throughout this passage (feed/tend, lambs/sheep, know/know). Verdict: the point is not the vocabulary but the threefold question, matching the threefold denial.

Feed my lambs. Love for Christ is shown in caring for his people. They are his lambs, not Peter’s (1 Peter 5:1–4).
verseByVerse.note: “More than these” probably means more than the other disciples love me — Peter had claimed he would never fall away.

parallels.desc: shepherd the flock of God

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him the third time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, "Do you love me?" and he said to him, "Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you." Jesus said to him, "Feed my sheep. Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grieved but honest, Peter casts himself on Jesus’ knowledge of his heart, and Jesus recommissions him and tells him the cost.

The third time. Each question undoes one denial. The pain is part of the healing.

You know everything. Peter no longer trusts his own claims. He appeals to Jesus’ knowledge (2:25; 16:30).

Feed my sheep. Restored to ministry. Failure is not final for a repentant disciple.

Where Christians differ: Peter’s primacy. Roman Catholic teaching sees here, with Matthew 16:18, Christ appointing Peter as chief shepherd of the whole church, with authority passed to the bishops of Rome. Protestants see Peter’s personal restoration and commissioning as an apostle and elder (1 Peter 5:1), without a line of successors with universal jurisdiction. Verdict: Peter’s leadership among the apostles was real, but Christ alone is the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4); the passage restores a fallen disciple, not an institution.

When you are old. Stretching out hands may refer to crucifixion. Early tradition (1 Clement; Tertullian; later reports) says Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero, about AD 64–67, according to some upside down.
verseByVerse.note: Three questions mirror Peter’s three denials. “Stretch out your hands” was an expression used of crucifixion; early Christian tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God. And after saying this he said to him, "Follow me." Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, "Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who once said “I will lay down my life for you” will now actually do so, by grace, and his whole calling is summed up in two words: follow me.

Glorify God. A martyr’s death brings glory to God, as Christ’s did (12:23; 13:31).

Follow me. The first call (Mark 1:17), renewed. Now Peter knows where it leads.

The beloved disciple following. John reminds us who he is: the one who leaned on Jesus at supper.

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, "Lord, what about this man?" Jesus said to him, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each disciple has his own path; our task is not to compare ourselves with others but to follow Christ.

What about him? Natural curiosity, perhaps rivalry.

What is that to you? A firm, loving rebuke. God’s plans for others are his business.

You follow me. Emphatic “you”.

On a Tuesday. Stop comparing your gifts, trials or path with another Christian’s. Ask only: am I following Jesus?

verseByVerse.quote: So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?" This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John corrects a misunderstanding of Jesus’ words and solemnly affirms his own testimony as true.

A rumour. Some thought the beloved disciple would live until Christ returned. Perhaps he had now died, or was very old, and the church needed reassurance that Jesus had not been wrong.

Read carefully. Jesus said “if”. A lesson in reading Scripture accurately, not adding to it.

This is the disciple. The beloved disciple is the author: he has “written these things”.

We know. Perhaps the elders of the church endorsing his testimony, or John himself speaking in the plural (1 John 1:1–4; 3 John 12).

True. The Gospel rests on eyewitness testimony (19:35).
verseByVerse.note: The rumour may have spread because the beloved disciple lived to a great age. Verse 24 identifies him as the author of the Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gospel ends by admitting that no book can contain Jesus: all we have is enough to believe, and there is always more of him to know.

Many other things. 20:30. The four Gospels are selections.

The world itself could not contain. A deliberate overstatement, as ancient writers used to praise an inexhaustible subject. The Word through whom the world was made (1:3) cannot be contained by its libraries.

For worship. John began with the Word in the beginning and ends with words that run out. Worship the one who is more than all that can be written.

21.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way.<sup>2</sup>Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.<sup>3</sup>Simon Peter said to them, “I am going fishing.” They said to him, “We will go with you.” They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing.<sup>4</sup>Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.<sup>5</sup>Jesus said to them, “Children, do you have any fish?” They answered him, “No.”<sup>6</sup>He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.<sup>7</sup>That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea.<sup>8</sup>The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.<sup>9</sup>When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread.<sup>10</sup>Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.”<sup>11</sup>So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn.<sup>12</sup>Jesus said to them, “Come and have breakfast.” Now none of the disciples dared ask him, “Who are you?” They knew it was the Lord.<sup>13</sup>Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish.<sup>14</sup>This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.<sup>15</sup>When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”<sup>16</sup>He said to him a second time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”<sup>17</sup>He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.<sup>18</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go.”<sup>19</sup>(This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God.) And after saying this he said to him, “Follow me.”<sup>20</sup>Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, “Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?”<sup>21</sup>When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?”<sup>22</sup>Jesus said to him, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!”<sup>23</sup>So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?”<sup>24</sup>This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.<sup>25</sup>Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
21.overview:
After the conclusion of chapter 20, John adds an epilogue set by the Sea of Galilee. Seven disciples go fishing with Peter and catch nothing all night. At dawn a figure on the shore tells them to cast the net on the right side, and they cannot haul it in for the number of fish. The beloved disciple recognises him: “It is the Lord!” Peter throws himself into the water. On the beach Jesus has a charcoal fire burning with fish and bread, and invites them to breakfast; the net holds 153 large fish and is not torn.

Beside that charcoal fire, the same kind as the one where Peter denied him, Jesus asks Peter three times, “Do you love me?”, and three times commissions him: “Feed my lambs… Tend my sheep… Feed my sheep.” Peter, grieved at the third question, answers, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus foretells that Peter will one day be bound and led where he does not want to go, signifying the death by which he would glorify God, and says, “Follow me.” When Peter asks about the beloved disciple, Jesus replies that this is not his concern: “You follow me!” John corrects a rumour that the beloved disciple would not die, identifies him as the author of the Gospel, and closes by saying that if everything Jesus did were written, the world could not hold the books. The Gospel ends not with failure but with a forgiven disciple, a renewed calling and the command to follow.
